entries.title_transcribed: Commentariolus (De hypothesibus motuum coelestium ... commentariolus) — manuscript
entries.subject: Astronomy
entries.editorial_note: A manuscript of the Commentariolus in the Österreichische Nationalbibliothek, Vienna, attributed to Tycho’s library by Norlind. Tycho owned the text: Hagecius gave him a copy at Regensburg in 1575, and he printed it in the Progymnasmata (Opera omnia II, 428). Whether the Vienna manuscript is that copy rests on Norlind’s attribution and on the Uraniborg-circle contents of the same Sammelhandschrift; the volume carries no mark of his, and its catalogue record names no former owner, so both the entry and the identification of the copy are graded C. Walde (1938) showed the Vienna manuscript to have been Longomontanus’s gift to the amanuensis Johannes Eriksen at Benátky on 18 July 1600 and left open whether it passed from Eriksen to Tycho; Eriksen’s books otherwise went into Queen Christina’s library with the Prague booty. The witness therefore belongs to the Uraniborg circle rather than, on present evidence, to Tycho’s own shelves. Jardine and Segonds note the copy that came from Hagecius (2008, p. 187 n. 4). The National Library's account of 2026 adds two points to the Regensburg gift: that the original Hájek exemplar is untraced (the same object as Norlind's ‘Tycho's exemplar not located’ if the Regensburg transfer was a gift), and the conjecture that it was Tycho who had Copernicus's name — absent from the anonymous letter as it circulated — set at the head of the transcripts he distributed (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 22 (scan 22); ‘zřejmě’, her conjecture, not a documented fact). The three surviving transcripts she names (Vienna, Stockholm, Aberdeen; p. 20) are those the history essay already records. Status disputed since 20 October 2026: the witness belongs to the Uraniborg circle rather than, on present evidence, to Tycho's shelves (Walde 1938 against the transfer), and a located C with the ownership in doubt is the Definitions' disputed, not located. Westman (2011, p. 248) describes the Regensburg manuscript as one ‘that evidently had been in Hagecius's family for many years’, citing TBOO II 428, which records the gift and nothing of the manuscript's earlier history.
open_questions: Whether the Österreichische Nationalbibliothek’s Commentariolus manuscript, Longomontanus’s gift to Johannes Eriksen in July 1600 (Walde 1938), ever passed from Eriksen to Tycho or reached Vienna by another route; a mark of Tycho’s in the volume or a record of its arrival in Vienna would decide.

Whether a second Commentariolus in the Tycho orbit — the quarto of 14 folios in Paul Wittich's own hand, received from his uncle Balthasar Sartorius of Breslau, which Dudith described to Praetorius on 12 February 1589 (Gingerich and Westman 1988, p. 10 n. 21) — came to Prague with the Wittich books in 1600 under Tycho's ‘other manuscripts, if there are any’ (1 November 1589), and how it relates to the Vienna manuscript and to Liddel's Aberdeen copy.

norlind.entry: Copernicus, Nicolaus: De hypothesibus motuum cœlestium commentariolus. [Manuskript.]
norlind.ownership_verdict: owned: received from Hagecius at Regensburg 1575 and had transcripts made (Tycho's own statement in Prog.); Tycho's exemplar not located — the transcript Longomontanus gave Eriksen in 1600 (probably one of Tycho's copies) is now in Wien; another, ex-Hevelius, in KVA
norlind.discussion: Copernicus' preliminära, endast i manuskript publicerade, förhandsmeddelande om de forskningsresultat han sedermera framlade för offentligheten i »De revolutionibus orbium cœlestium». – I »Prog.» (II, 428) skriver Tycho, att han erhöll ett exemplar av Hagecius vid deras möte i Regensburg 1575 och att han därpå lät göra avskrifter av detsamma, vilka han skickade till andra astronomer i Tyskland. En sådan avskrift var väl det exemplar som Longomontanus vid sin avresa från Benatky d. 18 juli 1600 skänkte Johannes Eriksen, en annan av Tychos lärjungar. Detta exemplar, ett av de få bevarade, finns nu i Wien. Ett annat, tidigare ägt av Hevelius i Danzig, som förmodligen förvärvat det med Keplers kvarlåtenskap, finnes nu i KVA.

entries.title_transcribed: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
entries.subject: Astronomy

marks.inscription: ‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis Jesu Pragae A° 1642. Ex Bibliotheca et Recognitione Tichoniana’ on the title (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 86, no. 11); the later note ‘Musei Mathematici’.; the 1642 line is written around the title woodcut: ‘Collegij Caesa=|rei Soc[ieta]tis IESV / Pragæ / A° 1642° / Ex Bibliotheca et Recognitione Tichoniana.’ (Vackářová 2026, Obr. 30 and 32, read 27 October 2026)
marks.annotations: marginalia by Paul Wittich, not Tycho (Gingerich); long exhibited as Tycho's
marks.binding: pale leather over boards, blind-tooled with ornament rolls and pictorial centre panels — the Crucifixion on the front board, the risen Christ on the back — with no owner's mark; a binding apart from Tycho's own, made before the volume reached him (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 9, Obr. 5–6; Prandtl 1932, p. 14); on the published photograph (Vackářová Obr. 5–6): outer floral roll, a figured roll in compartments, inner frame with a lettered strip above the centre panel, diagonal corner tools, three-line plaques below both panels — lettering too worn to read at reproduction size

entries.editorial_note: From Tycho’s library: Prandtl, Verzeichnis A no. 14, his Einzelband X (‘reichverzierter weißer Lederband’). Prandtl (1932) attributed the marginalia to Tycho; Gingerich and Westman showed them to be Paul Wittich’s. The acquisition is documented in the correspondence. After Wittich’s death (1586) two noble visitors, the barons Johann Septimius von Lichtenstein and Felician von Herberstein, took charge of Wittich’s books and papers in Tycho’s name (Tycho to Hagecius, 22 March 1589, Opera omnia VII 165–166) and pursued the purchase of Wittich’s whole library from the surviving sister for six years, 1589–1595 (Tycho’s letters of 1 November 1589 and 12 August 1595 — Hagecius’s reply of 10 May 1589 found the barons away from court and Dudith already rebuffed by the sister: ‘omnem eius supellectilem librariam... iusto pretio nanciscar’; ‘de libris VITICHIANIS... a sorore superstite... obtinere queam’). According to Mosley (2007, pp. 175–179; the despatch at p. 179, following Gingerich and Westman 1988) Jacob Monau is held to have succeeded in part: he is thought to have despatched three of Wittich’s four annotated De revolutionibus volumes to Prague, the fourth remaining in Wrocław — Gingerich’s Wrocław 9 (Biblioteka Uniwersytecka 437777), the copy Valentin von Sebisch transcribed c. 1604. Gingerich’s Annotated Census traces two of Wittich’s copies to Tycho through Monaw’s delivery of October 1600 — Prague 3, 14 B 16 (p. 23: ‘likely one brought to him in Prague from Wittich’s heirs in Wrocław by Jacob Monaw … in October of 1600’) and Vatican 1, Ottoboniana 1902 (p. 105: ‘presumably he got it in October 1600 through the help of Jacob Monaw’) — and gives the Liège copy, Res MS 69C, the provenance of an annotator from Reinhold’s circle, Wittich and the Université de Liège, with no Prague station (p. 8); in his essay of the same year Gingerich writes that ‘another of the Wittich/Tychonic copies was perhaps acquired by a Belgian Jesuit working in Prague, for today it is found in the University Library in Liège’ (Tycho Brahe and Prague, p. 325). Whether the Liège copy was among the books Monaw brought to Prague is thus left open between Gingerich’s two accounts and Mosley’s count of three. The pursuit was bound up with Tycho’s dispute with Ursus over plagiarism. This is the channel by which the Wittich-annotated De revolutionibus entered the Tychoniana. The count of Wittich’s annotated copies that reached Tycho stands at two values: Mosley has three despatched to Prague, Gingerich and Westman two of the four, as Jardine and Segonds cite them (2008, p. 3 n. 1); both stand until the Liège question below is settled. Gingerich and Westman describe the volume (1988, pp. 33–34): the blind-stamped pigskin binding carries roll-stamps dated 1550, which does not exclude Wittich's having had the book bound; 21 blank folios are bound before the text and 71 after it, never used; the year 1580 is used in a worked example on f. 93; slips are pasted over earlier notes on ff. 22v, 26 and 65; John Dee's Parallaticae commentationis of 1573 is cited on f. 124v; the star catalogue (ff. 46v–62v) is the one long stretch without notes. They take it as ‘one of three copies brought by Monaw to Tycho in October 1600, but the only one to have retained any connection with the Danish astronomer’ (p. 33). Westman (2011, p. 283 n. 7) counts the surviving Wittich copies as five — four treated in Gingerich & Westman 1988 and a fifth, with a single Wittich annotation, identified in Gingerich's census of 2002 — and records the efforts to obtain the library as continuing at Wandsbek in 1598, ‘in particular, the several copies of De Revolutionibus that he knew it contained’ (p. 349); his statement that Tycho sought the books ‘from his widow’ (p. 286) is at odds with Tycho's own letters, which name the surviving sister. No letter, inventory, Kepler or Tengnagel document records a price, a payment, a receipt or a delivery: the correspondence ends with Monau’s promise of 14 June 1600 (Opera omnia VIII 325–326), and Gingerich and Westman themselves write that ‘as far as the letters are concerned, this is unfortunately the end of the story’ (1988, p. 22); part of Wittich’s library was still being sold at Wrocław in 1606. The October 1600 delivery is carried as probable, not as documented (register dossier of 27 October 2026, §3 and §6).
open_questions: Whether the Liège De revolutionibus (Université de Liège, Res MS 69C; Nuremberg 1543, annotated by an early reader of Reinhold’s circle and by Wittich) passed through Tycho’s hands: Mosley counts three Wittich volumes despatched to Prague, Gingerich’s Census gives the Liège copy no Prague station, and Gingerich’s essay of 2002 supposes it acquired in Prague by a Belgian Jesuit; evidence of a Prague station in the Liège volume itself would decide.

27 Oct 2026 — nothing in 14 B 16 or its records bears on a Prague station of the Liège copy; the test remains the Liège volume itself (a Clementinum or Prague Jesuit mark) or a Liège record naming a Prague owner.

Lead, unadopted: the National Library's account names Andreas Dudith, with Hájek, Monau and Longomontanus, among those Tycho asked to secure Wittich's books (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 33 (scan 33), without a source). Dudith died in February 1589 at Breslau, where the Wittich estate lay, and Tycho was in correspondence with him (the Epistolarium's Dudith letters of 17 August 1588 and 10 May 1589; TBOO VII); the claim is plausible and would add a fourth agent to the three attempts Christianson counts, but it is not adopted until the letter is found — Gingerich & Westman 1988, pp. 17–22 (Desiderata row 4f) or the Dudith correspondence are the places to look.
27 Oct 2026 — no source held this round adds to the Dudith lead; G&W 1988 pp. 17–22 and the Dudith letters in TBOO VII (17 Aug 1588, 10 May 1589) remain the places to look.

entries.title_transcribed: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
entries.subject: Astronomy

dispersal.detail: Tycho (presumably acquired Oct 1600 via Monau) → Rudolf II → 1648 Swedish loot → Queen Christina → Rome 1655 → Ottoboni 1690 → BAV Ott. lat. 1902

entries.editorial_note: Scholarship argues that Tycho owned or used more than one De revolutionibus. This copy is the Nuremberg edition of 1543 now Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Ott. lat. 1902 (Gingerich: Ottoboniana 1902), described by Gingerich, Annotated Census (2002), pp. 105–108 (I.98, ‘Vatican 1’). The copy is annotated by Wittich; Tycho ‘eagerly sought’ it ‘and presumably he got it in October 1600 through the help of Jacob Monaw’. Gingerich conjectures its later route: from Rudolf II to the Swedish booty of 1648, to Christina, to Rome in 1655, to the Ottoboni library and so to the Vatican. The annotations are Wittich’s, not Tycho’s: Gingerich retracts the older belief, the flyleaf longitudes citing Vratislavia rather than Hven or Copenhagen. Tycho’s ownership therefore rests on the documented acquisition through Monau, not on any mark of his. The copy is distinct from the Wittich copy in the Clementinum (Sign. 14 B 16, the Basel edition of 1566). Gingerich and Westman (1988, pp. 31–32, 140): the volume is bound in red-orange morocco with the arms of Pius IX on the spine, so that the physical evidence of its earlier provenance is lost; it is entered in Queen Christina's catalogue of 1655 (Vatican, MS lat. 1871, pp. 88–91), the stage from which the Prague-loot conjecture is argued (Callmer 1977, pp. 116 ff.); ‘Andreae Osiandri’ is added in red ink on the Ad lectorem; observations of 8 November 1572 (f. 57v) and 16 September 1574 (ff. 54, 163) recur in the Liège copy; the manuscript leaves ff. 197v–211v are dated between 27 January and 17 February 1578, ff. 211–211v carrying star positions for 1578 and 1580.
open_questions: Whether a third of Wittich’s annotated copies, the Liège De revolutionibus of 1543 (ResMS 69C), also reached Tycho: Mosley (2007, p. 179, after Gingerich and Westman 1988) has Monau despatch three of the four to Prague, whereas Gingerich’s Census (2002) counts two as reaching Tycho, this copy and 14 B 16, and places the Liège copy outside his hands.

entries.title_transcribed: Epistola ad Bernardum Wapowski (the Letter against Werner), in a transcript
entries.subject: Astronomy
entries.editorial_note: Norlind 1970, p. 343: the letter Copernicus wrote at the request of Bernard Wapowski, canon of Kraków, on Johann Werner’s De motu octavae sphaerae; the comet book quotes a passage from it, and Tycho says there that he owns the text in a second- or third-hand transcript (Opera omnia IV, 292). No manuscript from his library is identified; the surviving transcripts of the letter have not been examined for the question.
open_questions: Which, if any, of the surviving transcripts of the Letter against Werner descends from the copy Tycho reports owning (Opera omnia IV, 292); the Vienna Sammelhandschrift that holds the Commentariolus (Cod. 10530) has not been examined for it.

norlind.ownership_verdict: owned in a second- or third-hand transcript (Tycho's own statement in the comet book, IV, 292); not located
norlind.discussion: På begäran av sin ungdomsvän och f.d. studiekamrat Bernhard Wapowski, domherre i Kraków, författade Copernicus detta brev, vilket utgör ett utlåtande över Johann Werners i Nürnberg skrift »De motu octavæ sphæræ». Copernicus kritiserar bl.a. Werners åsikt, att vårdagjämningspunkten förflyttade sig med ojämn hastighet. Vidare påpekar han, att Werner begått ett grovt fel vid beräkningen av årets längd. – I kometboken (IV, 292) citerar Tycho ett ställe ur detta manuskript, vilket han säger sig äga i en andra eller tredje avskrift.

entries.title_transcribed: Historia Lutheri
entries.subject: History/Theology

acquisition.channel: one of nine copies that reached Tycho from Wittenberg in September 1598 with letters for Rosenkrantz; he passed the parcel on and kept one copy to read (Opera omnia VIII, 115)

entries.editorial_note: A parcel of nine copies of the Historia Lutheri reached Tycho from Wittenberg with two letters for Rosenkrantz; he forwarded it and kept one copy to read at leisure (‘behåller han ett exemplar av boken för att i lugn och ro kunna studera den’; Tycho to Rosenkrantz, September 1598, Opera omnia VIII, 115). Dresser is not named in the letter; the identification is Norlind’s. The book was printed at Leipzig; only the parcel came from Wittenberg. Tycho’s copy has not been identified.

norlind.entry: Dresserus, Matthias: Historia Lutheri. Lipsiæ 1598.8°.
norlind.ownership_verdict: owned: one copy kept back from the parcel of nine received from Wittenberg (letter to Rosenkrantz, Sept. 1598); author identified by Norlind, not named by Tycho; no copy located
norlind.discussion: Innehåller en samling av 15 uppsatser rörande Luther, däribland predikningar av Melanchthon, dennes biografi över Luther m.m. – Ehuru Dressers namn inte nämns, måste denna bok åsyftas av Tycho i ett brev till Rosenkrantz (sept. 1598; VIII, 115). Tycho skriver, att han från Wittenberg fått ett paket med 9 exemplar av »Historia Lutheri» och tvenne brev till Rosenkrantz. Han låter försändelsen gå vidare till Rosenkrantz, dock behåller han ett exemplar av boken för att i lugn och ro kunna studera den. Han vill nämligen se efter, om vad som står häri skiljer sig från det han en gång i sin ungdom läste hos en författare, vars namn han dock inte nu kan påminna sig.

entries.title_transcribed: Ad Iacobi Auberti Vindonis de ortu et causis metallorum ... brevis responsio
entries.subject: Alchemy/Chymical medicine

dispersal.detail: owned by Tycho, then given to Hagecius at Regensburg, autumn 1575 (TBOO VII,95)

entries.editorial_note: Quercetanus (Joseph Du Chesne), Ad Iacobi Auberti … brevis responsio (Lyon 1575, 8vo): a Paracelsian book Tycho owned only briefly. Its preface is dated 1 April 1575, and he gave the copy to Thaddaeus Hagecius at their meeting in Regensburg in the autumn of that year; in August 1585 he asked Hagecius for another copy, unable to recall author or title (Tycho to Hagecius, August 1585, Opera omnia VII, 95). The work is identified from Hagecius’s marginal note ‘Libellus est Josephi Quercetani’ on Tycho’s letter (autograph in Vienna, Österreichische Nationalbibliothek), not from the book; Norlind gives the title as ‘med största sannolikhet’ (Norlind 1970, p. 359). The copy passed into Hagecius’s library; a copy recovered from it would carry his marks, not Tycho’s. Status attested, passed on, since 20 October 2026: the copy left the library in his lifetime as a gift to Hagecius (road 0), which is why no copy is sought — not a mass-survival text retired as unlocatable.

norlind.entry: Quercetanus, Josephus: Ad Iacobi Auberti Vindonis de ortu et causis metallorum contra chymicos explicationem Josephi Quercetani Armeniaci brevis responsio. Eiusdem de exquisita mineralium, animalium et vegetabilium medicamentorum spagyrica præparatione et usu, perspicua tractatio. Lugduni 1575.8°.
norlind.ownership_verdict: once owned (Tycho gave the book to Hagecius at Regensburg in autumn 1575 and sought another copy in 1585); identification of the work from Hagecius's marginal note on Tycho's letter, 'med största sannolikhet'; no located copy
norlind.discussion: [Preamble printed before the headword, leading into it:] I aug. 1585 (VII, 95) skriver Tycho till Hagecius, att denne vid deras sammanträffande i Regensburg hösten 1575 erhöll en bok, vars författare Tycho dock icke kan erinra sig. Boken handlade om beredning av »kemiska läkemedel» (»de Chymicis medicamentis præparandis»), titeln kan Tycho icke med bestämdhet uppge, men han minns, att formatet var oktav. Fastän han sökt efter den hos bokhandlare i Tyskland, har han inte lyckats komma över den, eftersom han inte kunnat uppge vare sig förf.-namnet eller titeln. Han ber nu Hagecius skicka ett exemplar, så vida ett sådant står att få köpa, eller också ge besked om författarens namn. Vi veta inte, om Hagecius lyckades tillmötesgå Tychos önskan, men i margen till Tychos brev (original i Wien) har han antecknat »Libellus est Josephi Quercetani». (»Quartani» i noten, VII, 407, är en felläsning av utg.) Den bok som här avses och som Tycho alltså en gång ägt är med största sannolikhet: [Here follows the entry line; text after the entry line:] Förf., vars franska namn var Joseph Du Chesne (1546–1609), ansågs som en framstående läkare och var sedan 1593 livmedikus hos Henrik IV. I sina talrika skrifter framträder han dock som en charlatan inom yrket. Att Tycho varit så intresserad av denna skrift, sammanhänger väl med den läkarverksamhet han bedrev på Hven. Quercetanus var en ivrig anhängare av Paracelsus, för vilken Tycho också hyste en viss böjelse. Bokens förord är daterat d. 1 april 1575, den var således alldeles nyutkommen, då Tycho skänkte den till Hagecius.

entries.editorial_note: The second piece of the Sammelband 44 F 38: Ratdolt's Euclid of 1482, the first printed edition, with its woodcut diagrams in the outer margins. On the blank recto of its first leaf a blacked-out ownership note, perhaps still of the late fifteenth century, read under the comparator as ‘Hic liber pertinet domui fratrum in Culmen’: the house of the Brethren of the Common Life at Kulm (Chełmno) in Royal Prussia, founded from Zwolle in 1473, with a school Copernicus probably attended before 1491 and, in the years about 1473 to 1478, one of the first presses of east-central Europe; its library was dispersed when the house ended in the 1530s or 1540s, and eleven volumes with twenty-six incunables are known from it (Boldan and Kazanskii 2023, p. 28, citing Szandorowska 1968 and 1973). How the Euclid came from Kulm to Tycho — bought, like his other student books, or through the Prussian connections of his circle — is not recorded; it was in his hands by 1576, when the binding was made. Boldan and Kazanskii call it the first scientific title recovered from the Kulm brethren's library.
open_questions: The route from the Brethren of the Common Life at Kulm to Tycho before 1576.
27 Oct 2026 — no source held records it.

marks.inscription: No Jesuit inscription of 1642. Title leaf: the ink ‘Bibliotheca Strahoviensis’ and two round purple BIBLIOTHECA STRAHOVIENSIS stamps of the series the library introduced from the late eighteenth century (Hlinovský & Pišna 2018, pp. 10–12); lower left, in graphite, the large ‘G. Crusio ‹K›’ of Gabriel Crusius — the formula ‘G. Crusio inservio’ that Kleinschnitzová printed from the National Library's 5 G 92 (1933, p. 89), where it stands beside the year 1673 — and faint strokes of an earlier inscription, effaced (read on the volume, 18 September 2026).
marks.annotations: marginal notes ‘in his hand’ (Pařez 2009: přípisky psané jeho rukou in margine; Pařez, 4 September 2026: a few notes, certainly Tycho's) — not yet examined graphonomically
marks.binding: front board: a plain blind-stamped two-line TYCHO / BRAHE above the central ornament and the date 1567 below it, on a Renaissance blind-tooled frame-composition binding; no supralibros on the back (Pařez 2009, with photograph; Katalog Tritius: ‘Supralibros Tychona Brahe z roku 1567’). The earliest dated appearance of his full name on a binding, of the family of the ‘Tycho Brade 1561’ and ‘Ty Brad 1563’ name-stamps

dispersal.detail: No 1642 inscription. The title carries Gabriel Crusius’s mark; the next recorded owner is Jan Josef Klauser (‘Clauser’ in the Tritius record), the Prague printer and gubernial archivist, whose library Strahov bought in 1775 (Neškudla 2021, p. 229). The book left Tycho’s library by a private route and bypassed the transfer of 1642: Crusius gave two other Tycho volumes (5 G 92, 5 J 103) to the Chomutov Jesuits on 5 August 1654, and Klauser died on 31 July 1771, so the book was on the private Prague market before the suppression of 1773.

entries.editorial_note: Found by Hedvika Kuchařová and published by Pařez in 2009. Not the Clavius Euclid that Norlind inferred (one of the editions of 1574–91, of which no copy has been located): this is the Zamberti–Campanus Elements of 1558, a working mathematician's Euclid a generation earlier. The 1567 date places the binding in the Rostock student years, nine years before the earliest dated T.B.O. cohort; Norlind (pp. 344, 363) already knew a ‘T. B.’ initials mark of 1567, so the year is not anomalous — the two-line full name is. Whether this is one of the eight books Mainx found in 1943 is tested by the mark: it is not the gilt portrait plaque Mortensen describes for all eight. The graphite ‘G. Crusio ‹K›’ on the title is Gabriel Crusius's (identified 19 September 2026 by the match of formula and ductus with the digitised title leaf of 5 G 92): the Euclid is the third or fourth known book of a named private collector of Tychoniana in mid-seventeenth-century Bohemia, whose holding scattered by more than one route. Munzar and Pařez already counted five books from Tycho's library at Strahov in 2002 (p. 369); whether that count includes this Euclid, found by Kuchařová between 1996 and 2009, or the Mechanica, is not stated.
open_questions: Whether the marginal notes — at Book I, prop. 4 and in the Campanus section — are in Tycho’s hand: Pařez (2009) gives them to him (‘přípisky psané jeho rukou in margine’); they have not been compared with his securely attributed specimens.
The effaced inscription beneath Crusius's mark on the title — ultraviolet or raking light may recover the earlier owner's name.
Klauser's printed ex-libris, which would confirm the 1775 route, has not been looked for on the endleaves; nor Strnad's name or stamp.

The trailing ‹K› glyph after Crusius's name on all three Prague instances — a second initial, a locative abbreviation, or a personal mark — is unresolved; if Gabriel Crusius was a Kraus z Krausenbergu the glyph has a candidate expansion.
Whether the ‘five books from Tycho's library’ Munzar and Pařez counted at Strahov in 2002 include this Euclid (Pařez 2009 credits its discovery to Kuchařová and calls it new) or the Mechanica.

entries.title_transcribed: Geometriae rotundi libri XIIII (Basel 1583)
entries.subject: Mathematics/Geometry

marks.inscription: No Tycho mark on either KB copy (both examined on their surrogates). The Geometria rotundi is dedicated to King Frederik II; in the dedication Fincke praises 'in Mathematis excellentissimum virum Dn. Tychonem Brahe' (printed text, present in every copy) — this is Norlind's whole basis, not a copy-level Tycho mark.

entries.editorial_note: Thomas Fincke, Geometriae rotundi libri XIIII (Basel: S. Henricpetri, 1583), dedicated to Frederik II. Both copies in the Royal Library, Copenhagen, have been examined in digital reproduction, and neither bears any mark of Tycho’s ownership. The first copy (LN 599 4, ex. 1) carries the autograph ‘Horrebow’ (the eighteenth-century family of Danish Royal Astronomers) on the title page and royal-cipher and BRH stamps, in an eighteenth-century marbled-board binding. The second (Hielmst. 1661a 4, ex. 2) is a contemporary Sammelband (Fincke 1583 with Ursus, Fundamentum astronomicum, Strasbourg 1588) in limp vellum, inscribed ‘Severinus Pauli[?] … Lipsiae Anno Dni 158[3]’ (mottoes ‘Superna curato, Humana contemnito’ and ‘Mens generosa ultra polos’) and ‘Christiernus Joannis Hafniensis Anno 1620’ (motto ‘Ex uno omnia’), later Hielmstierne’s. Norlind nonetheless placed the book in Tycho’s library — ‘fanns säkerligen i biblioteket på Uraniborg’ (Bilaga I, p. 346) — but his whole basis is Fincke’s printed praise of Tycho in the preface, a compliment present in every copy rather than a mark in any copy. No inventory, inscription or ownership mark attests Tycho’s ownership, and neither surviving Copenhagen copy is his.
open_questions: Who the two early owners of the second copy were — ‘Severinus Pauli[?]’, Leipzig c. 1583, and Christiern Jensen of Copenhagen, 1620 — is unknown beyond their inscriptions, and neither is Tycho; a full reading of the inscriptions and the university matriculation registers would identify them.

norlind.entry: Fincke, Thomas: Geometriæ rotundi libri XIIII. Basileæ 1583.4°.
norlind.ownership_verdict: certainly in the library at Uraniborg (Norlind, from the continuation on p. 346: author addresses Tycho warmly in the preface); no copy located
norlind.discussion: Fincke bedrev studier vid olika utländska universitet, bl.a. i Basel 1583, blev vid 30 års ålder professor i matematik i Köpenhamn 1591, i retorik 1602 och i medicin 1603. Erhöll 1597 uppdraget att jämte professor Iver Stub resa över till Hven för att undersöka om någon åverkan gjorts på Tychos instrument, vilket misstänkliggjorde dem i Tychos ögon. – Boken är tillägnad konung Fredrik II, men i förordet till läsaren, fol. 3r, talar Fincke mycket vänligt om Tycho och ber honom inte dölja, om det finns något lovvärt i den och icke spara kritik, om så behövs. Boken, som tillkommit under Finckes studievistelse i Basel, fanns säkerligen i biblioteket på Uraniborg.

entries.title_transcribed: Ægloga de eclipsi solari anno 1574 ... futura
entries.subject: Astronomy (eclipse)

marks.inscription: No Tycho ownership mark. Full 32-image EEB scan of KB Hielmst. 1226 4 read: only the Hielmstierne armorial bookplate (engr. C.M. Tuscher, datable 1743-51), the Bibliotheca Regia Hafniensis stamp, and plain 18th-c paper boards.

entries.editorial_note: That Tycho owned the work is well founded: the Aegloga is dedicated to him (17 October 1574), and Flemløse came to Hven early in 1578 as one of his very first pupils (Norlind 1970, p. 346). This copy, however, is not demonstrably Tycho’s. The only surviving copy known (a unicum, according to L. Nielsen as cited by Norlind 1970, p. 346) is KB Hielmst. 1226 4, an eighteenth-century Hielmstierne Danica acquisition carrying no mark of Tycho’s. No Prague or Clementinum copy is known: the work appears in none of Kleinschnitzová, Prandtl or Šolc, and the Czech National Library’s index of former owners records no copy of Brahe’s. Norlind uses no verb of ownership: he infers only that a copy was ‘högst troligt’ on Hven, from the dedication, not that the Copenhagen copy is Tycho’s. The copy is therefore rejected as Tycho’s, while ownership of the work is retained at grade C. Status attested, B, since 20 October 2026: the work-level ownership is sound on the dedication; the Royal Library's copy, judged in its own volume record, is not shown to be his.

norlind.entry: Flemlöse, Peder Jacobsen: Ægloga de eclipsi solari anno 1574. mense novembri futura, et tempore plenilunii ecliptici anno 1573. conspecti ... Hafniæ 1574.4°.
norlind.ownership_verdict: probably owned (dedicated to Tycho; "högst troligt" a copy was on Hven); no located Tycho copy — only one copy of the edition known (Copenhagen, KB), not claimed as Tycho's
norlind.discussion: Flemlöse blev en högt betrodd assistent hos Tycho, kom till Hven i början av 1578 såsom en av hans allra första lärjungar. Redan dessförinnan hade han emellertid stått i förbindelse med den omkr. 8 år äldre Tycho, såsom framgår av, att han tillägnat denne sin bok. Den utgör en episk herdedikt, behandlande den stundande solförmörkelsen i nov. 1574, vilken enligt Flemlöse bebådar Kristi snara återkomst. Förordet är dat. Köpenhamn i mitten av okt. 1574. Han har alltså avslutat boken vid den tid, då Tycho höll sina föreläsningar vid universitetet där. På dessa föreläsningar syftar Flemlöse fol. A3r; förmodligen har han varit en av åhörarna. Det får anses som högst troligt, att ett exemplar av boken fanns i biblioteket på Hven. – Enligt Lauritz Nielsen är endast ett exemplar numera känt (i Det kgl. Bibliotek i Köpenhamn).

entries.title_transcribed: Tractatus brevis et utilis de erigendis figuris coeli
entries.subject: Astronomy/Astrology/Mathematics

marks.inscription: the work number ‘3.’ at the head of the title (the later librarian's, matching the contents note on the front flyleaf)
marks.annotations: scattered marginalia in two registers of a sixteenth-century hand (brown and black ink): subject headings and section numbers in the calendar chapters (images 19–37 of the facsimile), the solar cycle for 1555 worked by long division (33), the dominical-letter table numbered with the years 1488–1501 and a 1–7 counter (34), numerals against the worked example of the Sun's true place (89), ‘obliquam’ correcting the misprint ‘aliquam’ (124), arithmetic checking the Elector August's nativity and part of fortune (129, 143, 155), the rule of the part of fortune written out below an ornament (136), the revolution of 1556 recomputed from Reinhold's tables (171), a note on the meridian of Reinhold's equinox table (174), ‘Directionis finis’ with underlining at Propositio XXII (176), a faint unread note (152); on the rear endleaf of the volume an unfinished index of the propositions (I–V: ‘Index monstrans quid quaelibet propositio in hoc libello contineat’) in the same hand, written in the bound volume after 1563; hand(s) not identified

dispersal.detail: Vedel’s name stands at the head of the first title of the volume. Walde (1920, p. 329) and Mortensen (1955, p. 27) read the volume as Tycho’s gift to Vedel, the memento of their Leipzig years; Norlind (1970, p. 366) held it more likely that the book was Vedel’s from the start, given to Tycho, who had it bound with the two others — on which reading it did not leave the library in his lifetime and its route to De la Gardie is undocumented.

entries.editorial_note: Prandtl Verzeichnis A no. 19; bound third in Band III. The manual Tycho followed at Leipzig for his first horoscopes (Thoren 1990, p. 17, n. 23, pointing to this copy).
open_questions: Whose hand are the marginalia of the Garcaeus — Tycho's student hand of 1563–65 or Vedel's? A comparison with the inscriptions in the student binding of 1561 (Museet for Søfart, inv. 1957:0030) and the earliest observation notebook would decide.
The faint six-line note in the outer margin of image 152 of the facsimile is unread.
The place at longitude 53½° against which the writer set Königsberg's 44¼° in the note below Reinhold's table (image 174).

entries.title_transcribed: De astrolabo catholico liber
entries.subject: Astronomy/Instruments
entries.editorial_note: Norlind 1970, p. 347: listed among the books of the library because Tycho discusses the tract in the Progymnasmata (Opera omnia III, 74); no copy, receipt or mark is recorded. Norlind’s introduction states the principle on which such tracts enter his catalogue: it may be regarded as fairly certain that nearly all the writings on the new star of 1572 and the comet of 1577 that Tycho reviews in the Progymnasmata and the comet book stood in the library on Hven (p. 335). Norlind shows by textual comparison which edition Tycho used: the sentence ‘Quicquid alii de ea scribant’ stands in the edition of 1556, published after the author’s death by his son Cornelius Gemma, and in Tycho’s text, but not in Everaert’s compendium of 1583 (Ortroy, nos. 129–130). Use is shown; ownership is the inference. If Tycho’s copy survives, it would carry no known mark by which it could be recognised.

norlind.ownership_verdict: used and cited in Progymnasmata; the 1556 edition (not the 1583 Everhardus compendium) established by textual comparison; no copy located
norlind.discussion: Efter denna upplaga, som utgavs efter förf:s död av sonen Cornelius Gemma, citerar Tycho i »Prog.» (III, 74) och icke efter det av Martinus Everhardus publicerade kompendiet, som trycktes i Antverpen 1583 (Ortroy, a.a. nr 130). Detta framgår av en jämförelse mellan de båda upplagorna och Tychos text. Såväl i uppl. 1556 som hos Tycho står så t.ex. satsen »Quicquid alii de ea scribant», som emellertid saknas i uppl. 1583.

entries.title_transcribed: De naturae divinis characterismis; seu raris & admirandis spectaculis, causis, indiciis, proprietatibus rerum in partibus singulis universi, libri II
entries.subject: Natural philosophy

marks.annotations: Numerous annotations in Tycho's hand, from a word or two to virtually filling the available margin (Martayan Lan 2001, which supplied a list of the annotated locations and a partial transcription); on pp. 124–125 of Book II the long note in the lower margin was written with the book held upside down (the colour plate at the front of Martayan Lan's catalogue; Gingerich 2002, fig. 1: the opening headed ‘COSMOCRIT. LIB. II’ / ‘CAPVT III’, with further notes in the outer margins beside the printed glosses on the new star's motion and distance). Tycho annotated heavily the section on Muñoz's observations of the new star of 1572 and quoted this passage explicitly in the Progymnasmata (Gingerich 2002, p. 327). The hand confirmed as Tycho's by Owen Gingerich (per litteras, 25 May 2001); Anthony Grafton's preliminary report for the dealer found a genetic relation between the notes and the Astronomiae instauratae progymnasmata (Prague 1602)
marks.binding: Contemporary flexible vellum with yapp edges: gilt medallion portrait of Tycho in the centre of the front cover, worn, with ‘Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei / pulchrius eniteat, quae latet interior’ in the surround; the back cover with the Brahe family arms and ‘Arma genus fundi pereunt durabile virtus / et doctrina decus nobilitatis habent’ in the surround; covers soiled, remnants of ties; an old shelfmark stencilled on the spine (Martayan Lan 2001; the same portrait-and-arms supralibros is illustrated by Prandtl 1932 and Christianson 2000, p. 139)

dispersal.detail: The copy carries a scored (cancelled) former ownership inscription and a later inscription dated 1647, both unread, unidentified later annotations on the front endleaf, and an old shelfmark stencilled on the spine (Martayan Lan 2001): the traces of its route between Tycho's heirs and Felix Mainx's purchase in Prague in 1938. Gingerich 2002 (p. 326) places the book ‘around 1955’ in Harald Mortensen's own collection: a misreading of Mortensen's paper, which reports Mainx's acquisition; Martayan Lan's provenance line (‘the private collection of a professor in Prague’) has it right.

entries.editorial_note: Tycho’s heavily annotated working copy of Gemma’s book on the new star of 1572, printed by Christopher Plantin at Antwerp in 1575. The notes on Muñoz’s observations are the passage he quotes in the Progymnasmata, and Grafton’s report for the dealer found a genetic relation between the marginalia and the printed work (Prague 1602). The copy was recorded as Tycho’s by Mortensen (1955, p. 30) on Felix Mainx’s report that he had acquired it in Prague in 1938, listed by Norlind (1970, p. 347) from Mortensen, and identified as annotated in Tycho’s hand only when Martayan Lan offered it in 2001 (Catalogue 28, item 55, US$ 300,000, with a colour plate of Book II, pp. 124–125); the hand was confirmed by Gingerich (per litteras, 25 May 2001) and is reproduced as fig. 1 of Gingerich 2002, p. 326, which records the sale to a private American collector. The binding is Tycho’s portrait-and-arms supralibros on flexible vellum. Mortensen’s own sentence says that Professor Felix Mainx acquired the Gemma in Prague in 1938 and told Mortensen of it; the book was never in Mortensen’s collection, and Gingerich’s ‘the same collector’ (2002, p. 326) misreads him.
open_questions: Who now owns the book: the private American buyer of 2001 (from Martayan Lan) is unidentified; the dealer’s records or a later sale would name him.

In which library the book sat before Mainx bought it in Prague in 1938 — possibly the monastery in which he found the eight further Tycho volumes in 1943; the scored former ownership inscription, the later inscription dated 1647 and the old shelfmark stencilled on the spine (Martayan Lan 2001) would name it once read.

What the annotations contain in full: Martayan Lan’s list of the annotated locations with partial transcription and Anthony Grafton’s report of 2001 are unpublished, and their publication or an examination of the volume would settle it.

entries.title_transcribed: De peregrina stella quae superiore anno primum apparere coepit
entries.subject: Astronomy (nova 1572)
entries.editorial_note: Norlind 1970, p. 347 (Ortroy, Gemma Frisius, no. 197): since Tycho writes that Postellus’s tract on the star was contained in it (Progymnasmata, Opera omnia III, 229), the edition can be no other than this one, printed without place in 1573 with Postellus’s De nova stella iudicium on its last three leaves; Norlind (p. 357) notes that Postellus is not known to have published a separate tract on the star, though Dreyer took it for one (Opera omnia III, 402). The attribution rests on Tycho’s own words about the copy in his hands. An unbound tract; a copy of Tycho’s would carry no known mark by which it could be recognised.

entries.title_transcribed: De omni rerum fossilium genere, gemmis, lapidibus, metallis
entries.subject: Natural science

marks.inscription: Laube’s stamp ‘Prof. Dr. G. C. Laube, Prag’ at the foot of the title, and no other inscription (the Ransom Center’s photographs, 7 October 2026)
marks.annotations: none by Tycho: a leaf-through of the whole volume at the Ransom Center (7 October 2026) found only a reader's pen drawing of a goat and one word in a German cursive hand on p. 103 of De figuris lapidum, and Prandtl, who owned the volume, noted none
marks.binding: parchment Prachtband, the gilt portrait-and-arms supralibros on both boards, each oval in a lozenge frame, struck from the larger die, with the distichs (Prandtl’s frontispiece of 1932; the Ransom Center’s photographs of 7 October 2026); the spine in four gilt-tooled panels, unlettered

dispersal.detail: Never traced at the Clementinum: the title page carries no Jesuit inscription of 1642, and the spine, which Studnička in 1901 found intact and numbered 2781 where the Jesuit library relabelled its Tycho volumes, shows no number at all — already in Prandtl's photograph of 1932, and in those of 2026. Surfaced in the Leipzig trade before 1901 and bought there by Gustav Laube of Prague, whose stamp is on the title page; Wilhelm Prandtl's by the late 1920s; to the University of Texas with his collection in the 1950s, whose bookplate is on the rear pastedown.

entries.editorial_note: Prandtl Verzeichnis A no. 46, bound alone as Band XXI — his own parchment Prachtband, the frontispiece of his catalogue of 1932. First noticed by Studnička in 1901 in Gustav Laube's possession at Prague, the number 2781 on its spine the source of the ‘several thousand volumes’ estimates. Located at the University of Texas at Austin (Harry Ransom Center) ex Prandtl (Gingerich 2002, p. 325).
open_questions: The number 2781 that Studnička read on the spine in 1901: the spine now shows no number, label or lettering, in direct or in raking light (the Ransom Center’s photographs of 7 October 2026). Whether the number was inked on the parchment and has faded, stood on a paper label since lost, or was never where Studnička placed it cannot be settled from photographs; ultraviolet light on the spine would show faded ink, and the hand that Studnička attributed to Tycho can no longer be examined at all.

The pencil note ‘Aus Tycho Brahes Bibliothek!’ on the front flyleaf and the number 760 on the front pastedown: whose hands — Laube's, the Leipzig bookseller's or Prandtl's — is not known; a comparison with Laube's or Prandtl's known hand would settle the note.

When and from whom Prandtl bought the volume (after Laube's death in 1923?), and when the University of Texas acquired the Prandtl collection: the catalogue record gives no accession date, and the bookplate none.

entries.title_transcribed: Thierbuch (German, transl. C. Forer)
entries.subject: Natural history/Zoology
entries.editorial_note: Norlind: ‘Tycho, som också hade Gesners Thierbuch’ — Tycho, who also had Gessner’s Thierbuch. The book is attested only by Tycho’s own letter to Landgrave Wilhelm of September 1591, which places the Oryx description on fol. 68 (Opera omnia VI, 244). No copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified. Whether his copy was the 1563 or the 1583 edition is unrecorded; Norlind holds it immaterial, the two editions being in his words identical: Zurich, Christoph Froschauer, 1563 (VD16 G 1728), reissued 1583 (VD16 G 1729), folio. It is a different book from the surviving Gessner, De omni rerum fossilium genere (Zurich 1565; Prandtl, Verzeichnis A no. 46; now at the University of Texas at Austin). The only Thierbuch physically traced in Tycho’s orbit is Landgrave Wilhelm’s own Kassel copy, not Tycho’s, destroyed in an air raid in September 1941.

norlind.entry: Gesner, Conradus: Thierbuch ... durch Cunrat Forer ... in das Teütsch gebracht ... Züryck 1563 (1583).2°.
letters: lantgreve Wilhelm till Tycho maj 1591; VI, 231
lantgreve Wilhelm till Tycho aug. 1591; VI, 240
norlind.ownership_verdict: owned, edition unknown (1563 or 1583, which Norlind calls identical) — attested by Tycho's own letter to the Landgrave, Sept. 1591
norlind.discussion: Lantgreve Wilhelm ägde upplagan 1563, efter vad han skriver till Tycho maj 1591 (VI, 231). Han uppger, att »in dem Deutschen Exemplari Gesneri de Animalibus Quadrupedibus» skulle på fol. 85 stå en beskrivning med bild av ett djur, kallat Rix eller Oryx (till Tycho aug. s.å.; VI, 240). Tycho, som också hade Gesners Thierbuch (om uppl. 1563 eller 1583 få vi ej veta, men det är betydelselöst, då båda upplagorna äro identiska), finner fol. 68 en beskrivning dock utan bild av det märkliga djuret (till lantgreven sept. 1591; VI, 244). Han menar därför, att lantgreven måste ha en annan upplaga. Lantgrevens uppgift är emellertid oriktig, ty i de båda upplagorna står fol. 68ᵛ en beskrivning utan bild under rubriken »Von der wilden Geyss Oryx genannt». Fol. 85ʳ finnes däremot bild och beskrivning av en älg (»Von dem Pferdthirtz»). – Lantgrevens exemplar (i Kassel) gick förlorat vid ett bombangrepp i sept. 1941.

entries.title_transcribed: De geographia liber unus. Friburgi Brisgaudiae 1536.

marks.inscription: title (canvas 5, read 27 October 2026): 'Sum And: Seuer: Wellej Danj. 1564' (struck through), 'Mensis Aug. die 26.'; 'Collegij Societatis IESV Commotouij Catalogo inscriptus Aº 1671.'
marks.annotations: red-ink glosses (Euclid, sphere, Ptolemy, coordinates), many struck through, pp. 9–71; a second hand p. 50 (re-read 27 October 2026); hands unattributed
marks.binding: modern half-binding, sprinkled paper boards (canvas 1)

entries.editorial_note: Kleinschnitzová 1933 no. 42; NK Clementinum Sign. 19 G 20. The title page carries the struck-through inscription of Anders Sørensen Vedel, 26 August 1564; on the back of the last leaf are instructions to a binder, in Tycho's hand according to Kleinschnitzová, naming a commentary on Alcabitius, an astrological fragment, Gauricus with Montulmo, and Albubater. A cost note on the first leaf of the Sacrobosco manuscript Sign. VII E 29, formerly bound before the Gauricus of Sign. 14 F 16, lists a Glareanus at 21 pfennigs before Gauricus with Montulmo, Albubater, Cardanus and the binder's fee (Studnička 1901, Bericht, p. 20). The volume carries no ownership mark of Tycho’s, and its route from Vedel is not documented. It is one of the four Clementinum volumes — with Sign. 5 G 42, 14 J 164 and MS XII A 12 — that Kleinschnitzová cites (p. 80) to show that Sammelbände from Tycho’s library were broken up and rebound with books of other provenance; the three works bound after the Glareanus she marks ‘Kein Tychonianum’.
open_questions: Kleinschnitzová concluded from the cost note on the first leaf of the Sacrobosco manuscript Sign. VII E 29 — ‘sichtlich sehr nahe verwandt’ to the binder’s instruction on the last leaf here — that the Glareanus, like the manuscript, belonged to the Sammelband no. 37, now Sign. 14 F 16, whose spine signature attests the Chomutov provenance also inscribed on the Glareanus (1933, p. 93); the cost note is headed ‘Andreas Schöner’, Vedel’s inscription on this title page is dated 26 August 1564, and the hands of the two notes have not been compared.

27 Oct 2026 — the comparison cannot be made from the facsimile: the binder's instruction is not on fol. 35v, the back of the Glareanus's last leaf (Manuscriptorium canvas 74, read at full size: printed Epilogus and colophon only), nor on fols 34v–35r (canvases 72–73). The note's present location (an undigitised leaf, the first leaf of the Apianus adligatum, or binding waste) must be asked of NK ČR before the hands can be compared.

entries.title_transcribed: Apodixis physica et mathematica de cometis
entries.subject: Astronomy (comet)

acquisition.channel: a copy sent by Bartholomaeus Scultetus from Görlitz (Tycho to Hagecius, October 1581; Opera omnia VII, 64)

entries.editorial_note: A copy was sent to Tycho by Scultetus in Görlitz (Tycho to Hagecius, October 1581, Opera omnia VII, 64). Tycho discusses the work in his book on the comet (Opera omnia IV, 293–295). No copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified, and the work belongs to the Hagecius gap: Tycho owned at least four works of Hagecius, each documented by a letter, and not one survives in the Clementinum. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 78) remarked on the absence: among the Clementinum Tychoniana there is not a single work of Hagecius, though his long friendship with Tycho and Norlind’s list make it likely that Tycho had many if not all of his works, and none of the Clementinum’s Hagecius copies carries a provenance note pointing to him. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 80) names the mechanism by which such a copy could lose its provenance: composite volumes from Tycho’s library were broken up and rebound with pieces of other provenance (5 G 42, 14 J 164, 19 G 20, XII A 12), and Richard Kukula, director of the university library 1897–1918, had old Sammelbände dissolved as a matter of principle, among them, to judge by its modern binding, the Scultetus of 14 F 284. Whether Tycho’s Hagecius copies were lost or survive unrecognised remains an open question. The National Library of the Czech Republic holds three copies of the Görlitz 1581 edition — in a Luther convolute, in a convolute from the Jesuit college at Litoměřice, and as the host volume (record 000030653) of the Hagecius composite owned by the Jesuit college at Chomutov — and none bears a Tycho mark.

Imprint: Prague, Jiří Melantrich z Aventinu, 1578, 4to (Zinner 2824; Hellman 48), issued with the Spongia contra … Hannibalis Raymundi. The National Library of the Czech Republic holds two copies — 14 K 191, and a second (record 000030662) bound as the second tract in the Hagecius composite from the Jesuit college at Chomutov (host volume, record 000030653) — and neither bears a Tycho mark.

entries.editorial_note: Norlind: ‘Måste Tycho ha ägt’ — Tycho must have owned it, since the Progymnasmata treat the work at length (Opera omnia III, 19–43). Hájek sent Tycho a copy with many manuscript corrections and additions in his own hand, hoping that Tycho would print the revised text or take selections into his own account of the nova; Tycho discussed the revised text in the Progymnasmata and did not print it (Dreyer 1890, p. 58 n. 2; Mosley 2007, p. 124 n. 42; Opera omnia VII, 99). Tycho’s copy, which would carry Hájek’s autograph corrections, has not been identified. The National Library of the Czech Republic’s two copies of the Frankfurt 1574 edition — one inscribed for the Chomutov Jesuit college in 1671 (‘Collegij Soctis IESV Commotonij Ao. 1671’, record 000154680), one stamped ‘REGIAE BIBLIOTH: ACAD: PRAGEN.’ (record 000014579) — have no earlier owner in the library’s records.

entries.editorial_note: Two copies reached Tycho: one sent by the author in August 1576 (Hájek to Tycho, Opera omnia VII, 38), a second in Maior’s parcel of June 1584 (VII, 83). A reply to Hannibal Raimundus of Verona, who held that the star of 1572 was not new. Neither copy is located. The National Library’s copy of the work, the first tract (record 000030657) of a Hájek composite from the Chomutov Jesuit college (record 000030653), carries no Tycho mark in the library’s record. The second copy came inside Maior's priced parcel of June 1584 (Opera omnia VII 83), so was probably bought, not given; the first copy of August 1576 was the author's gift (register dossier of 27 October 2026, §18).

acquisition.channel: the author’s dedication copy; the disputation was held at Wittenberg on 21 March 1599, while Tycho was in the town (Norlind 1970, p. 349)

entries.editorial_note: Dedicated to Tycho by the author, a son of Tycho’s friend Bishop Peder Jacobsen Hegelund of Ribe; Norlind: ‘har säkerligen befunnit sig i hans bibliotek’ — certainly in his library. The author enrolled at Wittenberg in November 1598, some months before Tycho and his sons.

norlind.entry: Hegelius, Iohannes: Themata pro disputatione quarta ψυχολογίας, decadem quartam problematum exhibentia ... sub præsidio ... Iacobi Coci ... respondebit Iohannes Hegelius, Ripensis, Danus. Witebergæ 1599.4°.
norlind.ownership_verdict: dedicated to Tycho by the author; certainly in his library (Norlind); no copy located
norlind.discussion: Hegelius är latiniserat Hegelund. Denne Jens Pedersen Hegelund var son till Tychos ungdomsvän, biskop Peder Jacobsen Hegelund i Ribe, och var född 1573. Han inskrevs vid Wittenbergs universitet i nov. 1598 (Alb. Vit. II 453 a 31), några månader innan Tycho och hans söner. Ifrågavarande avhandling var tillägnad Tycho av förf. och har säkerligen befunnit sig i hans bibliotek. Den behandlar sömnens problem och ventilerades d. 21 mars 1599, alltså vid den tid, då Tycho ännu var kvar i Wittenberg. I jan. 1600 rekommenderar Tycho Hegelund hos Praguniversitetets rektor Bacchatius (VIII, 238–239).

entries.editorial_note: Heidenstein’s history of Stephen Báthory’s Muscovite war in the Basel edition of 1588 (Waldkirch, 184 pp., 4°), in a white parchment binding with Tycho’s gilt portrait medallion on the upper cover and the arms medallion on the lower, each ringed by his distich — the livery he gave presentation copies and books he valued (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 81) — and with the Chomutov college’s catalogue inscription of 1671 on the title. The volume never reached the Clementinum: it is at the Biblioteka Kórnicka (Cim.Qu.2812), whose record notes the supralibros and the arms plate and whose digitisation shows the volume. The one Prague copy of the Cracow edition of 1584 (Sign. 22 B 201) carries no mark of his. How the book went from Chomutov to Kórnik is not established.
open_questions: How the volume passed from the Chomutov college, which catalogued it in 1671, to Kórnik: the older shelfmarks ‘H. VI. 365.’ and ‘C: 157.’ on the pastedown and ‘hh: 310.’ on the flyleaf, and the red stamp ‘Z HANKOWYCH’ at the foot of the title, have not been identified, and the Kórnik record names no former owner. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 81) supposed that the Chomutov stock reached the Clementinum only in part; this is the first located volume that took another road.

entries.editorial_note: Norlind 1970, p. 349 (Zinner 2827; Hellman 55): listed among the books of the library because Tycho discusses the tract in the comet book (Opera omnia IV, 362); no copy, receipt or mark is recorded. Norlind’s introduction states the principle on which such tracts enter his catalogue: it may be regarded as fairly certain that nearly all the writings on the new star of 1572 and the comet of 1577 that Tycho reviews in the Progymnasmata and the comet book stood in the library on Hven (p. 335). An unbound tract of this kind, if Tycho’s copy survives, would carry no known mark by which it could be recognised.

entries.author_identified: Hipparchus (ed. Petrus Victorius), the copy annotated by Joseph Justus Scaliger
entries.title_transcribed: In Arati et Eudoxi Phaenomena libri III (the Greek editio princeps, with Scaliger’s annotations)
entries.subject: Astronomy

acquisition.channel: given by Scaliger — ‘pro utroque libro mihi tam benigne concesso’ and ‘libris mihi dono missis’ (Tycho to Scaliger, 17 April 1599, Opera omnia VIII 151): a gift, not a loan; the earlier ‘lent or given’ resolves (register dossier of 27 October 2026, §18)

entries.editorial_note: Hipparchus’s commentary on the Phaenomena of Aratus and Eudoxus in the Greek editio princeps of Petrus Victorius (Florence 1567), Scaliger’s own copy, annotated in his hand. Christiernus Johannis Ripensis, formerly in Tycho’s service on Hven, met Scaliger in Holland and reported that he owned the Greek text. Tycho asked in August 1598 for the book or for transcripts of the passages he needed (Opera omnia VIII, 102); Scaliger sent excerpts, acknowledged in March 1599 (Opera omnia VIII, 151); and in April 1599 Tycho thanked him for two books granted him (‘pro utroque autem libro mihi tam benigne concesso’), of which the Hipparchus is the one identified. Norlind (1970, p. 362) considers that the other may be the Cyclometrica elementa duo of 1594 with Scaliger’s dedication, now Sign. 14 A 59 (Prandtl A 42). That Tycho had the annotated book itself Kepler states to Herwart von Hohenburg in January 1603: Scaliger had once sent Tycho his Hipparchus with his own notes, and it was still in the possession of the heirs (Norlind 1970, p. 350, citing the letter as Caspar nr. 242, p. 354). On 16 November 1624 Kepler asked Tycho’s son Georg Brahe for ‘Hipparchum de fixis graecè, ist ein klains folium, vnd vil drinnen manu Scaligerj’ (KGW XIX, no. 7, pp. 202–203), so the annotated book was still with the heirs two years after Tengnagel’s death. Whether Kepler obtained it is not recorded, and no copy has been traced since.
open_questions: Where the Victorius Hipparchus of 1567 with Scaliger’s annotations went after November 1624, when it was last recorded with Tycho’s heirs; it has not been found.

norlind.entry: Hipparchus Bithynus: In Arati et Eudoxi Phænomena libri III. Eiusdem liber asterismorum. Achillis Statii in Arati Phænomena. Arati vita et fragmenta aliorum veterum in eius poëma. Florentiæ 1567.2°.
letters: Tycho till Scaliger mars 1599; VIII, 151 (in the continuation, printed p. 350)
Kepler till Herwart jan. 1603; Caspar nr 242, s. 354 (in the continuation, printed p. 350)
Kepler till Jörgen Brahe nov. 1624; Caspar till nr 242, s. 499 (in the continuation, printed p. 350)
Tycho till Scaliger aug. 1598; VIII, 102 (cited on printed p. 349)
Kepler till Herwart jan. 1603; Caspar nr 242, s. 354
Kepler till Jörgen Brahe nov. 1624; Caspar till nr 242, s. 499
norlind.ownership_verdict: owned: Scaliger sent Tycho his own annotated copy, attested by Kepler 1603 and 1624 as still with Tycho's heirs (argued in the continuation on printed p. 350); no present location
norlind.discussion: Ed. princeps, utg. av Petrus Victorius, av det enda originalverk vi äga av antikens store astronom. – Christiernus Johannis Ripensis, tidigare i Tychos tjänst på Hven, hade under en resa i Holland träffat Scaliger. Ripensis meddelade Tycho, att Scaliger ägde en bok på grekiska om Hipparchus' observationer, tryckt »för några år sedan» i Italien. Att härmed avses ovanstående verk är otvivelaktigt. Tycho ber Scaliger (aug. 1598; VIII, 102), att antingen skicka boken eller ock en avskrift av vissa partier. Varför Tycho var så intresserad av Hipparchus' skrift, beror på att de häri meddelade noggranna uppgifterna om den heliakiska uppgången resp. nedgången för vissa stjärnor samt observationerna av deras läge på himmelssfären, jämförda med sådana uppgifter från följande århundraden, voro viktiga för hans undersökningar av precessionen. Scaliger måste ha tillmötesgått det ena alternativet i Tychos anhållan, eftersom denne i mars 1599 (VIII, 151) tackar honom bl.a. för hans besvär med excerpering av vissa ställen hos såväl Hipparchus som Ptolemeus. Härav framgår alltså icke, att Tycho erhållit boken utan endast Scaligers excerpter ur densamma. Men från annat håll veta vi, att Tycho verkligen ägt ett exemplar av boken med Scaligers egenhändiga anteckningar. I jan. 1603 (Caspar nr 242, s. 354) skriver nämligen Kepler till Herwart, att Scaliger en gång skickade till Tycho Hipparchus' skrift med sina egenhändiga anteckningar och att den ännu befinner sig i Tychos arvingars ägo. Kepler har tydligen varit mycket intresserad av att förvärva exemplaret, ty så sent som i nov. 1624 (Caspar till nr 242, s. 499) skriver han till Tychos son Jörgen Brahe: »Sonderlich hett ich gern Hipparchum de fixis græce, ist ein klains folium, und vil drinnen manu Scaligeri.»

entries.subject: Astronomy (eclipse)
entries.editorial_note: Jöstel was Tycho’s collaborator in Prague, and the eclipse times in the tract were computed by Tycho’s lunar theory. Norlind: ‘Att Jöstelius’ skrift ingått i hans bibliotek är otvivelaktigt’ (that Jöstel’s tract entered his library is beyond doubt). The discrepancy at the eclipse of 31 January 1599 forced Tycho to revise his lunar theory, delaying the Progymnasmata.

S. 5–6 redogöres för hans världssystem och månteori. Det var den bristande överensstämmelsen mellan de beräknade och observerade tiderna för denna förmörkelse som tvang Tycho att omarbeta sin månteori, därmed fördröjande avslutandet av »Prog.». – Att Jœstelius' skrift ingått i hans bibliotek är otvivelaktigt.

marks.annotations: none known (the June positives are printed side-notes)
marks.binding: plain vellum, tie slits, no supralibros; labels 'T. Brahe 48' (front) and 'Tres. M 48' (back)

entries.editorial_note: A Prague imprint of 1606, five years after Tycho’s death, carrying ‘Ex Biblioth. Tijchoniana’, the Clementinum inscription of 1642 and the Tychonian shelf-mark ‘T.B. 27’; bound with it is Kepler’s De Jesu Christi servatoris nostri vero anno natalitio (Frankfurt 1606). Kukula, who published the volume in 1906–07 (no. VII), took the two tracts as proof that the family and Kepler kept the library together and added to it after 1601 and 1604; Prandtl (1932, p. 16) read it the same way — the heirs had apparently left the working library to Kepler, who carried it on for some years. The volume belongs to the Tychoniana as the Jesuits marked them, not to Tycho’s own library. Šolc 2006 (printed p. 192 (scan 6)) names the heirs' additions ‘for example’ as De Stella Nova in pede Serpentarii and De stella tertii honoris in Cygno (both Prague 1606) and the Frankfurt ‘pars altera’ of 1606 — the two Prague titles one book, the Frankfurt piece the De Jesu Christi … vero anno natalitio bound with it here, the identification being the house's — and has them given to the Clementinum Jesuits together with the harder-to-sell, predominantly astronomical part of the library.

entries.title_transcribed: Prodromus dissertationum cosmographicarum (Mysterium cosmographicum)
entries.subject: Astronomy (cosmology)
entries.editorial_note: Kepler to Tycho, Graz, 13 December 1597 (Opera omnia VIII, 14–15), sent no copy of the Mysterium cosmographicum (Tübingen 1596), supposing that Tycho already had one: ‘Exemplaria non dubito, quin antea habeas: quare facile patior, ut difficultas transmittendi per tantum intervallum a mittendo me avocet’. Tycho to Kepler, Wandsbek, 1 April 1598 (Opera omnia VIII, 44), replied that he had seen and read the book before: ‘Librum tuum, quem Prodromum vocas Dissertationum Cosmographicarum, iam ante videram et … perlegeram’. So already Norlind 1970, p. 350. How and when his copy reached him is not recorded; no copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified.
open_questions: How and when Tycho’s copy of the Mysterium cosmographicum reached him, and whether it survives: Kepler sent none, and Tycho had read the book before April 1598; a copy bearing his marks, or a passage in the correspondence naming the sender, would decide.

norlind.entry: Kepler, Johannes: Prodromus dissertationum, continens mysterium cosmographicum. Tubingæ 1596.4°. Z. 3664.
letters: Kepler till Tycho dec. 1597 (Keplers första brev); VIII, 14
Tycho till Kepler från Wandsbek april 1598; VIII, 44
norlind.ownership_verdict: owned: Tycho already had the book before Kepler's first letter and had read it (his reply of April 1598); no dedication copy at first; no copy located
norlind.discussion: Keplers berömda ungdomsverk. – Egendomligt är, att Tycho åtminstone icke till att börja med fick något dedikationsexemplar. Kepler skriver nämligen i sitt första brev till Tycho (dec. 1597; VIII, 14), att han förmodar, att Tycho redan förut äger boken; därför skickar han icke något exemplar. Tycho svarar från Wandsbek i april 1598 (VIII, 44), att han fick brevet från Helmstedt. Boken hade han förut och han hade tagit del av densamma. Tychos brev innehåller många lovord över boken. Jfr s. 199 ff.

entries.title_transcribed: Observationes aliquot Eclipsium Solis et Lunae per Joh. Krabbe, mathematicum ducis H. Julii factae
entries.subject: Astronomy (observations)

acquisition.channel: procured through Georg Rollenhagen in Magdeburg at Tycho's request of April 1600 (Opera omnia VIII, p. 295)

entries.editorial_note: Not a book: a single manuscript leaf of another astronomer’s eclipse observations, obtained by Tycho, annotated in his hand and kept among his own observation books. In April 1600 Tycho asked Georg Rollenhagen in Magdeburg to procure the eclipse observations that Johannes Krabbe, since 1585 mathematician to Duke Heinrich Julius of Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel, was said to have made, together with the method by which the times had been taken, so that a comparison with his own observations would give the difference in meridian between the observing places (Tycho to Rollenhagen, April 1600; Opera omnia VIII, 295). The leaf arrived. Headed ‘Observationes aliquot Eclipsium Solis et Lunae per Joh. Krabbe, mathematicum ducis H. Julii factae’, it records seven lunar and six solar eclipses of 1581–1600 observed at Helmstedt, Berlin, Braunschweig, Wolfenbüttel and Gröningen near Halberstadt, the times as a rule derived from star altitudes; the solar eclipse of September 1595 could not be observed. The last observation is dated 30 June 1600, so the leaf reached Tycho after that date. In the margin Tycho wrote the mean times for Krabbe’s observations and for his own. Dreyer did not print the leaf in the Opera omnia; his commentary records it as sewn among Tycho’s observations of 1600–1601 in the Royal Library’s codex GKS 318 2°, which his edition numbers codex I, with Tycho’s annotations (Opera omnia VIII, 438, note to p. 295 line 2), and Norlind describes it from the codex (Norlind 1970, p. 351). It is entered because Norlind’s list of Tycho’s books includes the manuscripts he is known to have possessed, and because the leaf is a text by another author that Tycho acquired, owned and annotated; the observation codices themselves, being Tycho’s own writing, are not entries.
open_questions: On which folio of GKS 318 2° the leaf is sewn: Dreyer’s commentary gives fol. 157, Norlind fol. 159; the codex itself would decide.

norlind.entry: Krabbe, Johannes: [Manuskript med observationer.]
surviving_copy_locations: Gl. kgl. S. 2° 318, fol. 159r (a leaf among Tycho's own observations; Norlind prints only the shelfmark, i.e. Köpenhamn, KB, Gammel kongelig Samling)
ownership_inscriptions: Observationes aliquot Eclipsium Solis et Lunæ per Joh. Krabbe, mathematicum ducis H. Julii factæ
letters: till Rollenhagen i Magdeburg april 1600; VIII, 295
norlind.ownership_verdict: received (some time after 30 June 1600) through Rollenhagen; the leaf survives among Tycho's own observations with Tycho's autograph annotations; not printed by Dreyer
norlind.discussion: I april 1600 (VIII, 295) skriver Tycho till Rollenhagen i Magdeburg, att han fått veta, att Krabbe (som sedan 1585 var astronom hos hertigen av Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel) anställt noggranna observationer av sol- och månförmörkelser. Tycho ber Rollenhagen skaffa honom detta observationsmaterial. Det räcker emellertid inte endast med vederbörliga observationsresultat utan han måste också få veta på vad sätt dessa resultat erhållits (om genom stjärnhöjder eller på annat sätt). Anledningen till att Tycho önskade alla dessa uppgifter var, att han ur en jämförelse mellan Krabbes och sina egna observationer ville bestämma meridianskillnaden mellan de båda observationsorterna. Rollenhagen har tydligen lyckats skaffa materialet, eftersom det nu befinner sig på ett blad bland Tychos egna observationer (Gl. kgl. S. 2° 318, fol. 159r). Det är icke utg. av Dreyer. Under rubriken »Observationes aliquot Eclipsium Solis et Lunæ per Joh. Krabbe, mathematicum ducis H. Julii factæ» upptagas 7 månförmörkelser och 6 solförmörkelser (den ena i sept. 1595 kunde dock icke iakttagas) för tiden 1581–1600. Tycho har gjort egenhändiga anteckningar i manuskriptet. Den sista observerade förmörkelsen är för d. 30 juni 1600; någon gång efter detta datum har Tycho således mottagit materialet. Observationsorten är icke en och densamma, utan olika (Helmstedt, Berlin, Braunschweig, Wolfenbüttel och Gröningen, vid Halberstadt). Tiderna ha i regel bestämts ur stjärnhöjder. I margen har vidare Tycho antecknat medierna dels för Krabbes tider dels för sina egna.

entries.editorial_note: Norlind 1970, p. 351 (Zinner 2632), lists the tract among the books of the library because Tycho discusses it in the Progymnasmata (Opera omnia III, 218–225); no copy, receipt or mark is recorded. Norlind’s introduction states the principle on which such tracts enter his catalogue: it may be regarded as fairly certain that nearly all the writings on the new star of 1572 and the comet of 1577 that Tycho reviews in the Progymnasmata and the comet book stood in the library on Hven (p. 335). The edition Tycho discusses is the Lauingen edition, not the reprint De nova stella iudicia … Leovitii et Gemmae (s. l. 1573, Zinner 2633). As an unbound tract, Tycho’s copy would carry no known mark by which it could be recognised, and none has been identified.

entries.title_transcribed: [Themata]
entries.subject: Astronomy (world-system)
entries.editorial_note: Norlind: ‘Tycho har ägt ett exemplar, ty han citerar’ — Tycho owned a copy, since he cites its proposition 2 in a letter to Cramer of September 1599 (Opera omnia VIII, 185), where Liddel, in a section ‘Parerga mathematica’, names Tycho in connection with the new world-system in terms that leave the reader unsure whether Tycho was its author. Title and imprint are Norlind’s conjecture, bracketed by him and unverified (‘Omöjlig att belägga’); the tract is not the Themata de melancholia (Helmstedt 1596) that P. J. Anderson’s Liddel bibliography (1910) lists as no. 4, and Anderson did not know it.
open_questions: Which tract carried the ‘Parerga mathematica’ Tycho cites, and whether its wording claimed the geoheliocentric system for Liddel, as Tycho suspected (to Cramer, September 1599, Opera omnia VIII, 185; Norlind 1970, pp. 351 and 355).

norlind.entry: Liddelius, Duncanus: [Themata. Helmæstadii 1595.]
norlind.ownership_verdict: owned — Tycho cites proposition 2 of the piece in a letter to Cramer, Sept. 1599; the print itself cannot be traced (omöjlig att belägga) and is not Anderson's no. 4 (Themata de melancholia, 1596)
norlind.discussion: Omöjlig att belägga. – Liddel, som var född i Aberdeen, blev 1591 professor i Helmstedt men återvände 1607 till sin fädernestad. – Tycho har ägt ett exemplar, ty han citerar i ett brev till Cramer sept. 1599 (VIII, 185) proposition 2 i skriften, där Liddel i »Parerga mathematica» visserligen nämner Tychos namn i förbindelse med det nya världssystemet men på ett sådant sätt, att läsaren ej får klart för sig, om Tycho är den verklige upphovsmannen till detsamma. – P. J. Anderson, »Duncan Liddel», Aberdeen 1910, känner icke till ovannämnda skrift av Liddel. Den skrift som Anderson anför som nr 4 i sin förteckning: »Themata de melancholia», Helmæstadii 1596,4°, är icke den, varpå Tycho syftar. En annan skrift av Liddel, också okänd för Anderson, är »Disputatio de elementis», Helmæstadii 1596. Se s. 400.

entries.subject: Medicine

acquisition.channel: bought as a student — if the cipher is Tycho’s (ownership C): the pigskin binding of the volume is blind-stamped ‘T. B. 1560’ and the Bayrus bound first in it is printed in 1560 (Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 47; Christianson 1967, pp. 200–201); no inscription, annotation or Jesuit note of 1642 supports it

entries.editorial_note:
Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 47:3; Norlind 1970, p. 352; the library’s record 18 J 318/adl.2. The third piece of the volume in the ‘T. B. 1560’ binding. The ‘T. B. 1560’ volume is the earliest dated binding of Tycho’s and, while the purchase note of the Ptolemy 5 B 70 is disputed, the earliest book securely his (Christianson 1967, pp. 200–201: ‘two of his own “textbooks”’).

Ownership graded B on 28 October 2026: the attribution rests on the blind-stamped cipher T·B and the year 1560 on the binding alone — no inscription, no annotation, no 1642 or Chomutov mark, and Kleinschnitzová 1933 gives no argument. The cipher is consistent with Tycho's documented series of initial-and-year bindings 1561–1583 (Helsingør 1561, Uppsala 1563, Strahov and 10 G 47 1567, T.B.O. 1576–1583) and the contents fit the Copenhagen curriculum of 1560, but T·B alone identifies no one. The NK ČR photographs requested on 28 October 2026 (the three edges, both boards, the three title pages at 600 dpi) and an EBDB identification of the panel stamps are the tests.

Reviewed again on 29 October 2026, the literature pack read whole: ownership graded C (was B). Beyond the cipher the literature holds nothing — no inscription, no annotation, no hand, no note of 1642. Kleinschnitzová (1933, pp. 76–78) herself sets the volume outside the twenty-three Clementinum volumes that carry the note of 1642 and says it ‘verirrt sich’, strayed, into the Jesuit professed house on the Malá Strana — an explanation that assumes what it should show; Norlind’s ‘T. B. O. 1560’ (1970, p. 339) reads a letter the board does not carry; the library’s record gives Tycho the year 1567 in its former-owner field without a basis; Šolc (1999, 2006, 2018), Christianson (1967, 2020), Thoren and Pařez all derive from Kleinschnitzová. If the cipher is Tycho’s, the year 1560 places the binding before his departure from Denmark; whether it is Tycho’s is the whole question, and the National Library’s photographs are the test. Decided on 29 October 2026.

entries.title_transcribed: Demonstratio astronomica loci stellae novae (in Frischlin, Consideratio novae stellae, Tübingen 1573)
entries.subject: Astronomy (nova)
entries.editorial_note: Tycho reprinted Maestlin’s tract in full in the Progymnasmata (Opera omnia III, 58–67) and praised it (‘liten till omfånget men till innehållet mera betydande’). Reprinting the tract in full implies that the Frischlin volume containing it was in Tycho’s hands, but Norlind frames the passage as discussion rather than ownership, and the attestation is accordingly graded C. There is no documented receipt, no inventory entry, and no copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified.
open_questions: Whether the Swedish words ‘liten till omfånget men till innehållet mera betydande’, given as Tycho’s praise of the tract, are Norlind’s own wording or his rendering of a passage of Tycho’s; Norlind’s page and the Progymnasmata passage (Opera omnia III, 58–67) would decide.

Ingår på s. 27–32 i: Frischlin, Nicodemus: Consideratio novæ stellæ ... Tubingæ 1573.4°. Z. 2622.
Tycho har avtryckt den lilla skriften helt i »Prog.» (III, 58–67), där han också diskuterar den; den är, skriver han, liten till omfånget men till innehållet mera betydande och gedigen än de flesta större avhandlingar i ämnet. Dock nämner han ej, att den ingår i Frischlins verk.

entries.subject: Prophecy/History

acquisition.channel: commissioned copy

entries.editorial_note: Herwart had the Revelatio ascribed to Methodius transcribed for Tycho because the volume that contained it was too bulky to send, and despatched the copy from Munich with the Alphonsine tables (Herwart to Tycho, 10 December 1600; Opera omnia VIII, 393: ‘METHODIJ uti fertur Revelationem, quam describi curavi, cum liber, cui inserta fuerat, ob molem transferri nequeat’). The transcript is not among the Clementinum volumes and has not been identified at the Royal Library, Copenhagen, or the Austrian National Library; the text survives in many copies, and a transcript without Tycho’s own mark cannot be told from them. Status lost since 20 October 2026: a unique transcript made for Tycho and sent, not a mass-survival text.

entries.title_transcribed: Observatio und Beschreibung der newen Cometen, so 1572 und noch in diesem 73. Jar erschienen
entries.subject: Astronomy (nova 1572)
entries.editorial_note: Norlind 1970, p. 355 (Zinner 2637), lists the tract among the books of the library because Tycho discusses it in the Progymnasmata (Opera omnia III, 263–279); no copy, receipt or mark is recorded. Norlind’s introduction states the principle on which such tracts enter his catalogue: it may be regarded as fairly certain that nearly all the writings on the new star of 1572 and the comet of 1577 that Tycho reviews in the Progymnasmata and the comet book stood in the library on Hven (p. 335). As an unbound tract, Tycho’s copy would carry no known mark by which it could be recognised, and none has been identified.
