entries.title_transcribed: De crepusculis liber unus (with Alhazen, De causis crepusculorum)
entries.subject: Optics/Astronomy
entries.editorial_note: Norlind: ‘sannolikt denna första upplaga Tycho ägt’ — Tycho probably owned this first edition (1542), the work in which the ‘nonius’ auxiliary scale is described; in the comet book Tycho calls it ‘Libello de crepusculis dudum edito’ (Opera omnia IV, 327). The ownership is Norlind’s inference from Tycho’s discussion of the nonius scale; no receipt and no inventory record it, and no copy bearing Tycho’s marks has been identified. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).

norlind.entry: Nonius, Petrus: De crepusculis liber unus ... Item Allacen Arabis ... De causis crepusculorum liber unus ... Olyssipone 1542. 4°.
norlind.ownership_verdict: probably owned, this first edition (Lisbon 1542) — inferred from Tycho's wording »Libello de crepusculis dudum edito» in the comet book
norlind.discussion: Nonius' skrift innehåller fol. e3v i proposition 3 beskrivning över en av honom uppfunnen hjälpskala (»nonie») för uppnående av större noggrannhet vid observationer av stjärnhöjder. – Det är sannolikt denna första upplaga Tycho ägt (en senare upplaga utkom i Coimbra 1573 och skriften trycktes ibland tillsammans med andra skrifter av Nonius). Härför talar, att han i kometboken (IV, 327) nämner den som »Libello de crepusculis dudum edito». Skriften omfattar endast ett 70-tal blad och kan alltså rubriceras som en »libellus» och »dudum edito», »för länge sedan utgiven», passar bra med första upplagan.

entries.title_transcribed: De divina astrorum facultate in larvatam astrologiam
entries.subject: Astronomy/Astrology/Mathematics

acquisition.channel: received from Hagecius at their meeting at Regensburg in November 1575 (Opera omnia VII, 184; II, 421)

entries.editorial_note: Norlind 1970, p. 355: Tycho received a copy of the printed book from Hagecius at their meeting at Regensburg in November 1575 (Opera omnia VII, 184; II, 421) and was particularly taken with its section on the planets’ influence at their varying distances from the earth; in May 1588 he wrote to Hagecius that he could no longer find the book in his library and asked him to procure another copy (VII, 121; Hagecius’s answers of November 1588 and May 1589, VII, 147 and 184). A book that left the library, or was mislaid in it, in Tycho’s own lifetime. Norlind adds that a copy stood in Queen Christina’s library which he could not find among the Reginenses in the Vatican — a lead he did not pursue, and one worth the question, since books from Prague reached her library in 1648. The store's separate entry for ‘Francius, De astris’ (the Regensburg gift of 1575, lost by 1589) was this book: Hagecius describes the book he gave as ‘librum … de astris … IO. FRANCI, Parisijs impressum, et Reginae Galliae dedicatum’ (20 May 1589, Opera omnia VII 184), ‘Io. Franci’ being Iofrancus, Offusius's given name; Tycho's account of its content (3 May 1588, VII 120–121) fits Offusius, and Norlind (p. 355) already read it so. The two entries were
open_questions: Whether Hagecius sent the second copy Tycho asked for in 1588; and whether the Offusius Norlind records in Queen Christina’s library, unfound among the Reginenses, is a copy from Prague (Norlind 1970, p. 355).

norlind.entry: Offusius, Iofrancus: De divina astrorum facultate in larvatam astrologiam ... Parisiis 1570. 4°.
letters: Hagecius till Tycho nov. 1588 (»brev nov. s.å.»); VII, 147
norlind.ownership_verdict: owned — received from Hagecius at their meeting in Regensburg Nov. 1575; by May 1588 Tycho could no longer find it in his library and asked Hagecius for another copy
norlind.discussion: Förordet är dat. d. 8 jan. 1556, men verket trycktes först 14 år senare. I Turin fanns före branden 1904 två manuskriptexemplar av verket (Thorndike, 6, s. 109²⁰). Ett exemplar fanns i drottning Kristinas bibliotek men kunde ej återfinnas av mig bland Reginenses i Vatikanbiblioteket. – Tycho erhöll ett exemplar av den tryckta boken genom Hagecius vid deras sammanträffande i Regensburg nov. 1575 (VII, 184, II, 421). Han var särskilt intresserad av det avsnitt som behandlade planeternas inverkan på jorden på olika avstånd från denna. Härom skriver han till Hagecius i maj 1588 (VII, 121). Han säger vidare, att han nu inte längre kan finna boken i sitt bibliotek och han ber Hagecius skaffa ett annat exemplar. Denne synes först inte ha vetat vad det gällde för bok (brev nov. s.å.; VII, 147); hans efterforskningar efter denna i biblioteken i Prag hade ej lett till något resultat. I ett senare brev maj 1589 (VII, 184) skriver han emellertid, att han nu minns, vilken bok det varit.

entries.title_transcribed: Thesaurus linguae sanctae
entries.subject: Hebrew lexicography
entries.editorial_note: Norlind (p. 356) holds that Tycho probably owned some edition (‘Någon upplaga har väl ägts av Tycho, som citerar Pagninus’), since Tycho cites Pagninus in biblical exegesis in a letter to Peucer of 1590 (Tycho to Peucer, 1590; Opera omnia VII, 234); Norlind takes the citation to suggest that Tycho had some Hebrew. The ownership rests on this inference, which Norlind himself phrases weakly; the edition is undetermined, and no copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified.

entries.title_transcribed: Commentationes in integra Biblia (manuscript)
entries.subject: Theology/Alchemy
entries.editorial_note: The only authority is Joachim Morsius, who in 1625 — in the dedication to the pseudo-Paracelsian lion-prophecy — reported on Cort Aslakssøn’s word that Tycho had owned a copy, and who further supposed that the manuscript was by then in Prague with Tycho’s heirs. Norlind relays both. No inventory and no Clementinum catalogue records it, and no copy has been identified: the ownership is attested at second hand only and remains unverified. Status attested, not located, since 20 October 2026: no one contests the ownership — Norlind relays only Morsius's report — so the Definitions' 'disputed' does not fit.

norlind.entry: Paracelsus, Theophrastus: Commentationes in integra Biblia. [Manuskript.]
norlind.ownership_verdict: reported owned (manuscript) on Joachim Morsius's 1625 testimony citing Cort Aslakssøn; Morsius conjectured it was with Tycho's heirs in Prague; no copy located
norlind.discussion: Enligt Cort Aslakssön skall Tycho ha ägt ett exemplar. Rosenkreutzaren Joachim Morsius, från vilken denna uppgift härrör (i dedikationen till den pseudoparacelsiska lejonprofetian, tryckt 1625, se Nordström i: »Samlaren» 1934, s. 36 f.), förmodar, att detta manuskript nu förvaras i Prag hos Tychos arvingar. Paracelsus' inflytande på Tycho har varit betydande bl.a. i kemi och medicin såsom framgår av brevsamlingen och även annorstädes. Se t.ex. Dreyer, s. XI och registret, S. Lindroth, »Paracelsismen i Sverige», Upps. & Sthm 1943, s. 68, not 9.

entries.title_transcribed: Nova de universis philosophia
entries.subject: Natural philosophy
entries.editorial_note: Norlind (1970, p. 356): ‘Ett exemplar har Tycho säkerligen ägt’ — of either the Ferrara edition of 1591 or the Venice edition of 1593, perhaps the later. His basis is a note in Tycho’s hand in the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences copy of the Progymnasmata (p. 165), naming Patritius among the authors whose writings reached him only after the chapters they belonged to were printed. Tycho complained to Kepler that Patrizi misrepresented his world-system (Tycho to Kepler, December 1599, Opera omnia VIII, 206). The only surviving evidence of Tycho’s ownership is that annotation in his own Progymnasmata, not a mark in a copy of Patrizi; the work is common, and no copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified.
open_questions: Which edition Tycho owned, the Ferrara folio of 1591 or the Venice issue of 1593: Norlind (1970, p. 356) inclines to the later on the strength of Tycho’s note in the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences copy of the Progymnasmata (p. 165), which names Patritius among the authors whose writings reached him only after the chapters they belonged to were printed.

norlind.entry: Patritius, Franciscus: Nova de universis philosophia. 2°.
norlind.ownership_verdict: certainly owned, edition uncertain (Ferrara 1591 or Venice 1593, perhaps the latter, judging from Tycho's note in the KVA copy of the Progymnasmata); no copy located
norlind.discussion: Ett exemplar har Tycho säkerligen ägt av endera upplagan Ferrara 1591 eller Venedig 1593 (kanske den senare att döma av en hans anteckning i KVA:s exemplar av »Prog.», se ovan s. 165). Till Kepler skriver han i dec. 1599 (VIII, 206), att Patritius i sin bok lämnat en helt vilseledande framställning av Tychos världssystem. Tycho menar väl vad Patritius skriver fol. 91ʳ (=Pancosmia, liber XII), att enligt Tychos världssystem skulle Merkurius' och Venus' banor skära solbanan i två punkter. Enligt Tychos framställning i kometboken var det dock endast Mars-banan som skar solbanan.

dispersal.detail: Sächsische Landesbibliothek Dresden; reported by the library as lost in the Second World War (Norlind 1970, p. 356).

entries.editorial_note: A book by another author that Tycho owned (Paulus Alexandrinus, edited from Heinrich Rantzau’s library, Wittenberg 1588), in its original Tychonic binding. Reported by Isak Collijn to Flora Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 78 n. 1) as a Tychonianum in the Landesbibliothek Dresden, the companion to the Waldstein (Mnichovo Hradiště) copy of Tycho’s own De nova stella, which, as a copy of one of Tycho’s own works, lies outside this library. The volume is lost: Norlind (1970, p. 356) records the Dresden library’s own communication that the copy ‘gått förlorat under senaste världskrig’ — was lost in the Second World War. Šolc still lists the volume in Dresden — ‘befand sich … in der Sächsischen Landesbibliothek Dresden’ (1999, § 2.533, printed p. 150) and, in the present tense, ‘se nachází v Zemské knihovně v Drážďanech’ (2006, p. 192) — and nowhere mentions the loss Norlind reports from the library itself; neither text cites a sighting. The entry keeps ‘lost’ on Norlind's report; a question to the SLUB (its war-loss records, and whether a Paulus Alexandrinus, Wittenberg 1588, in a Tychonic binding has since been acquired) would close it. Falkenstein's description of the Dresden library (1839, pp. 574–575; quoted by Šolc 2018, pp. 194 and 201–202) shows what the volume was: a Sammelband of three works — this Paulus Alexandrinus first, then Rantzau's own Horoscopographia (Wittenberg 1588, 4°) and Michael Boiemus's Historia de somniis (Wittenberg 1587, 4°) — in a parchment binding with Tycho's portrait stamp on the front board (‘Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei. Pulchrius eniteat quae latet interior’) and his arms on the back, and on the flyleaf two distichs by a M. Johannes Schmidt sending the book to a nobleman he addresses as Smil (‘Promissum transmitto librum, Doctissime Smile, / Invenies, legito, quae Tibi forte placent, / Somnia pars narrat, sed somnia vera loquuntur / Interdum. Ast illis credere multa cave. — Generositatis tuae officioss. M. Johannes Schmidt’; read on the page image 29 October 2026 — the OCR's ‘Praemissum’ and the elided name corrected). The address is to a Smil, not to Tycho: Schmidt's leaf and Tycho's portrait binding are the two facts recorded on the object, and no source reconciles them. Šolc presents the Boiemus as a further Dresden volume; Falkenstein's ‘Daran:’ makes it the third piece of this one. The loss of 1945 therefore covers all three works, which this library enters as the two bound companions. The SLUB's war-loss register carries a card for the Boiemus — Lit.Graec.B.1976, earlier ‘Phil. gr. B. 93a. Misc. 3’, and ‘Misc. 3’ matches Falkenstein's order, in which the Boiemus is the third piece; no card was found under the other two headings, and the register does not say whether the volume was removed in 1945–46 or destroyed (Nachweiskatalog image 00504111, read 27 October 2026; the identification with the Tycho volume is inference, C). The whole literature on the volume was read on 29 October 2026 (the volumelit table, nine passages): the attribution is Collijn's, printed by Kleinschnitzová in 1933 on the binding alone and naming only the Paulus; Mortensen 1955 (p. 28, the ‘two books’ Collijn reported, no title), Norlind 1970 and Šolc 1999, 2006 and 2018 repeat her — Šolc copying her misprint ‘natalatiis’ in all three, writing ‘leather bindings’ in 2006 where Falkenstein has a parchment binding, and in 2018 counting the one volume as two (the Paulus–Rantzau pair on p. 194, the Boiemus as ‘ein weiteres Tychonisches Buch’ on p. 201) while omitting the verses. Falkenstein himself, the only writer who had the volume in hand, makes no statement about Tycho's library; nobody after 1839 reports seeing it. The Rantzau literature (Oestmann 2004, Zeeberg, Lohmeier 2000, Ilsøe 2005) and the Tycho biographies name the editions, not this copy.

open_questions: Who ‘Smil’ (Falkenstein's ‘Doctissime Smile’, addressed ‘Generositatis tuae’) and M. Johannes Schmidt were, and how a volume Schmidt sent to a Smil came to carry Tycho's portrait binding. The name is Bohemian/Moravian; a book-collecting Moravian nobleman of the right years, Smil Osovský z Doubravice (1548–1613), is a lead from the name alone, unverified, not an identification.

entries.title_transcribed: De cometis qui antea visi sunt et de eo qui ... Novembri apparuit, narratio
entries.subject: Astronomy (comet)
entries.editorial_note: Tycho treats the work at length in the comet book (Opera omnia IV, 356–358; cf. Progymnasmata, Opera omnia III, 153–157). Thorndike (History of Magic and Experimental Science VI, p. 84) held that neither Tycho nor Hagecius owned a copy. Norlind shows that Thorndike misread the three passages of the correspondence on which he relied (Opera omnia VII, 120, 147 and 212), which concern Apianus and Pena and not this book, and so defends Tycho’s ownership against Thorndike’s denial. The Czech National Library holds the work as the fourth tract of a Hagecius composite volume from the Jesuit college at Chomutov; its record notes no mark of Tycho’s.

entries.title_transcribed: Almagest (old Venetian edition, c. 1515)
entries.subject: Astronomy
entries.editorial_note: Tycho states that he owns an old Venetian Almagest, some seventy years old in 1587 (letter of 20 January 1587: ‘vetus quoddam exemplar Almagesti, ante annos proxime 70. Venetijs editum’), that is, the Latin Almagest printed at Venice by Petrus Liechtenstein in about 1515. It is distinct from the Ptolemy volumes among the Clementinum copies — the Opera (Basel), the Geographia (Cologne 1597) and the De analemmate (Rome 1562). Norlind identified the edition in print (Fund og Forskning XII, 1965, p. 156, ‘Efterslæt’): the Latin Almagest printed at Venice in 1515 (Petrus Liechtenstein; Gerard of Cremona’s version), whose prefatory life of Ptolemy — ‘indledningen til en oversættelse af Almagesten, trykt i Venedig 1515, som Tycho Brahe har ejet og nævner i et brev’ — is the source of the royal descent and the physical description of Ptolemy in Tycho’s elegy In effigiem Cl. Ptolemaei (Epistolae astronomicae, 1596, p. 239). No copy of the Venice Almagest with Tycho’s marks has been identified. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).
open_questions: Whether a copy of the Venice Almagest of 1515 with Tycho’s marks survives; such a copy coming to light would decide.

entries.editorial_note: Prandtl Verzeichnis A no. 31; Kleinschnitzová no. 4; National Library of the Czech Republic (Clementinum), shelfmark 5 B 70, bound as Band I. Friis (1868–69, p. 267) and Dreyer (1890, p. 14) read the title-page note «emptus Haffniae 2 Joachimicis 1560 ultimo Novembris» (bought at Copenhagen for two Joachimsthaler on the last day of November 1560) as Tycho’s own hand, and Dreyer made this the first book of the library, procured after the predicted eclipse of 21 August 1560. The same title page carries the name of Johannes Pratensis (1543–1576) and the binding his stamped initials «I P 1561»: Studnička (1901, p. 39) took Pratensis for the seller; Boldan & Vackářová (2024, pp. 143–144) take him for the first owner and suppose the book passed to Tycho from his estate. The hand of the note has not been examined. Norlind (1970, p. 358) took the ‘Ptolemaeum Tychonis’ that Benjamin Ursinus asked Kepler to request from the Rožmberk librarian (March 1614; Caspar no. 681, p. 105) to be this copy, and found the work entered in Václav Březan’s catalogue of Peter Vok of Rožmberk’s library at Třeboň, drawn up 1602–08 and now in the Royal Library, Stockholm. The copy survives, is digitised, and carries an early note beside the 1642 inscription that the marginalia are Tycho’s. Šolc (2006, printed p. 190 (scan 4)), explaining how the Ptolemy came from Pratensis ‘by 1576 at the latest, after the friend's death’, has Tycho visit him often and observe at his house ‘for example on 3 December 1573’ the lunar eclipse whose beginning and course he had computed from the Prutenic tables to within 20 minutes. Tycho's own observation note places that eclipse on 8 December 1573 at Knutstorp (‘Hanc ego Eclipsin in curia mea Knusdorpiana observavi’, TBOO X, 38–39), with the new gilt-brass quadrant and his sister Sophie's help (the loci record of the Knutstorp years); Šolc's date and place are not adopted, and the visit is not evidence for when the book passed to Tycho. Christianson (1967, p. 201 n. 13) wrote that the volume ‘has now been shown to have belonged to Johannes Pratensis, from whom Tycho probably inherited it in 1576’, and printed a note in Dreyer’s hand (Royal Library, NKS 3077 4°, p. 101) recording Friis’s later opinion that the marginalia are few, insignificant and Pratensis’s. The title page is image 3 of the Manuscriptorium facsimile. The hands were compared on the facsimile on 25 October 2026: the purchase note is not shown to be Tycho’s (the capital I without his J-descender, the final s at x-height) and not shown to be Pratensis’s (the h built on different limbs, the minims), every pair inconclusive at the facsimile’s resolution; the marginalia share Tycho’s u-marks and looped g but use a German-cursive e, final s and final i that his secure hands show nowhere, and lean away from him. Reviewed on 29 October 2026 in the lecture session, the six student volumes read through their literature packs: no positive evidence makes the volume Tycho’s before he left Denmark on 14 February 1562. The reading of the purchase note as his own hand began with Friis (1868–69) and Dreyer (1890) and was repeated without a comparison by Prusík (1901), Studnička (1901), Kukula (1906), Prandtl (1932) and Šolc (1999); Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 74) saw that a binding stamped for Pratensis in 1561 contradicts a purchase by Tycho in 1560 and called Studnička’s binder’s error improbable; Šolc (2006, 2018) and Boldan & Vackářová (2024) make Pratensis the purchaser and first owner; the National Library’s own record gives Pratensis the year 1561 and Tycho none; and the comparison of 25 October 2026 found nothing in the note that points to Tycho. The volume is carried from today as Pratensis’s purchase of 30 November 1560, bound for him in 1561, and Tycho’s later — not before 1561, probably after Pratensis’s death on 1 June 1576 — on the Jesuit note of 1642 that the marginalia are Tycho’s and on the college’s acquisition from his heirs; ownership graded B (was A), and the ‘first book’ of Dreyer’s account withdrawn. Decided on 29 October 2026.

entries.title_transcribed: Arithmeticae libri duo, geometriae septem et viginti
entries.subject: Mathematics (arithmetic, geometry)

marks.inscription: No Jesuit inscription. Title leaf: in ink beside the printer's device, ‘G: Crusio ‹K› / inservio.’ — the ownership formula of Gabriel Crusius, as on the National Library's 5 G 92 (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 89) — and the two round Strahov stamps (read on the volume, 18 September 2026).
marks.annotations: One reader's note seen: p. 7, cap. V De divisione, ‘Divisio igitur’ underlined and ‘Analogia divisionis & multiplicationis’ in the margin; hand not assessed.
marks.binding: gilt portrait supralibros on the front board (bust in cloak and ruff, the Order of the Elephant on a long chain; legend HIC PATET EXTERIOR TYCHONIS FORMA BRAHEI PVLCHRIVS ENITEAT QVAE LATET INTERIOR) and the arms supralibros on the back (ARMA GENVS FVNDI PEREVNT DVRABILE VIRTVS ET DOCTRINAE DECVS NOBILITATIS HABENT), each 76 × 59 mm, on a binding of gilt-tooled brown calf over boards — not the parchment Pařez 2009 (with photographs) reports — Katalog Tritius: ‘vazba se zlacenou podobou Tychona de Brahe’

dispersal.detail: Route to Strahov undocumented beyond the Crusius layer: no Jesuit inscription, no Klauser ex-libris photographed, no later owner named in the catalogue. The same collector's other volumes went to the Chomutov Jesuits (1654) and, in the Euclid's case, to Klauser.

entries.editorial_note: One of the two Strahov volumes with the full-size portrait/arms supralibros (Pařez 2009); the other, the Opus palatinum Σ V 5/a, is bound in parchment, this one in gilt-tooled brown calf. Books carrying this plaque were printed 1584–1598 (Norlind) — this 1580 imprint sits at the lower edge, and Pařez leaves open whether the plaques were applied as the books came or in one campaign after 1598. The title inscription ‘G: Crusio ‹K› / inservio.’ is Gabriel Crusius's — the same hand and formula as on 5 G 92 (compared 19 September 2026 on the digitised leaf) — which ties this volume to the Euclid AV II 2 and to the two Chomutov gifts of 1654.
open_questions: The endleaves and spine for a Klauser ex-libris, Strnad's name or a Mathematical-Museum spine — the volume's last step into Strahov.

entries.title_transcribed: Horoscopographia, sive de inveniendo stellarum situ astrologia
entries.subject: Astrology

marks.binding: the volume's binding (the Paulus Alexandrinus entry)

dispersal.detail: Sächsische Landesbibliothek Dresden, in the Sammelband with the Paulus Alexandrinus; reported by the library as lost in the Second World War (Norlind 1970, p. 356).

entries.editorial_note: Heinrich Rantzau's Horoscopographia (Wittenberg 1588, 4°), bound after the Paulus Alexandrinus in the Dresden Sammelband that Falkenstein described in 1839 (pp. 574–575: ‘Daran: Henrici Rancovii (v. Ranzau) Horoscopographia, Wit. 1588. 4.’) — the volume in Tycho's portrait-and-arms parchment binding that Collijn reported to Kleinschnitzová and that the Dresden library reported lost in the Second World War (Norlind 1970, p. 356). Rantzau's book of the same year as the Paulus edited from his library, in the same binding: a pair that reached Tycho together, by gift or purchase, in 1588 or soon after. Entered on 20 October 2026 from Šolc 2018 (p. 194) and Falkenstein's entry; grade B by the document rule — Tycho's binding described by a librarian, the copy not seen since 1945. The SLUB's war-loss register carries a card for the Boiemus — Lit.Graec.B.1976, earlier ‘Phil. gr. B. 93a. Misc. 3’, and ‘Misc. 3’ matches Falkenstein's order, in which the Boiemus is the third piece; no card was found under the other two headings, and the register does not say whether the volume was removed in 1945–46 or destroyed (Nachweiskatalog image 00504111, read 27 October 2026; the identification with the Tycho volume is inference, C). Šolc 2018 (p. 194) infers from the words ‘ex Henrici Rantzovii bibliotheca’ that the volume's ‘paths once led through both libraries’, Rantzau's and Tycho's; the words belong to the Paulus edition's title (its Greek text printed from a manuscript in Rantzau's library) and Falkenstein records no Rantzau mark on the volume, so nothing documents that this copy was ever Rantzau's.

acquisition.channel: inscribed by Heinrich Rantzau to Henrik Ramel in 1584 (the flyleaf dedication); Tycho's acquisition undocumented — a second-hand gift by inference, Ramel ‘formodligen’ passing it on (Norlind 1970, p. 359)

marks.inscription: Heinrich Rantzau’s autograph dedication to Henrik Ramel, 1584, on the flyleaf; the Jesuit inscription of 1642 with ‘Ex Bibliotheca Tijchoniana’ on the title (Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 3); title (canvas 2, read 27 October 2026): 'Collegij … Cæsarei / Soc[ieta]tis IESV … Pragæ A° 1642' and 'Ex Bibliotheca Tÿchoniana.'; the Rantzau–Ramel dedication not visible in the facsimile
marks.annotations: reader's marginal nota-dashes on pp. 17–73 (canvases 38–94) against the astrologer-kings; a cursive note beside Alphonsus X (canvas 76); hands never compared
marks.binding: plain, no mark of Tycho’s

entries.editorial_note: Prandtl Verzeichnis A no. 33; Prandtl Einzelband XXII (National Library of the Czech Republic, Clementinum, shelfmark 1 H 56; Kleinschnitzová no. 3). The volume carries Rantzau’s autograph dedication of 1584 to Henrik Ramel, who probably passed it to Tycho (Norlind 1970, p. 359). Šolc 2002 (p. 330) lists ‘Astrologicae quaedam praedictiones; adiectus est tractatus De annis climactericis’ as a second item of the volume; it is the continuation of this print’s title. Three further works are bound with it (Kleinschnitzová 3:2–4). Heinrich Rantzau’s own library of more than six thousand volumes reached the same National Library by another road: taken from Breitenburg by Wallenstein in 1627 (1626 in Walde), given to the Jesuit professed house on the Malá Strana, partly confiscated by the Swedes on 2 September 1648, and in the Clementinum since the suppression of 1773 (Veselá 2025, pp. 9–10, 180–183; Lohmeier 2000, pp. 103–104). This copy came by the road of 1642 from Tycho’s heirs; the two are not to be conflated. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C). The earlier reading of the store and of the library-history — Rantzau's presentation copy to Tycho — is withdrawn (27 October 2026, register dossier §18-10): the dedication names Ramel, and only the Tycho step is inference.

norlind.entry: Rantzau, Henrik: Catalogus imperatorum, regum ac virorum illustrium, qui artem astrologiam amarunt, ornarunt et exercuerunt. Collecta ab Henrico Rantzovio ac edita a Theophilo Silvo. Lipsiæ 1584.4°. Z. 3400. Pr. nr 33. Kl. nr 3: 1. – Prag, UB.
ownership_inscriptions: [not quoted by Norlind: Rantzau's autograph dedication, dated 1584, to Henrik Ramel (later rigsraad) on the front flyleaf]
letters: (poem, not a letter) Tychos dikt till Rantzau, tryckt på Uraniborg 1585, daterad 1 mars 1585; IX, 187–190
norlind.ownership_verdict: located copy, Prague (Sammelband; probably given to Tycho by Henrik Ramel, to whom Rantzau had dedicated it in 1584); Tycho had read the Catalogus by March 1585 but in an edition Norlind cannot determine — the Prague copy, he says, was certainly acquired later
norlind.discussion:
I ett saml.-bd. På försättsbladet egenhändig dedikation 1584 av Rantzau till sedermera riksrådet Henrik Ramel, som förmodligen har skänkt exemplaret till Tycho. Av en dikt, som Tycho skrev till Rantzau och som trycktes på Uraniborg 1585, daterad d. 1 mars d.å. (IX, 187–190), framgår, att Tycho blivit smått På försättsbladet egenhändig dedikation 1584 av Rantzau till sedermera riksrådet Henrik Ramel, som förmodligen har skänkt exemplaret till Tycho.
Av en dikt, som Tycho skrev till Rantzau och som trycktes på Uraniborg 1585, daterad d. 1 mars d.å. (IX, 187–190), framgår, att Tycho blivit smått förargad över, att Rantzau i en bok kallat Uraniborg för »specula», varav det är uppenbart, menar Tycho, att Rantzau icke haft klart för sig, hur byggnaden såg ut:
»Cuius fama tuas siquidem pervenit ad aures,
Intuitu vero forte minora refert:
Quippe vocas speculam, quas Divæ struximus Ædes,
Vnde liquet, formam te latuisse domus.»
Den bok av Rantzau som Tycho här åsyftar, är just hans »Catalogus». Första upplagan trycktes i Antwerpen 1580 och såväl här som i alla de senare upplagorna står om Uraniborg följande: »Tygonique Braden (cuius vix similem in disciplinis Mathematicis hic Septentrionalis tractus habet) rex insulam nomine Vueen cum omnibus reditibus inter Zelandiam et Schaniam ad tempus vitæ concessit, ingentemque speculam erigi curavit» etc. Detta står som sagt i alla upplagorna. Vi kunna således inte med säkerhet avgöra i vilken Tycho läste det, men det kan ha varit i upplagan 1584 (s. 75–76), vars förord är daterat d. 1 febr. 1584. Exemplaret i Prag fick han dock säkerligen först senare.

entries.title_transcribed: Rantzovianum calendarium ad elevationem poli 55. grad. tam in usum medicorum quam astrologorum
entries.subject: Calendar/Astrology

acquisition.channel: from the author (Tycho to Rantzau, April 1590; Opera omnia VII, 243)

entries.editorial_note: Norlind records the book as received from the author (‘Erhöll Tycho av förf.’), on the evidence of Tycho to Rantzau, April 1590 (Opera omnia VII, 243). Rantzau’s own copy, into which a transcript of Tycho’s elegy to Denmark was bound and which King Christian leafed through on a visit to Rantzau (Opera omnia VIII, 63), is a different book. Two copies of the 1590 edition in the Royal Library, Hielmst. 547 2° and Hielmst. 146 2°, examined in facsimile, descend from Henrik Hielmstierne and bear neither a mark of Tycho’s nor the bound-in transcript. No copy with Tycho’s marks has been identified.

norlind.entry: Rantzau, Henrik: Rantzovianum calendarium ad elevationem poli 55. grad. tam in usum medicorum quam astrologorum ... Hamburgi 1590.2°. Z. 3399.
norlind.ownership_verdict: received from the author (letter April 1590); no copy located
norlind.discussion: Erhöll Tycho av förf. (brev till denne april 1590 [VII, 243]). I Rantzaus eget exemplar var inhäftad en avskrift av Tychos elegi till Danmark, däri han beklagar sig över den behandling han rönt hemma. När konung Kristian vid ett besök hos Rantzau bläddrade i boken, fick han även se Tychos dikt, läste den och avlägsnade sig sedan utan att säga ett ord (VIII, 63). Jfr s. 265.

entries.title_transcribed: De cometae magnitudine longitudineque ... problemata XVI
entries.subject: Astronomy (comet)
entries.editorial_note: Norlind holds that the tract was certainly in Tycho’s library, perhaps in several copies (‘fanns säkerligen i hans bibliotek, kanske i flera exemplar’), since Tycho cites it repeatedly, above all in the comet book. The tract was also reprinted within Regiomontanus’ Scripta (Nuremberg 1544), a volume Norlind likewise places in Tycho’s library.

norlind.discussion: Detta verk, som på flerfaldiga ställen citeras av Tycho, framförallt i kometboken, fanns säkerligen i hans bibliotek, kanske i flera exemplar. Skriften ingick emellertid också på fol. 75ʳ–88ʳ i Regiomontanus' »Scripta», som fanns i Tychos bibliotek.

entries.title_transcribed: Ephemerides ab anno 1482 ad annum 1506

marks.inscription: the title 'Ephemerides Iohannis Regiomontani ab anno 1482 ad annum 1506' on the blank fol. [b1r] (Tycho's hand per the library's record of 40 F 39), with the damaged 'Collegii Caesarei Societatis Jesu Prag[ae …] 1642. Ex bib[liotheca Tychon]iana' below it
marks.annotations: the marginalia are the unknown first owner's — family entries, deaths of friends of the Leipzig, Dresden and Meissen circle, weather notes, many dated 1487–1506, partly cropped at the rebinding (the library's record)
marks.binding: rebinding of the 16th/17th century: pasteboard covered in light leather, blind-tooled centre-and-frame with German Scripture quotations (a foreign workshop), the boards mounted upside down; rear board of waste Danish manuscripts of the 16th century; the front pasteboard lost; the spine overpainted white-grey with the Clementinum college's red title and shelfmark (the library's record). Formerly 14 H 188, re-shelved 40 F 39 after c. 1950.

entries.editorial_note: Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 14; NK Clementinum, formerly Sign. 14 H 188, now 40 F 39 (Boldan 2025, no. 33.b). The title is written in Tycho’s hand on fol. [b1r] (Kleinschnitzová; Boldan) — one of the two volumes she names (p. 80) to show that he did not mark all his books with his name. The copy lacks the first gatherings a4 and a10, which survive at Strahov before the Augsburg Ephemerides of 1492 (DR VII 19), both halves inscribed by the Jesuits in 1642.
open_questions: Whether the Venice 1481 Ephemerides were divided — the tables here, the prefatory gatherings before the Augsburg 1492 edition at Strahov — in Tycho’s own time or in the Clementinum; Boldan (2025) leaves open whether Tycho acquired the book only after coming to Bohemia.

marks.inscription: fol. a2r: ‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis Jesu Pragae Anno 1642. Ex Bibliotheca Tichoniana’ (Straka 1913; Boldan 2025; Katalog Tritius 1064031). Later hands: ‘Ex libris Johannis Nachlovsky’ (fol. a1v) and ‘Nachlovsky’ (a2r) — later than Tycho per Boldan 2025; ‘Joannes Josephus Worell’ and ‘Anna’, with a drawn basket, on the second leaf (Straka 1913)
marks.annotations: A 34-line Latin note on the winter of 1495/96 on the verso of the leaf carrying December 1495 (‘fol. 75.b’ in the old foliation, Straka; ‘e4v’, Boldan 2025; ‘e14b (75v) druhého přívazku’ — of the second constituent, the 1492 almanac — Katalog Tritius). Munzar and Pařez's transcription (2002, p. 372): ‘Haec hiems tanta frigoris in Bruma asperitate referta erat tantaeq(ue) nivium moles passim conglomoratae, ut agrestium casarum culmina superantes desup(er) homines in redis iter expeditissime facerent at sequuta est in sequente aestate maxima lues wulgo gallica scabies dicta Germanis & Danis ante ea tempora non solum incognita sed pro(r)sus inaudita q(uod) multa hominum milia infecit. Ratio e(st) quod omnes planete sint in frigidis & humidis signis praesertim introeunte ☉ in initia solstitii hiberni. Ex quibus certissimum inditium frigoris & copiosae nivis sumi poterat. Rarum exemplum.’ — then a table of the seven planets' signs. Attributed to Tycho's own hand by Straka in 1913 on an undocumented comparison by eye; compared letter by letter, again by eye, with the DG IV 25 motto and the AG XI 56 dedication by Munzar & Pařez (2002, pp. 372–373), who find the hand ‘with a high probability’ Tycho's and at the least that of his immediate circle, who read the note as a retrospective astrometeorological reconstruction from historical reports rather than a weather record, and who date the winter to 1495/96 from independent climate records and a reconstruction of the planetary positions; called ‘vlastnoruční’ by Boldan (2025) — and called hypothetical by Pařez himself (2026). Their fig. 5 (p. 371) reproduces the note. Never examined graphonomically. Other hands in the volume: the reference-meridian note above the Tabula regionum (‘Nota hec Ephemerides sunt supputate ad longitudinem …’) and three front flyleaves of mathematical calculations running onto fol. 1a1a, signed ‘Josephus Worel’ above a drawn basket (Katalog Tritius dates the hand c. 1766; Straka read ‘Joannes Josephus Worell’ and ‘Anna’), which also foliated the volume.
marks.binding: Contemporary binding: wooden boards 230 × 150 mm covered in leather for a third of their width only, the leather nailed to the boards with small brass nails and blind-tooled in a frame composition now almost worn away; the spine damaged at the head, undecorated; a faint ‘ALMANACH’ on the front board; the central clasp removed; yellow edges (Katalog Tritius 1064031; Straka 1913: bare boards with a glued and nailed leather spine; Boldan 2025: a contemporary tanned-leather binding with the blind-tooling worn).

dispersal.detail: Carries the 1642 inscription yet stands at Strahov. Straka 1913: Clementinum → the astronomer Antonín Strnad (d. 1799) → Strahov, whose purchase of Strnad's library is documented (Munzar 2001); Strahov's present cataloguer objects that the volume is in neither published catalogue of Strnad's library (Seydl 1939; Kouklová 1989) and suspects Straka confused it with Stoeffler–Pflaum's Almanach nova (Venice 1507), which did come from Strnad and bears AG VII 87. Boldan 2025 leaves it open whether Tycho acquired the volume before or after coming to Bohemia. The library's own record agrees with Straka on the first step and doubts the second: ‘then the volume became part of the so-called Mathematical Museum in the Clementinum, from which it passed to Strahov (original shelfmark AG VII 84)’ — but Seydl and Kouklová do not list it in Strnad's library, and Straka may have confused it with the Stoeffler–Pflaum almanac AG VII 87. Munzar and Pařez (2002, p. 369) supposed the Strahov purchase ‘probably not before the abolition of the Jesuit Order in 1773’. The calculations signed by Worel, which the catalogue dates c. 1766, would then have been written while the volume was still in the Clementinum.

entries.editorial_note: Not a second copy of Kleinschnitzová 14. Boldan 2025 (33.b, 33.c, 36.a): the National Library's Venice 1481 Ephemerides (his shelfmark 40 F 39; our Kleinschnitzová no. 14 records 14 H 188) LACKS its first gatherings a4 a10, and the Strahov volume CONTAINS exactly those gatherings, bound before the Augsburg 1492 Ephemerides 1492–1506 — the two are halves of one Tycho book, both inscribed by the Jesuits in 1642. Straka's ‘first incunable, Ephemerides c. 1476–82, a fragment lacking eight leaves and its end’ is the 1481 prefatory gatherings; his second, ‘Almanach … ad annos XV … 1492’, lacking seven leaves in the text and eighteen at the end, is the almanac that carries the note. The weather note is the case Pařez calls hypothetical; its attribution rests on Straka's eye and on content — the ‘Germanis et Danis’ of the plague sentence is the strongest internal pointer — and the note stands as attributed, not as autograph. The 1481 part is 358 leaves short: only gathering 1a4 (Ratdolt's and Regiomontanus's prefaces) and fol. a5–6 of gathering 2a (Mariensüss's Expositio) survive, their printed initials uncoloured and the rubrics unfilled (Katalog Tritius).
open_questions: The National Library twin (Kleinschnitzová no. 14, now 40 F 39 according to Boldan 2025) is reported by Boldan to lack gatherings a4 and a10; the two copies have not been compared.

The published halftone of the note (Munzar & Pařez 2002, fig. 5, p. 371) allows a first comparison with the securely attributed specimens of Tycho’s hand; a photograph of fol. e4v at specimen scale would allow a full one.
Who Josef Worel was, and whether a hand dated c. 1766 inside a volume the Jesuits held until 1773 belongs to a Clementinum student or shows the volume outside the college earlier than supposed.

acquisition.place: Copenhagen — inferred from the binding’s year 1561 and Tycho’s departure from Denmark on 14 February 1562; no source names the place
acquisition.channel: bought as a student: the purchase note ‘Eptg [emptus] thalero & 4 Groshj’ on the fly-title; the year is that stamped on the binding, ‘Anno 1561’, read as the year of purchase by Klem (Årbog 1957, p. 8)

marks.inscription: fly-title (before this, the first title in the volume), read on the leaf 20 October 2026: recto ‘tico brade ven:’ in a thin early hand, struck through once in the same ink; a name obliterated under heavy black strokes (Thykier: ‘Tyge Brahe’); ‘Sum Pauli’ in a firmer hand with a flourish, complete, what followed lost with the torn-away part; two short words, read 21 October 2026 as ‘Brÿſſe’ or ‘Chrÿſſe’ (inside a wet-wiped erasure of an earlier inscription) and ‘to bra[h/n][e/o]’; verso ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ under a heavy bar, the purchase note ‘Eptꝰ thaliro & 4 Groſs.’ — emptus thalero et 4 grossis, the sign after Ept being the -us abbreviation, not a g (read 21 October 2026), and an intact two-branch memorandum on oblique ascension; a companion note in ink on the front pastedown (the museum's record: ‘tico brade ven:’, ‘Tycho Brade’ and further ownership inscriptions, the leaf half torn and repaired; ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’, ‘Eptg [emptus] thalero & 4 Groshj’; Prandtl: ‘emptus thalero & 4 Gross und dreimal Brahes Name’)
marks.annotations: a grey marginal note in an early hand on the Octavum problema page of the preface (‘pro g. m. / 60 / sec. / 15 / tert. / differentia’ — Thykier's note on the tenth page), tallies ij iij iiij beside ‘Ille autem numerus polaris’, a red-brown stepped line through the Tabula declinationum, a large pen flourish at the head of the Tabula ascensionum rectarum (photographed 20 October 2026; the museum's record: ‘enkelte notater over klummen’); Latin plant names at the head of the preface leaves in a later hand (Pulmonaria, Ranunculus aquaticus, Hedera arborescens, Lamium, Lysimachia flore luteo, Hyacinthus — read 21 October 2026), the Octavum problema column read as ‘p[ro] g[radu] m[inuta] iiij[?] / 60 / ſecũdꝫ / 15 / tertiꝫ / differentia’, a crossed tally iii on a table leaf; no hand attributed — the hand of the memoranda compared with the Graphonomicon's dated specimens on 21 October 2026, inconclusive
marks.binding: Band II: brown calf, blind-ruled mirror panels on both boards, originally gilt floral stamps, TVCHO BRADE stamped on the front board, ANNO 1561 on the rear, three raised bands; on the spine the remnant of a label with a library shelfmark 204 (the museum's record, 1957:0030)

entries.editorial_note: Prandtl, Verzeichnis A no. 34, the first work in his Band II. The volume is at the M/S Museet for Søfart, Helsingør, inventory 1957:0030, the gift of Lia and Oscar Ekman in 1957. The museum’s record collates the work (title, [43] pp. text, [268] pp. tables) and notes a few annotations in the head margin; the ownership inscriptions and the purchase note are on its fly-title. The volume is in the museum’s own keeping, as the museum confirms; the deposit at the Royal Library reported in 1987 and 1992 has ended. Offered by Maggs Bros., London, in 1933 (Catalogue 582, item 155, £125), 1934 and c. 1938, and by Herbert Reichner, New York, in [1939] (Catalogue 1, item 72); Prandtl's ‘sold to America’ was wrong about the first step (the dossier of 20 October 2026). Examined at the museum on 20 October 2026: the inscriptions read on both sides of the leaf, the memorandum intact, the herbarium confirmed. Read letter by letter from the frames on 21 October 2026: the purchase note corrected to ‘emptus thalero et 4 grossis’, the two memoranda read in full, the hands labelled and the hand of the memoranda compared (inconclusive). Reviewed on 29 October 2026: of the six volumes the house has carried as the student’s, this is the one documented as Tycho’s before he left Denmark on 14 February 1562 — by the boards stamped with his name and the year 1561, and by nothing else: the purchase note and the ownership entries are undated, and no hand in the volume is attributed. Copenhagen as the place of purchase is an inference from the year (the Kronik of 1987 read the Leipzig register’s ‘16 October 1561’ as the matriculation; it is the winter-semester heading, Norlind 1970, p. 16, and Tycho and Vedel matriculated in the spring of 1562); the price in thaler and groschen is German money of account, which no source explains for a Copenhagen purchase; Klem’s ‘i 1561’ (Årbog 1957, p. 8) is the binding’s year, not the note’s. The volume came back to Denmark as Oscar Ekman’s bequest, entered in January 1957 by his widow Lia in the dead man’s name (he died 16 September 1956; the sale catalogue of 1965, lot 497: ‘according to the last will of ingeniør Ekman’, not for sale).

entries.title_transcribed: Practica auff das Jhar 1574, sampt einer Erklerung aller Umbstende des neuen Sternes
entries.subject: Astronomy (nova 1572)
entries.editorial_note: Norlind 1970, p. 361 (Zinner 2681): listed among the books of the library because Tycho discusses the tract in the Progymnasmata (Opera omnia III, 212–216); no copy, receipt or mark is recorded. Norlind’s introduction states the principle on which such tracts enter his catalogue: it may be regarded as fairly certain that nearly all the writings on the new star of 1572 and the comet of 1577 that Tycho reviews in the Progymnasmata and the comet book stood in the library on Hven (p. 335). The Practica is the work of the astronomer’s son, the physician Erasmus Reinhold the younger, whom Norlind’s headword does not distinguish from the author of the Prutenic tables. An unbound tract of this kind, if Tycho’s copy survives, would carry no known mark by which it could be recognised.

norlind.discussion: I slutet Rheticus' »Dialogus de canone doctrinæ triangulorum», som innehåller en bekväm metod för lösning av sfäriska trianglar. – Kl. nr 12: 1. – Prag, UB. I ett saml.-bd. Det framgår av flera yttranden av Tycho, hur viktigt detta arbete var för honom. Till Herwart skriver han sålunda i nov. 1599 (VIII, 200), att han för 20 år sedan hade börjat syssla med detta verk. Något eller några exemplar funnos förmodligen redan i biblioteket på Uraniborg.

marks.binding: gilt portrait supralibros on the front board (bust in cloak and ruff, the Order of the Elephant on a long chain; legend HIC PATET EXTERIOR TYCHONIS FORMA BRAHEI PVLCHRIVS ENITEAT QVAE LATET INTERIOR) and the arms supralibros on the back (ARMA GENVS FVNDI PEREVNT DVRABILE VIRTVS ET DOCTRINAE DECVS NOBILITATIS HABENT), each 76 × 59 mm, on a parchment binding (Pařez 2009, with photographs); the binding is by the Prague ‘Knihvazač rudolfínského okruhu II’ (NUSK workshop 33; Schunke's Dürerbuch-Meister), dated by comparison with the National Library's Reinhold 14 J 176 to 1599–1601 (Voit 2020, pp. 250–252)

dispersal.detail: Carries the 1642 inscription yet stands at Strahov: a volume that left the Clementinum core — the documented route is Ungar's post-1773 duplicate screening and Strnad's purchase of the surplus, whose library Strahov bought after 1799; not yet documented for this volume.

entries.editorial_note: Norlind: ‘kanske detta stora verk som Tycho erhöll som gåva av lantgreve Moritz’ — perhaps the ‘Opus illud Palatinum’ Tycho received as a gift from Landgrave Moritz and thanked him for in November 1600 (Opera omnia VIII, 388; the relevant lines are struck in the draft). The copy at the Strahov Library, Σ V 5/a, carries Tycho’s portrait and arms supralibros on a parchment binding of the Rudolfine circle and the Jesuit inscription of 1642 (Pařez 2009; Voit 2020, pp. 250–252; Katalog Tritius 1046995). Whether it is the ‘Opus illud Palatinum’ of the November 1600 letter is an open question. The binder is no guide to the route: Voit (2021, p. 117) counts about seventy volumes of the Rudolfine-circle binder II at Strahov, arrived by several hands — Pontanus’s gifts of 1595, Troilo von Lessoth’s books, Pistorius z Lucka. The library’s record cites, beside Voit 2020, his Boj o volnou plochu (2023), pp. 209 and 560, and lists the copy in the NUSK binding database (exemplar 5089). The Czech National Library holds two copies of the Neustadt (Harnisch) edition of 1596, 14 A 12, complete, and a second, defective copy; neither record names a former owner. Tycho had bought four copies of the work before June 1597 — ‘cuius quidem antea quaterna exemplaria coëmeram’ (to Moritz, 17 June 1597, Opera omnia XIV 105–108) — the largest multiple purchase of one work in his correspondence, so that five copies were in his hands by 1597; the gift copy is the one Norlind had in view.
open_questions: Whether this is the ‘Opus illud Palatinum’ for which Tycho thanked Landgrave Moritz in November 1600 (Opera omnia VIII, 388): neither Pařez 2009 nor the Tritius record reports a gift inscription, and the wording of the Jesuit inscription of 1642 is unpublished; a reading of the inscriptions in the volume would decide.
By what route the volume passed from the Clementinum to Strahov, which is undocumented for this copy; a Mathematical Museum spine signature or Strnad’s name-stamp would settle it.

entries.title_transcribed: Libellus de sphaera
entries.subject: Astronomy/Astrology/Mathematics

acquisition.channel: bought as a student — if the cipher is Tycho’s (ownership C): the pigskin binding of the volume is blind-stamped ‘T. B. 1560’ and the Bayrus bound first in it is printed in 1560 (Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 47; Christianson 1967, pp. 200–201); no inscription, annotation or Jesuit note of 1642 supports it

entries.editorial_note:
Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 47:2; Norlind 1970, p. 350; the library’s record 18 J 318/adl.1. Bound after Bayrus’s Enchiridion in the blind-stamped pigskin binding lettered ‘T. B. 1560’, a binding of Tycho’s student years. Christianson (1967, p. 200) has Scavenius lecturing four times a week, ‘beginning with arithmetic, then going on to Sacrobosco’s treatise On the Sphere, and the Cosmography of Peter Apian’, and counts this volume with the volume of 1561 as ‘two of his own “textbooks”’ still preserved (pp. 200–201). While the purchase note of the Ptolemy 5 B 70 is disputed, the ‘T. B. 1560’ volume is the earliest book securely Tycho’s.

Ownership graded B on 28 October 2026: the attribution rests on the blind-stamped cipher T·B and the year 1560 on the binding alone — no inscription, no annotation, no 1642 or Chomutov mark, and Kleinschnitzová 1933 gives no argument. The cipher is consistent with Tycho's documented series of initial-and-year bindings 1561–1583 (Helsingør 1561, Uppsala 1563, Strahov and 10 G 47 1567, T.B.O. 1576–1583) and the contents fit the Copenhagen curriculum of 1560, but T·B alone identifies no one. The NK ČR photographs requested on 28 October 2026 (the three edges, both boards, the three title pages at 600 dpi) and an EBDB identification of the panel stamps are the tests.

Reviewed again on 29 October 2026, the literature pack read whole: ownership graded C (was B). Beyond the cipher the literature holds nothing — no inscription, no annotation, no hand, no note of 1642. Kleinschnitzová (1933, pp. 76–78) herself sets the volume outside the twenty-three Clementinum volumes that carry the note of 1642 and says it ‘verirrt sich’, strayed, into the Jesuit professed house on the Malá Strana — an explanation that assumes what it should show; Norlind’s ‘T. B. O. 1560’ (1970, p. 339) reads a letter the board does not carry; the library’s record gives Tycho the year 1567 in its former-owner field without a basis; Šolc (1999, 2006, 2018), Christianson (1967, 2020), Thoren and Pařez all derive from Kleinschnitzová. If the cipher is Tycho’s, the year 1560 places the binding before his departure from Denmark; whether it is Tycho’s is the whole question, and the National Library’s photographs are the test. Decided on 29 October 2026.

entries.editorial_note: Prandtl, Verzeichnis A no. 41, listed in his Band IV; Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 24, Sign. VII E 29. The manuscript was separated from Sign. 14 F 16 before 1901, at an earlier revision of the manuscripts (Prusík 1901, pp. 198–199; Studnička 1901, p. 21; Kukula 1906–07, p. 22); the printed pieces A 20, A 1 and A 11 remain in 14 F 16.
open_questions: Whose hand the main text is in: Prandtl (1932, Verzeichnis A no. 41) records the manuscript as Tycho’s own copy (‘eigenhändige Abschrift Tycho’s’), but the Truhlář catalogue, followed by Manuscriptorium, dates the codex 1539–1550, before Tycho’s birth; whether the hand is Tycho’s, the codex a later copy of a work of 1539, or the writer another scribe with Tycho only as owner, a comparison with his securely attributed specimens would decide.

Whose account the cost note on f. 1r is — it is headed ‘Andreas Schöner’ and reckons in pfennigs — and whether the monogram beside it, read as T B, is Tycho’s: Studnička (1901) took both for Tycho’s; a comparison of hands, none of which has been published, would decide.

entries.title_transcribed: De emendatione temporum (revised ed.; Leiden, Plantin 1598)
entries.subject: Chronology

acquisition.channel: purchase or gift (disputed: the author’s gift according to Norlind 1926, an ordinary purchase according to Walde 1938)

dispersal.detail: seen by Walde in the library of the Staatliche Akademie at Braunsberg in 1937; the library burned in January 1945; not traced since

entries.editorial_note: Sought in 1584 through Johannes Maior, Tycho’s agent at the Frankfurt fairs; the first edition of 1583 then reached Tycho twice in June 1584, from Maior at Augsburg on 8 June (Maior to Tycho, 8 June 1584, Opera omnia VII, 83: ‘Inprimis autem mihi curae fuit SCALIGERI de emendatione temporum’) and from Heinrich Brucaeus at Rostock on 12 June (Brucaeus to Tycho, 12 June 1584, Opera omnia VII, 86: ‘Mitto IOSEPHUM SCALIGERUM de emendatione temporum’). One of the two copies survives: Prague, National Library, Sign. 19 A 46, initialled ‘T. B.’ on the title-page; Kleinschnitzová (no. 41, p. 92) could not say which: ‘Dürfte das von Brucaeus oder Major an Brahe gesandte Exemplar sein.’ The entry concerns the revised edition of 1598, which Tycho acknowledged to Scaliger from Wandsbeck on 14 March 1598 (Tycho to Scaliger, 14 March 1598: ‘redintegratum de Temporum Emendatione... primum accepi’); Norlind (1926, no. 28) read the copy as the author’s gift, Walde (1938, p. 14 n. 2) as an ordinarily procured copy, the letter containing no thanks. A copy of this edition from Tycho’s library was found by Walde in the summer of 1937 in the library of the Staatliche Akademie at Braunsberg: white parchment with Tycho’s portrait on the upper and his arms on the lower board, both blind-stamped, and the decor usual on his bindings; not bound on Hven, which he left in 1597, perhaps at Wandsbeck in 1598; many marginalia in several hands, photographs of which Hans Ræder judged not to be Tycho’s; no dedication; the only later note ‘M. Braunhardt i Gotha 1761 … Ex bibliotheca Oppeliana’, which Walde could not explain (a person named Oppel, or the town of Oppeln near Neisse, where Tycho’s great globe was found in 1632). Mortensen cited the find in 1955 without the title; nothing later is recorded of the volume, and Norlind’s catalogue of 1970 does not include it. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).
open_questions: Whether the Braunsberg copy survived the Second World War. The Hosianum library's wartime losses and the post-war route of its rescued early prints — to Moscow, back to Poland and to the seminary library at Olsztyn, with East Prussian library material also gathered at Toruń — are not documented in anything held here and are not asserted; a Scaliger, De emendatione temporum, Leiden 1598, in white parchment with the blind-stamped portrait and arms plaques and the note of M. Braunhardt, Gotha 1761, ‘Ex bibliotheca Oppeliana’, in one of the successor collections would decide.

Tycho till Scaliger mars 1598 (the Opera number, VIII, 32, is printed in the p. 362 portion of the entry)
norlind.ownership_verdict: located copy, Braunsberg (original binding with portrait and arms), received shortly after publication, perhaps via Pontanus; a second, dedication copy from Scaliger received at Wittenberg 1598 and lent (not given) to Taubmann; Kästner/Dreyer's Conjecturae in Varronem story rejected
norlind.discussion:
Originalbd med porträtt och vapen.
I sept. 1595 (VII, 373) skriver Tycho till Pontanus, som då befann sig i Holland, att han önskade, att denne skulle sända Scaligers »de Emendatione Temporum præstans illud opus recognitum, ubi illud consummatum fuerit» – varmed tydligen menas föreliggande upplaga, som då ännu icke förelåg färdigtryckt. Måhända var det Pontanus, som sedan skickade det exemplar som nu finns i Braunsberg. Tycho måste ha fått verket kort efter dess publicering. Förordet är nämligen dat. d. 11 jan. 1598 (g.st.) och i mars s.å. (VIII, 32) tackar han Scaliger för dennes omnämnande av honom i boken, som han fått »just i dagarna». Tycho syftar på den tabell över sina observationer av ekvinoktierna som Scaliger på ett smickrande sätt meddelat på s. 728–729: »Tabella æquinoctii utriusque in Dania observati ab eximio artifice nobiliss. Tychone Brahe.» Denna tabell är den som Tycho tryckte i »Prog.» (II, 15) och som han måste ha skickat Scaliger tidigare, väl genom samme Pontanus, som i ett odaterat brev, sannolikt från slutet av 1597 eller början av 1598 (VIII, 20), omtalar, att Scaliger satt in Tychos observationer i verket och att Tycho snart skall få se dem.
Dreyer menar i en not (»Tycho Brahe», s. 270,¹ efter Kästner, »Geschichte der Mathematik», 2, Gött. 1797, s. 409), att Scaliger som tack för några böcker Tycho skickat honom sänt honom ett exemplar av sina »Conjecturæ et notæ in Varronem», vilket exemplar Tycho skänkte eller lånade professor Taubmann i Wittenberg. Denna notis grundar sig på en fullständig missuppfattning av ett ställe i Taubmanns kommentar till Plautus »Pœnulus», vers 34 ff. (M. Acci Plauti »Comœdiæ XX. superstites ...». Wittebergæ 1612, s. 309). Taubmann hänvisar här dels till Scaligers »Conject. Varron.», dels till sammes »in Appendice operis, De emendatione temporum». Längre ned refereras till Scaliger »in Emendata quidem prædicti Operis editione». Detta syftar givetvis icke på hans »Conject. Varron.» – som Kästner och efter honom Dreyer trott – utan på den strax förut nämnda »De emendatione temporum». Vi kunna också fastställa, att upplagan 1598 avses. Endast i denna och ej i någon annan upplaga står det av Taubmann citerade stället i ett appendix, »In Fragmentum Berosi Babylonii», s. XXV. Vidare berättar Taubmann i sin Plautus-kommentar, att Scaliger skickat Tycho boken, som just lämnat pressen. Tycho var då i Wittenberg, skriver Taubmann. Det var vid ung. samma tid som han skänkte Taubmann ett exemplar av sin »Mech.» (Berlin-exemplaret) och Taubmann å sin sida sjöng hans lov i ett alkaiskt ode till kejsar Rudolf (dat. d. 21 okt. 1598; avskrift bl.a. i slutet på ett exemplar av Resen, »Inscriptiones Haffnienses», Det kgl. Bibliotek, Köpenhamn). Dreyer har varit tveksam om Tycho skänkte eller lånade Taubmann sitt exemplar (det står concessit hos Taubmann). Att det varit fråga om ett lån, framgår dock av vad Taubmann själv skriver om detta exemplar i ett brev till Scaliger, sannolikt från våren 1599 (i: P. Burmannus' »Sylloge epistolarum a viris illustribus scriptarum», T. 2, Leidæ 1727, s. 339): »quem hisce diebus ab amicissimo et pœne mihi domestico, Tychone Brahe utendum habui».
Taubmanns uppgift i Plautus-kommentaren är emellertid icke fullt klar. Ty det exemplar av verket varom Tycho talar i brevet till Scaliger i mars 1598 var säkerligen icke något gåvoexemplar från denne. Hade så varit fallet, skulle Tycho omtalat det som en gåva och framfört sitt tack därför, vilket han icke gör – utan han tackar Scaliger för dennes omnämnande av hans observationer. Och vidare befann sig Tycho då på Wandsbek, icke i Wittenberg. Inget tyder på, att detta exemplar varit en skänk från Scaliger. Däremot synes Tycho, om vi få tro Taubmann, ha erhållit ett dedikationsexemplar från Scaliger under vistelsen i Wittenberg, vilket exemplar dock icke var så färskt som Taubmann skriver. entries.editorial_note: Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 41; National Library, Clementinum, Sign. 19 A 46. The Paris edition of 1583, with Tycho’s initials ‘T. B.’ on the title, marginal glosses in his hand and, at the foot of the title, an epigram in a hand Kleinschnitzová queries as his; she took the volume for the copy sent by Brucaeus or Maior (p. 92). Norlind (1970, p. 362) records two copies received in 1584, from Maior at Augsburg (Opera omnia VII, 83) and from Brucaeus at Rostock (Opera omnia VII, 86). The revised edition of 1598, which Tycho acknowledged to Scaliger from Wandsbeck on 14 March 1598, is a separate book.

entries.title_transcribed: De astronomicis hypothesibus, seu de systemate mundano
entries.subject: Astronomy (world-system polemic)

acquisition.channel: several copies in 1598: one received at Wandsbek with Kepler’s first letter (Tycho to Kepler, April 1598; Opera omnia VIII, 46), one from Rollenhagen (VIII, 51), one from Hagecius by way of Denmark and Helmstedt (VIII, 56)

entries.editorial_note: Norlind records that Tycho received the book (‘erhöll boken’). It was printed ‘Absque omni privilegio’; in it Ursus denies having stolen the system, dedicates the work to Landgrave Moritz, prints a laudatory letter from Kepler (Graz, 15 November 1595), and violently attacks Tycho and Rothmann. Tycho lent his copy, with the offending passages marked, to Holger Rosenkrantz in 1598 and complained that it was not returned (Opera omnia VIII, 126). Jardine, Launert, Segonds, Mosley and Tybjerg (2005, pp. 98–103) found the Royal Library’s copy from the Rosenkrantz sale of 1695 unmarked; the copy now in the Danish National Library of Science and Medicine, 4° Astr. 8050, perhaps transferred from the Royal Library between 1918 and 1926, is inscribed ‘Donum Autoris’ on the title and carries sixteen clear marginal marks, all against passages insulting to Tycho and all but two of them in the dedication to Landgrave Moritz or in the invective poem that follows it. They argue that this is the copy prepared for Lange and lent to Rosenkrantz. The identification rests on the pattern of the marks, not on a mark of ownership; the hand of the marks has not been compared with Tycho’s or with those of his assistants. A book lent out of the library in 1598 and never returned is a survivor of the library’s lifetime, not of its dispersal. The Czech National Library holds a copy of the Prague 1597 edition, 14 J 81/adl.2, bound second in a re-bound convolute after della Faille’s Theoremata (Antwerp 1632); its record, recatalogued under Kukula, carries no provenance. Jardine and Segonds restate the identification in 2008: the copy is the one Caspar Lehmann obtained from Ursus himself and sent through Rollenhagen in the spring of 1598; Tycho had the marks made for Erik Lange’s testimony and lent the volume to Holger Rosenkrantz, who did not return it despite the demands of 9 September 1598 (Opera omnia VIII, p. 112) and 5 December 1598 (pp. 125–126); their ‘about a dozen’ marked passages answers to the twelve puncta Lange attested, the article of 2005 counting sixteen clear marks and two doubtful (2008, pp. 175, 195–196, 243 n. 3). Three copies of the book reached Tycho in the spring of 1598 — from a student of Helmstedt, from Lehmann through Rollenhagen, and from Hagecius (pp. 157 n. 3, 191–192). A second surviving copy of the book Jardine and Segonds call rare: Västerås Stadsbibliotek, from the Olomouc Jesuit college (‘Collegij Olomu. Soctis JESV Catalogo inscriptus an: 1604’), through the Stockholm royal library of 1650–51, in a parchment binding cut from a coloured Hebrew manuscript (the Swedish-booty database, record SJ 203; Gawryś, Slavica Arosiensia III, no. 213). Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).
open_questions: Whether the marginal marks in 4° Astr. 8050 (Royal Danish Library, formerly the Danish National Library of Science and Medicine) are in Tycho’s hand or in that of an assistant, and by what route the volume left the Royal Library; the ink and hand of the marks set against the Uraniborg hands, the binding and any earlier shelfmark would test the identification argued by Jardine et al. 2005.

norlind.entry: Ursus, Nicolaus Raimarus: De astronomicis hypothesibus, seu de systemate mundano, tractatus astronomicus ... Pragæ 1597.4°. Z. 3739.
letters: Hagecius (the copy sent via Denmark and Helmstedt); VIII, 56
norlind.ownership_verdict: owned — several copies received (one at Wandsbek together with Kepler's first letter, one from Rollenhagen, one from Hagecius); one copy with marginal annotations (probably Tycho's own) lent to Rosenkrantz; no located copy
norlind.discussion: I denna skrift, tryckt »Absque omni privilegio» såsom det står på titelbladet, förnekar Ursus, att han tagit idén till sitt i »Fundamentum» framställda världssystem från Tycho vid besöket på Uraniborg. Skriften är tillägnad lantgreve Moritz, son till lantgreve Wilhelm. I början är (fol. D) avtryckt ett mycket berömmande brev från Kepler, dat. Graz d. 15 nov. 1595. Bokens innehåll utgöres till en del av våldsamma personliga angrepp på såväl Tycho som på Rothmann. Tycho erhöll boken på Wandsbek samtidigt med Keplers första brev (Tycho till Kepler april 1598; VIII, 46). Från flera andra håll fick han emellertid exemplar, så från Rollenhagen (april 1598; VIII, 51) och Hagecius, som hade skickat boken till Danmark, varifrån den eftersändes över Helmstedt till Tycho på Wandsbek (VIII, 56). Ett lånade han till Rosenkrantz, vilket han var angelägen att återfå på grund av de däri (förmodligen av honom själv) införda marginalanteckningarna (brev till Rosenkrantz dec. 1598; VIII, 126).

entries.subject: Astronomy (world-system)

acquisition.channel: several copies: one from Rantzau (Tycho to Rantzau, December 1588; Opera omnia VII, 387), one from Georg Rollenhagen in Magdeburg, one probably through Christian Ripensis (Tycho to Rothmann, February 1589; VI, 179)

entries.editorial_note: Ursus set out in this book a world-system that, in Norlind’s words, differs only slightly from Tycho’s. Tycho held that Ursus had taken it from a sketch seen during his stay at Uraniborg in the autumn of 1584, in Erik Lange’s company, and pressed the charge of plagiarism in the correspondence with the Landgrave and Rothmann printed in 1596; Norlind, with Dreyer, holds the charge probably unwarranted. Tycho received several copies: one sent by Rantzau (Tycho to Rantzau, December 1588; Opera omnia VII, 387), a second probably from Christian Ripensis, which may be the other copy Tycho mentions in that letter, and one from Georg Rollenhagen in Magdeburg (Tycho to Rothmann, February 1589; Opera omnia VI, 179). Rollenhagen sent a copy to Rantzau on 16 October 1588 (Landesarchiv Schleswig-Holstein, Breitenburg-Archiv Abt. 127.21, Hss. 293, p. 552); Tycho already had one from elsewhere, ‘aliunde’ (to Rantzau, 21 December 1588, Opera omnia VII, p. 387) (Jardine & Segonds 2008, pp. 120–121). A copy with a Prague provenance of 1595 — ‘Daniel Muller à Mollenberg, '95 Prag’ on the title, ‘Raymari’ on the fore-edge, interleaved and annotated in a hand the Kepler-Kommission declared in 1964 not to be Kepler's — is at Leiden, 538 E 2, from Isaac Vossius's library; Balsem declines to call it Swedish booty for want of any trace of Christina's shelfmark on its ruined spine (2020, p. 37 and Cat. Math. 730). Not Tycho's copy, but a Prague copy of the year of the quarrel.

norlind.entry: Ursus, Nicolaus Raimarus: Fundamentum astronomicum, id est nova doctrina sinuum et triangulorum. Argentorati 1588.4°. Z. 3316.
norlind.ownership_verdict: owned — several copies received (one from Rantzau, one probably from Ripensis, one from Rollenhagen in Magdeburg); no located copy
norlind.discussion: I denna skrift framlägger Ursus bl.a. ett eget världssystem, som endast obetydligt avviker från Tychos. Denne misstänkte därför, att Ursus plagierat en skiss av detta under besöket på Uraniborg. I sin korrespondens, särskilt i den 1596 tryckta brevväxlingen med lantgreven och Rothmann framför Tycho mot Ursus kraftiga beskyllningar för plagiat. Ursus svarade med nedanstående skrift. Tycho erhöll flera exemplar. Ett skickade Rantzau (Tycho till denne dec. 1588; VII, 387), ett annat kom förmodligen från Ripensis och kan vara det andra exemplar, varom Tycho talar i brevet. Från Rollenhagen i Magdeburg fick han ett, efter vad han skriver till Rothmann i febr. 1589 (VI, 179). Se vidare s. 113 ff.

entries.title_transcribed: De iis quae scripta sunt physice in libris sacris, sive de sacra philosophia
entries.subject: Natural philosophy/Theology
entries.editorial_note: Norlind (p. 365): ‘Tycho, som möjligen ägt upplagan 1588’ — Tycho possibly owned the second edition (Lyon 1588). Tycho discusses Valles’ view that the new star of 1572 was not new in the Progymnasmata (III, 87–93). The ownership rests on Norlind’s ‘möjligen’ alone: no inventory and no marked copy attests it.

norlind.entry: Vallesius, Franciscus: De iis quæ scripta sunt physice in libris sacris sive de sacra philosophia. 8°.
norlind.ownership_verdict: possibly owned (perhaps the second edition, Lyon 1588); discussed in Progymnasmata
norlind.discussion: Behandlar i kap. 1 den nya stjärnan 1572, som Vallesius icke höll för »ny» utan för en redan existerande. – Tycho, som möjligen ägt upplagan 1588, tr. i Lyon (detta är andra uppl., den första trycktes i Turin året innan), diskuterar Vallesius' åsikt i »Prog.» (III, 87–93).

entries.title_transcribed: Two tracts newly published in 1600 (‘libelli duo’), one of them probably the Apollonius Gallus
entries.subject: Mathematics

acquisition.channel: gift/exchange

entries.editorial_note: Herwart von Hohenburg sent Tycho from Munich two booklets Viète had just published, without naming them (Herwart to Tycho, 26 April 1600; Opera omnia VIII, 305: ‘libelli duo, quos … FRANCISCUS VIETA, nuper in lucem prodire voluit … his iunctos ad te mitto’); Tycho acknowledged receipt in his letter to Herwart of 28 August 1600. Norlind (1970, p. 208) identifies one of them from Kepler’s letter to Herwart of July 1600 (Caspar no. 168), which reports that Kepler had seen at Tycho’s Viète’s ‘Opus de aequationibus’: not the De aequationum recognitione, printed only in 1615, but the Apollonius Gallus of 1600, whose second appendix (problems I and IV) determines a planet’s apogee and eccentricity from three observations. On 8 November 1600 Herwart described Viète’s Canon mathematicus under the title ‘Francisci Vietaei opera Mathematica’ and offered to procure it if Tycho wished (Herwart to Tycho, 8 November 1600; Opera omnia VIII, 386: ‘Quod si eum desideres, curabo omnino, ut habeas’) — an offer, not a sending, and not the Opera of 1646. Grade set on 20 October 2026 under the document rule (a surviving copy with his marks, or a document naming the book as his, is A; a dedication, the 1642 note alone or a queried mark is B; a third party's report or the compiler's inference is C).
open_questions: Which was the second of the two tracts of 1600: Norlind identifies only the Apollonius Gallus, and the De numerosa potestatum resolutione, printed at Paris the same year, is the other candidate; a letter naming it, or a copy with Tycho’s marks, would decide.

entries.title_transcribed: Libellus super vigintiduobus elementis conicis; Commentarius in undecim modos conficiendi eius problematis quod cubi duplicatio dicitur; De motu octavae sphaerae tractatus duo
entries.subject: Astronomy/Astrology/Mathematics
entries.editorial_note: Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 6:5, with marginalia in Tycho’s hand, ‘dürfte mit dem bei Norlind sub Nr. 32 zitierten Exemplare identisch sein’ — the Werner of Norlind’s list of 1926 (no. 32), there said to have come through Hagecius from Fabricius in Vienna; the library’s record 5 G 42/adl.4 notes his marginalia. Tycho sought the book for years for its De motu octavae sphaerae and had it at last from Hagecius, who sent on 1 November 1588 (O.S.) the copy he had had from Paul Fabricius in Vienna, acknowledged by Tycho in 1589; a second copy sent by Magini was lost on the way (Norlind 1970, p. 365; Opera omnia VII, pp. 104, 213, 295). The fifth piece of the Clementinum composite 5 G 42.

norlind.entry: Werner, Johannes: In hoc opere hæc continentur: Libellus Ioannis Verneri super vigintiduobus elementis conicis ... Norimbergæ 1522.4°. Z. 1193. Kl. nr 6: 5. – Prag, UB. I ett saml.-bd.
norlind.ownership_verdict: located copy, Prague (Kl. nr 6:5, in a Sammelband); obtained through Hagecius 1589 after several attempts; a second copy sent by Magini from Bologna lost in transit
norlind.discussion: – Tycho sökte flera gånger komma över denna skrift, vilken han till slut erhöll genom Hagecius (brev till denne nov. 1589; VII, 213). Hagecius hade dock tidigare skrivit (maj 1586; VII, 104), att boken icke stod att få. Ett annat exemplar sändes av Magini i Bologna men gick förlorat under vägen (till Magini dec. 1590; VII 295). Att Tycho varit så angelägen att skaffa sig boken, berodde nog helt visst på den däri ingående skriften »De motu octavæ sphæræ». I denna hade Werner ur egna och andras observationer dragit den slutsatsen, att den åttonde sfären (fixstjärnesfären) var underkastad en oscillerande rörelse – vilket han ansåg bekräfta den av senantika och medeltida astronomer omfattade s.k. trepidationsteorien. Tycho kritiserar emellertid Werner i bl.a. ett brev till Magini (dec 1590; VII, 295) och menar, att Werner använt fingerade

entries.title_transcribed: Observations of the comet of 1577 (sent to Tycho)
entries.subject: Astronomy

acquisition.channel: gift/exchange

entries.editorial_note: Wilhelm IV’s observations of the comet of 1577 reached Tycho through the Rothmann and Kassel correspondence (Tycho to Rothmann, 11 June 1588: ‘Recensui etiam in hoc libro... Observationes’) and were collated into his comet book, the Progymnasmata; they were not held as a discrete Wilhelm IV codex. Wilhelm IV’s own observation manuscripts survive at the Universitätsbibliothek Kassel — Landesbibliothek und Murhardsche Bibliothek, in the ‘2 Ms. astron.’ series (the observation corpus 1–7; the star catalogue 2 Ms. astron. 74; the handbook 2 Ms. astron. 5; Schrimpf and Verbunt 2021), with Wilhelm’s correspondence at the Hessisches Staatsarchiv, Marburg; those are Wilhelm’s copies, not Tycho’s. Status attested since 20 October 2026: nothing is contested — the observations reached Tycho and were collated into the comet book; no discrete codex was ever held. They had reached him earlier than the 1588 letter: through Paul Hainzel in March 1579 (Opera omnia VII 50) and from Kassel with Rothmann's letter dated in its own text ‘Cassellis 18 Calend. Maij … 1586’ = 14 April 1586 (VI 53–58; the Epistolarium's brahe-t_15850518001, re-dated) — register dossier of 27 October 2026, §18.

entries.title_transcribed: Cometa pogonias, qui anno labente 1577 apparuit
entries.subject: Astronomy (comet)
entries.editorial_note: Norlind 1970, p. 366 (Zinner 2871; Hellman 109), lists the tract among the books of the library because Tycho discusses it in the comet book (Opera omnia IV, 348–356); no copy, receipt or mark is recorded. Norlind’s introduction states the principle on which such tracts enter his catalogue: it may be regarded as fairly certain that nearly all the writings on the new star of 1572 and the comet of 1577 that Tycho reviews in the Progymnasmata and the comet book stood in the library on Hven (p. 335). As an unbound tract, Tycho’s copy would carry no known mark by which it could be recognised, and none has been identified.
