entries.title_transcribed: Vitellionis ... Peri optikes, id est De natura, ratione et proiectione radiorum visus, luminum, colorum atque formarum ... libri X (Nuremberg: Petreius, 1535)
entries.subject: Optics/Geometry

marks.inscription: 'T O' initials on the front cover; 'Collegij Caesarei Societatis JESU Pragae Anno 1636. Musei mathematici'; Šolc 2002 p. 332 prints the front-cover initials as ‘T O O’ (not ‘T O’); the college's note is dated 1636 on both titles in the library's provenance notes, 1638 in its former-owner field
marks.annotations: two pages of verse annotations; ‘Two pages contain annotations — verses’ (Šolc 2002 p. 332) — no hand named by any source
marks.binding: wooden boards, the spine half covered in leather, four bands, clasp holes (the library's Dürer record); spine lettered ‘Vitellio Mathematicus, Albertus Durerus’ (Šolc)

entries.editorial_note: Not in Kleinschnitzová; identified as Tycho’s by Šolc in 2002. National Library of the Czech Republic, Sign. 14 B 38: Witelo, Peri optikes (Nuremberg: Petreius, 1535), with Dürer’s Institutiones geometricae in four books (Paris: Wechel, 1532), the Latin Underweysung der Messung, bound after it as the first adligatum (adl. 1; the spine reads ‘Vitellio’ before ‘Durerus’). It is the only Witelo–Dürer Sammelband in the library, and distinct from Dürer’s star charts, which Tycho is attested to have owned but of which no copy has been identified. Wooden boards, the spine in brown leather lettered ‘Vitellio Mathematicus, Albertus Durerus’. Šolc (p. 332) prints the shelfmark as XIV B 38 and the imprints as Nuremberg 1585 and Paris 1582, ‘Geometriae lib. III’; the library’s records give 1535, 1532 and four books, and the entry follows them. The library’s provenance note names the Jesuit college (‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis JESU Pragae Anno 1636’) and the Mathematical Museum and records no Tycho note, so the identification rests on Šolc’s reading of the initials on the front cover and of the verse annotations. The volume has been digitised by the library with Google Books. Šolc 2006 (p. 192) has the volume reach the Jesuits ‘probably by sale’ in 1636 — six years before the transfer of 1642 and by a different act; his chapter of 1999 (§ 2.532) says the same with ‘presumably’. Dürer's Institutiones geometricae, bound before it, have their own entry since 20 October 2026 (the unit rule).

entries.title_transcribed: Commentarius in C. Plinii de naturalia librum secundum

acquisition.channel: bought in Tycho’s name by Magnus Bartholin from Johannes Aurifaber, one of Tycho’s assistants at Uraniborg, for a barrel of Rostock beer — the note on the title, ‘Hunc librum Magnus Bartolinus emit ab J. A. nomine Tychonis Brahe una Tonna Cerevisiae Rostochiensis’

marks.inscription: ‘Johannes Aurifaber’ and ‘Hunc librum Magnus Bartolinus emit ab J. A. nomine Tychonis Brahe una Tonna Cerevisiae Rostochiensis. n: Haec plus sapit palato, quam cerebro liber’ on the title (Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 7); the title read on the facsimile (canvas 5, 27 October 2026): 'Iohannes Aurifaber'; the purchase note '… unâ Tonnâ Cerevisiae Rostochiensis …' (beer, not rye); 'Collegij Caesarei Societatis IESV / Pragae A.o 1642.o' with 'Bibliothecae Mathematicae'
marks.annotations: notes in Tycho’s hand on the last leaf (Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 7); the Brevis descriptio cursus septem planetarum, ex libro octavo Martiani Capellae (Ziegler, pp. 447–454) annotated in Tycho’s hand, the hand matching his notes of April 1600 on Kepler’s Deliberatio and Conditiones (Gingerich 2002, pp. 323–328; Jardine & Segonds 2008, pp. 188–189 n. 4); the notes stand on p. 454 (canvas 490, below FINIS and in the left margin) and pp. 453 and 175 (canvases 489, 211); attribution to Tycho never compared in the Graphonomicon
marks.binding: plain limp vellum with tie stubs, no stamp, initials or date (canvases 1, 496)

entries.editorial_note: Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 7; NK Clementinum Sign. 7 B 27. Kleinschnitzová prints the title as ‘de naturalia librum secundum’; it is normalised here to ‘de naturali historia librum secundum’, the reading of the book itself (Ziegler’s commentary on Book II of Pliny’s Natural History, Basel 1531). The inscription on the title records the purchase: Magnus Bartholin bought the book in Tycho’s name from Johannes Aurifaber, one of the assistants on Hven, for a barrel of Rostock beer (‘Hunc librum Magnus Bartolinus emit ab J. A. nomine Tychonis Brahe una Tonna Cerevisiae Rostochiensis. n: Haec plus sapit palato, quam cerebro liber’); Norlind (1970, p. 366) takes Aurifaber to be Hans Crol, who died on Hven in 1591. The last leaf carries notes in Tycho’s hand (Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 7). Jardine and Segonds connect the annotated Martianus Capella passage with the formal refutation of Ursus’s Demonstratio that Johannes Müller drew up on 23 August 1600, the transcriptions of Martianus being authenticated the same day by Tycho’s advocate Johannes Fritsch; they hold it likely that Müller used Tycho’s notes and possible that Tycho annotated the commentary in direct response to the Demonstratio, in 1599–1600 — their inference, so marked (2008, pp. 188–189 and n. 4). Whether these are the notes on the last leaf that Kleinschnitzová records is not settled by either source.

norlind.entry: Ziegler, Jacobus: In C. Plinii de naturali historia librum secundum commentarius ... Basileæ 1531. 2°. Kl. nr 7. — Prag, UB.
norlind.ownership_verdict: located copy, Prague; bought in Tycho's name from Johannes Aurifaber (Hans Crol) by Magnus Bartolinus for a barrel of Rostock beer (‘unâ Tonnâ Cerevisiae Rostochiensis’ — Norlind's ‘råg’ is a slip)
norlind.discussion: Kl. nr 7. — Prag, UB. Enligt en anteckning på titelbladet har boken tillhört Johannes Aurifaber (väl identisk med Hans Crol, en av Tychos lärjungar på Hven, död där 1591), av vilken Magnus Bartolinus (Bertelsen) köpte den i Tychos namn för en tunna Rostock-råg.

entries.title_transcribed: Theatri humanae vitae volumen decimum-octavum [the last tome, volumina XVIII–XXIX: 33 books, pp. 3251–4373 and the index]
entries.subject: Encyclopaedia/commonplace (humanae vitae)

marks.binding: Gilt superexlibris: Tycho’s portrait on the upper board and his arms on the lower, each in an oval medallion ringed by a distich, ‘Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei / pulchrius eniteat quae latet interior’ and ‘Arma genus fundi pereunt, durabile virtus / et doctrina decus nobilitatis habent’. Brown leather over wooden boards, blind-tooled in three frames, the inner one with fourteen portrait medallions of scholars, four gilt rosettes, two chased brass clasps, seven raised bands (Zeitschrift für Bücherfreunde X, 1906–07, pp. 42–43). Mortensen (1955, pp. 28–30) takes it for a Renaissance trade binding that Tycho probably acquired bound (‘vistnok har erhvervet i indbunden Stand’) and then had stamped with the superexlibris, which he calls especially finely struck and well preserved; the 1906 notice supposed the binding made at Basel for Tycho, Bargum (1906–07) held it Danish work under Tycho’s direction, and Prandtl (1932) lists the volume among the Prachtbände. The superexlibris was imitated in press gilding on the cover of Lauritz Nielsen, Tycho Brahes Bogtrykkeri (1946) (Mortensen, p. 30).

dispersal.detail: The route out of the library and to Sweden is undocumented. In 1906 with the Munich bookseller Ludwig Rosenthal; with Baron Per Hierta (1864–1924) of Främmestad, Västergötland, so Prandtl 1932 (Band XXV); by 1955 in the Röhsska Konstslöjdmuseum, Göteborg (Mortensen 1955, pp. 28–30). Whether it came to the museum with Hjalmar Wijk’s donation of Hierta’s books in 1915 or from the sale of Hierta’s library after his death (Björck & Börjesson, Stockholm, October–November 1932, catalogue 272) is not established.

entries.editorial_note: Prandtl, Verzeichnis A no. 57, his Einzelband XXV, then with Per Hierta at Främmestad. Mortensen (1955, pp. 28–30) places the same volume in the Röhsska Konstslöjdmuseum, Göteborg, and Norlind (1970, p. 366) describes it as the last tome of the Theatrum, volumina XVIII–XXIX, 33 books (pp. 3251–4373 with the index). The volume was first published in 1906, when the Munich bookseller Ludwig Rosenthal sent it to the Zeitschrift für Bücherfreunde (the plaques reproduced, Heft 1, pp. 42–43); Bargum replied in the same volume (Beiblatt, pp. 124–126) that the binding was Danish work made under Tycho’s direction, that Gellius Sascerides may have procured the book at Basel or at the Frankfurt fair after the summer of 1588, and that Tycho may have taken from Zwinger’s title the name of his projected Theatrum astronomicum.
open_questions: How the volume came to the Röhsska museum — with Hjalmar Wijk’s donation of Hierta’s books in 1915, or from the sale of Hierta’s library after his death (Björck & Börjesson, 1932, catalogue 272) — is not established; the museum’s accession record would decide.

norlind.entry: Zwingerus, Theodorus: Theatri humanæ vitæ volumina XVIII-XXIX. Basileæ 1587. 2°. Pr. nr 57. — Göteborg, Röhsska konstslöjdsmuseet (tidigare ägare: frih. P. Hierta).
norlind.ownership_verdict: located copy, Göteborg (Röhsska), formerly P. Hierta; Prachtband with Tycho's portrait and arms
norlind.discussion: Pr. nr 57. — Göteborg, Röhsska konstslöjdsmuseet (tidigare ägare: frih. P. Hierta). Endast den sista delen, omfattande 33 böcker (s. 3251-4373, index) av denna gigantiska universal-encyklopedi. Praktbd med Tychos porträtt och vapen (se: H. Mortensen, s. 28-29).

entries.title_transcribed: [Eight unidentified Tycho-owned books, superexlibris and autograph marginalia, found in a Prague monastery, 1943]
entries.subject: (various)
entries.editorial_note: Felix Mainx reported to Mortensen that in 1943 he had found, in a Prague monastery library, eight further books, not further specified, bearing Tycho’s superexlibris and many autograph marginalia; he intended to describe the find in a later paper (Mortensen 1955, p. 30: ‘otte andre ikke nærmere angivne Bøger, som foruden Tycho Brahes Superexlibris havde mange egenhændige Marginalnoter’). The books have not been traced since.
open_questions: Which Prague monastery held the eight Tycho books Mainx saw in 1943, and whether he published them; the monastery's catalogue or Mainx's papers would settle it.

Strahov is excluded: its only Tycho volume with autograph-attributed marginalia and a mark on the binding is the Euclid AV II 2, and its mark is a blind-stamped name and date of 1567 (Pařez 2009), not the gilt portrait plaque Mortensen ascribes to all eight; the Regiomontanus DR VII 19 has the 1642 inscription and no supralibros. Strahov's Tychoniana were surveyed by its own librarian in 1996 and 2009 and its bindings by Straka (1919, 1920), Hamanová–Nuska (1966) and Voit (2020). On Mortensen's description Strahov is not Mainx's monastery; the question stays open for Emauzy, Břevnov and the others. Mainx's own notice on Strahov of 1940 (S_MAINX1940) names no supralibros volume and predates the find: it neither names nor excludes Strahov, the exclusion resting on Mortensen's description; the leaves of the three plaque volumes — Σ V 5/a and Σ VI 3 unexamined, AG XIV 7 with one reader's note recorded — are the residual test.

entries.title_transcribed: Ordo studiorum et lectionum in Academia Iulia
entries.subject: Education

concordance.norlind_headword: Ordo studiorum et lectionum in Academia Iulia...

entries.editorial_note: Norlind 1970, p. 355: the Helmstedt lecture list of 1599, of which Tycho owned a copy — he quotes from it the title of Duncan Liddel’s lectures, in which Liddel presented the world-system as the one described in Tycho’s comet book and left the reader to think Tycho was not its author (Tycho to Cramer, September 1599 (Opera omnia VIII, 185); Norlind, pp. 188 ff., on the Liddel affair). An academic broadside; a copy of Tycho’s would carry no known mark by which it could be recognised.

norlind.headword: Ordo studiorum et lectionum in Academia Iulia ...
norlind.entry: Ordo studiorum et lectionum in Academia Iulia ... Helmstædii 1599. 4°.
norlind.ownership_verdict: owned (Tycho quotes Liddel's lecture title from his own copy)
norlind.discussion: Av denna föreläsningskatalog från universitetet i Helmstedt ägde Tycho ett exemplar, varur han citerar titeln på Duncan Liddels föreläsningar. Liddel anger här – till Tychos stora förargelse – att Tycho beskrivit världssystemet i kometboken; läsaren får alltså det intrycket, att Tycho icke är upphovsmannen till detsamma (brev till Cramer sept. 1599; VIII, 185). Tycho misstänker därför, att Liddel själv avsett att utge det som sitt eget. Se vidare s. 188 ff.

entries.title_transcribed: Programma of the Helmstedt promotion of September 1596 (Duncan Liddel’s doctorate in medicine)
entries.subject: Education
entries.editorial_note: Norlind 1970, p. 358: at this promotion, in September 1596, Duncan Liddel was created doctor of medicine; the promotor, Franciscus Parcovius, spoke of Liddel in terms that made Tycho, who quotes the passage, suspect Liddel of claiming the world-system Tycho had published. Tycho owned a single copy and therefore sent Cramer a transcript (Tycho to Cramer, September 1599 (Opera omnia VIII, 186)). Norlind could not trace the print itself. No copy of the programme is traced, and a copy of Tycho’s would carry no known mark by which it could be recognised.

norlind.entry: [Promotions-program, Helmstedt 1596.]
norlind.ownership_verdict: owned a single copy (letter to Cramer 1599, who was sent a transcript); the print itself not traced by Norlind
norlind.discussion: Vid denna promotion, som skedde i sept., kreerades Duncan Liddel till medicine doktor. Av denna skrift ägde Tycho endast ett exemplar, varför han skickar Cramer en avskrift (till Cramer sept. 1599; VIII, 186). I programmet hade promotor, professor Franciscus Parcovius, uttalat sig på ett sådant sätt om Liddel att Tycho, som citerar denna passus, misstänkte, att Liddel tillskrivit sig äran av det världssystem, som Tycho framlagt. Det har icke varit mig möjligt att belägga denna skrift.

entries.title_transcribed: Typus pompae funebris 5. Junii anno 1588 habitae Rodtschildii in exequiis Friderici II Daniae regis, opera et consilio Henrici Rantzovii efformatus (Frans Hogenberg and Simon Novellanus, twenty engravings)
entries.subject: History and antiquities

acquisition.channel: Rantzau’s gift (Tycho to Rantzau, December 1588; Opera omnia VII, 386)

entries.editorial_note: Norlind 1970, p. 364: twenty engravings of the funeral procession of Frederik II at Roskilde on 5 June 1588, made at Rantzau’s instance and dedicated to Christian IV. Tycho acknowledged the gift to Rantzau in December 1588 — ‘delineationem exequiarum ac sepulturae regiae Hamburgi per te aeneis figuris procuratam’ (Opera omnia VII, 386). A print series from the Rantzau connection rather than a book of the study; no copy with a mark of Tycho’s is known.

norlind.entry: Typus pompæ funebris 5. Junii Anno 1588. habitæ Rodtschildii in exequiis Serenissimi ac Potentissimi Domini Friderici II. Daniæ ... regis opera et consilio ... Henrici Rantzovii efformatus et D. Christiano IIII. dedicatus a Franc. Hogenbergio et Sim. Novellano. s. l. et s. a. 2°.
norlind.ownership_verdict: received as a gift from Rantzau (letter)
norlind.discussion: Består av 20 kopparstick visande begravningsprocessionen vid konung Fredrik II:s likbegängelse. Åsyftas av Tycho i ett brev till Rantzau dec. 1588 (VII, 386), där han skriver, att han av denne fått »delineationem exequiarum ac sepulturæ regiæ Hamburgi per te æneis figuris procuratam».

survivors.marks_securing_id: brown stamped leather with the blind initials ‘I. P. 1561’ (Johannes Pratensis); the purchase note ‘Emptus Haffniae 2 Joachimicis 1560 ultimo Novembris’ (hand disputed: Tycho — Dreyer, Studnička 1901; Pratensis — Boldan & Vackářová 2024); marginalia Kleinschnitzová gives to Tycho; on the title ‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis Jesu Pragae A°. 1642’, ‘NB. Marginales notae sunt Tichonis Brahe’ and, in another hand, ‘Bibliothecae Mathematicae’ (Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 4) | binding period: another owner’s binding (I. P. 1561) || Prague catalogue (National Library, Staré tisky), copy-level provenance note, verbatim: Na titulní straně dole rukou: Emptus Haffniae 2 Joachimicis 1560 Vltimo Nouembris. | Na titulní straně dvakrát rukou: Ioannes Pratentis. | Na titulní straně rukou poznámka: NB. Marginales notae sunt Tichonis Brahe. Na přídeští je nalepená cedulka s rukopisným textem upozorňujícím na vlastnictví a rukopisné poznámky Tychona Brahe. | Na titulní straně exlibris pražských jezuitů: Collegij Caesarei Societatis JESV Pragae A[nn]o 1642. | Na titulní straně dodatečně jinou rukou: Bibliothecae Mathematicae. || Read on the Manuscriptorium facsimile, 27 October 2026 (canvas 3, native crop): the purchase note at the title foot reads ‘Emptus Haffniae 2 Ioachimicis / 1560 Vltimo / Nouembris’ in three lines below BASILEÆ; the Jesuit inscription ‘Collegij Cæsarei Socie[ta]tis IESV Pragæ A° 1642.’ is written large round the printer's device (the year 1642); to its right, below the year, ‘NB. Marginales notæ / sunt Tichonis Brahe.’ (spelled Tichonis); ‘Bibliotheca’ and ‘Mathematica’ flank BASILEÆ; ‘Iohannes Pratensis’ stands at the head and again below the printed title. The facsimile does not show the 1561 binding: canvases 1–2 and 551–552 are a modern grey archival wrapper (canvas 1 pencilled ‘5 B 70’; canvas 2 the NK label with barcode 1002620412).
survivors.identified_by: Prandtl, Die Bibliothek des Tycho Brahe (Verzeichnis B)
survivors.notes: Prandtl’s Band I, his Einzelband 31, a single volume of 1551: the book Dreyer made Tycho’s first; on the evidence reviewed on 29 October 2026 it is Johannes Pratensis’s purchase of 30 November 1560, bound for him in 1561, and Tycho’s only later — not before 1561, probably after Pratensis’s death in 1576 (below). Friis described the volume in 1868: ‘Johannes Pratensis’ twice on the title, the purchase note, which he read as written by Tycho himself, and the Jesuit inscription, which he printed with the year ‘Ao. 1644’ — a transcription slip, since the National Library’s record and the title page read 1642 (Friis 1868–69, p. 267). Prusík listed the volume in 1901 as group A, no. 7, Sign. 5 B 70, with the purchase note read as Tycho’s and the Jesuit note on the title, ‘Marginales notae sunt Tichonis Brahe. 1642’. The hand of the purchase note is disputed. Reproduced in colour by Šolc (2018, figs 4, 4b–c, p. 198 (the binding with ‘I. P. 1561’, the title with the purchase note)). Šolc (2018, pp. 195–196, figs 4, 4b–c) has the volume Johannes Pratensis's — the brown binding blind-stamped ‘I. P. 1561’, his name twice on the title — until Tycho took it over ‘spätestens 1576 nach dessen Tod’, and reads the purchase note as the book's purchase of 30 November 1560 for two Joachimsthaler without assigning its hand: a third position in the hand dispute, consistent with the Pratensis reading. Christianson (1967, p. 201 n. 13) held the volume Pratensis’s — ‘it has now been shown to have belonged to Johannes Pratensis, from whom Tycho probably inherited it in 1576’ — and printed a note in Dreyer’s hand (Royal Library, NKS 3077 4°, p. 101) recording Friis’s later opinion, against his own print of 1868, that the marginalia are few, insignificant and Pratensis’s. In the Manuscriptorium facsimile the first two images show a modern cover, not the binding; the title page, with Pratensis’s name twice, the Jesuit inscription of 1642 and the purchase note in a smaller hand at the foot, is image 3 (read 25 October 2026). The hands were compared on the facsimile on 25 October 2026 (the comparison method, every pair audited against the images): the purchase note agrees with the Pratensis signatures and with Tycho’s dated specimens of 1583 and 1599 only in the common forms of the period and differs from each in one or two constructions — from the signatures in the h (the second leg descending in the note, the first stem in the signatures) and in the minims, from Tycho’s hand in the capital I (no J-descender) and the final s (at x-height, not descending) — and from both hands of the volume of 1561 likewise; the marginalia share Tycho’s u-marks and looped g but draw on a German-cursive repertoire his secure hands show nowhere (the open e, the 3-shaped final s, no ſt/ct arch, the final i with a descender). Every pair: inconclusive; the note is not shown to be Tycho’s and not shown to be Pratensis’s, the marginalia lean away from Tycho. The facsimile’s c. 15–20 px x-height for the note is the limit; a sharper photograph of the title foot and a Pratensis prose specimen would decide it. || Re-read of the June 2026 census positives, 27 October 2026 (ch. III): 69 manuscript pages, 3 possible, 22 printed only (base: the 94 June positives); the re-reader sees one main sixteenth-century italic annotating hand with possibly a second (the star-name glosses at pp. 249–250), a Greek cursive (pp. 75, 426, 445) and a rapid German-style cursive (pp. 340, 350, 358) — a provisional separation, never compared. || 29 October 2026 — the literature pack read whole (41 passages, 26 documents) in the lecture session: the chain of the ‘first book’ is Friis 1868–69 → Dreyer 1890 → Prusík 1901 (‘seine eigenhändige Bemerkung’) → Studnička 1901 (‘Die eigenhändige Bemerkung des 14-jährigen Studiosus’, the binding’s 1561 put down to the binder) → Kukula 1906 → Prandtl 1932 → Šolc 1999 (‘kaufte Tycho Brahe aus dem Besitz von Johann Pratensis 1560’), none of them comparing the hand; against it Kleinschnitzová 1933 (p. 74), Christianson 1967 (p. 201 n. 13, with Friis’s own retraction in Dreyer’s note), Šolc 2006 and 2018 (‘spätestens 1576 nach dessen Tod’), Boldan & Vackářová 2024 (Pratensis the first documented owner, the inheritance ‘pravděpodobné’) and the National Library’s record (Pratensis 1561; Tycho without a year). Nothing in the volume dates Tycho’s ownership; what makes it his at all is the college’s note of 1642 and the donation from his heirs. Ownership of the entry graded B; the volume no longer stands as the first datable object of Tycho’s library (the Q&A of the lecture folder, 29 October 2026).

annotation_scan.state_note: Re-read 27 October 2026 (ch. III): 69 manuscript, 3 possible, 22 printed only of the 94 June positives; the June p. 299 transcription is a printed note.

custody.basis: The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931). Norlind (1970, p. 358) read Benjamin Ursinus’s letter to Kepler of March 1614 (Caspar no. 681, p. 105), asking him to request ‘Ptolemaeum Tychonis’ from the Rožmberk librarian, as referring to this copy, and found the work in Václav Březan’s catalogue of the Rožmberk library at Třeboň (1602–08; Royal Library, Stockholm).

custody.station: Jesuit college in the Clementinum (Collegium Caesareum), Prague — the Mathematical Museum
custody.basis: The inscription ‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis JESV Pragae A[nn]o 1642.’ on the title, as the National Library’s record transcribes it; the later note ‘Bibliothecae Mathematicae.’ places the volume in the college’s mathematical library.

custody.station: The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague
custody.basis: The college library passed to the state with the suppression of 1773 and became the public University Library in the Clementinum; the Tychoniana were mixed with the other mathematical books and reassembled by the librarians around 1900 (Šolc 2002, p. 329).

open_questions: Whether the purchase note ‘Emptus Haffniae 2 Joachimicis 1560 ultimo Novembris’ is in Tycho’s hand (Dreyer; Studnička 1901) or in that of Johannes Pratensis (Boldan and Vackářová 2024); a comparison of the note with dated specimens of both hands would decide.

27 Oct 2026 — the comparison this question asks for was run on 25 October 2026 against Tycho's dated hands of 1583 and 1599, the Pratensis signatures and both hands of the 1561 Helsingør volume: every pair inconclusive (Hand_comparison_5B70_2026-10-25.md; borderline.md holds note and marginalia as candidates). The limit is the facsimile's c. 15–20 px x-height (confirmed on the native crop of canvas 3, 27 October 2026) and the want of any Pratensis prose specimen; a macro photograph of the title foot from NK ČR and a Pratensis prose autograph are the tests that remain.

Who wrote the slip pasted on the front pastedown drawing attention to Tycho's ownership and manuscript notes (the library's provenance note), and when — a pastedown photograph from NK ČR (the reproduction desk) would show it.

How many hands annotate the volume: the re-read of 27 October 2026 suggests a main italic hand, a star-gloss hand, a Greek hand and a German cursive; a specimen set from the 69 manuscript pages compared through the Graphonomicon would settle the count before any attribution.
Whether ‘NB. Marginales notæ sunt Tichonis Brahe.’ is in the hand of the 1642 inscription beside it or a later addition — a higher-resolution photograph of the title's lower right would decide it.

29 Oct 2026 [reframed] - the question is no longer whether the note is Tycho's but when the book became his: the evidence as it stands makes it Pratensis's purchase of 1560, bound for him in 1561, and Tycho's later; the 1642 note and the donation are the only grounds, and a Pratensis estate record or a dated Tycho note in the volume would close it.

survivors.institution_raw: M/S Museet for Søfart, Helsingør (formerly Handels- og Søfartsmuseet på Kronborg)
survivors.later_owners: Antiquariat Weiss & Co., Munich (by 1932) → Maggs Bros., London (Catalogue 582, 1933, item 155, £125; Catalogue 600, 1934, item 260, £125; Catalogue 666, 1938, item 451, p. 166, £125) → Herbert Reichner, New York (Catalogue 1, [1939], item 72, probably $850) → unknown, c. 1940–1956 → Oscar Ekman (1885–1956), engineer, and Lia Ekman (1894–1965), Copenhagen → their gift to the Handels- og Søfartsmuseet på Kronborg in the museum year 1956–57 (inventory 1957:0030) → deposited by the museum at the Royal Library, Håndskriftafdelingen, in 1986 (Acc. 1986/116), lent from there to the Ole Rømer Museum's exhibition of October–December 2001 → in the museum's own keeping again, the deposit ended (the museum's curator, 13 October 2026)
survivors.marks_securing_id:
front board: TVCHO BRADE, rear board: ANNO 1561 (stamped, originally gilt); fly-title: ‘tico brade ven:’ (struck through), ‘Tycho Brade’ and further ownership inscriptions (leaf half torn, repaired); fly-title verso: ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ [I am Tycho Brahe's] (struck through), ‘Eptg [emptus] thalero & 4 Groshj’ [bought for a thaler and 4 groschen], beneath it an astronomical note, partly lost; a note in ink on the front pastedown; fol. 53r–v of the Apianus: four places with their positions in Tycho's hand; on the spine the remnant of a label with a library shelfmark 204; Latin plant names at the head of a run of recto pages in a hand other than Tycho's, and small plant remains between leaves (Magasin 1987, p. 31; Björklund 1992, p. 26; confirmed 20 October 2026); at the head of the front pastedown the pencil figure ‘+125’, Maggs's price of 1933, and a second figure (the museum's photograph).

Thykier (1985 inspection; report of 13 January 2003) reads the front of the fly-title (his ‘forperm’) as the autograph ‘Tyge Brahe’ struck through and ‘tico brahe ven’ struck through (‘en lidt barnlig skrift’ [a somewhat childish hand]), and in another hand ‘Sum Paul…’, the rest lost on the torn-off part; on its back, under a struck line where ‘Brade’ can be glimpsed, the price ‘… 4 taliro & 4 Gross.’; short astronomical notes in Tycho's hand inside the binding and on the back of the leaf, and one in the margin of the preface's tenth (unpaginated) page; Latin plant names at the head of 36 unpaginated pages in a hand other than Tycho's, plant remains in the gutter of 26 of them (microscoped by Jette Baagøe, re-housed in annotated envelopes of acid-free silk paper), further remains between pages without names, one plant name unattested before c. 1623 (Peter Wagner and Baagøe).

Examined and photographed at the museum on 20 October 2026. Fly-title recto: ‘tico brade ven:’ in a thin early hand, struck through once in the same ink; beside it a name obliterated under heavy black strokes (Thykier: ‘Tyge Brahe’), ringed in pencil; to the right, in a firmer hand with a flourish, ‘Sum Pauli’ [I am Paul's], complete to its last letter, what followed lost with the torn-away part; above it a smudged short word in another ink, and at the head, right, a short word in a darker ink, both unread; at the head, left, pencil ‘Acc. 1986/116’. Fly-title verso: ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ under a heavy bar, ‘Sum’ and ‘Brade’ legible beside it; below it the purchase note ‘Eptg thaliro & 4 Grossj’ [bought for a thaler and 4 groschen]; beneath that, intact, a two-branch memorandum in bracket form — ‘Decl: Merid: … obliqua {Adde / Subtr.} diff. asc. ab Ascensione Recta — Septen: … obliqua {Subtr. / Adde} diff. Asc. ab Asc. R.’, ‘obliqua’ struck and ‘Recta’ written above it — a rule for passing from right to oblique ascension by the sign of the declination. Front pastedown: an ink note in the same early hand (‘Ascens: decl: Merid: … ex Asc: Recta / Septm: Sub S … hoc modo’, a companion rule); a pencil collation in German (‘… 70 (von 1–74) … 31–34 … 1 Doppelbl. …’, the trace of the Munich trade); pencil ‘1986/116’. Spine: a paper slip in the second compartment with ‘20’ and a damaged third figure consistent with 4, the figures written by hand in ink; nothing else lettered, no label surviving at the tail. Rear flyleaf: a faint ‘N 36’ at the head and a small blind-stamped cartouche near the gutter, both unread. Rear pastedown: in ballpoint ‘Gave jan. 1957 fra civiling. Oskar Ekman’ [gift, January 1957, from the engineer Oskar Ekman], the stamp HANDELS- OG SØFARTSMUSEET PÅ KRONBORG HELSINGØR – DANMARK [the Trade and Maritime Museum at Kronborg, Helsingør, Denmark], and ‘30:57’ in blue. Box: brown cloth clamshell, its gilt spine label lettered in English — JOHANN DE MONTEREGIO TABULAE DIRECTIONUM 1550 BOUND WITH PETRUS APPIANUS COSMOGRAPHIA 1553. TYCHO BRAHE'S COPY WITH AUTOGRAPH OWNERSHIP NOTES, ETC. — with ‘30:57’ written on it.

Reader's marks in the Regiomontanus: a grey marginal note in an early hand on the Octavum problema page (‘pro g. m. / 60 / sec. / 15 / tert. / differentia’ — Thykier's note on the tenth page of the preface); tallies ij iij iiij beside ‘Ille autem numerus polaris’; a red-brown stepped line drawn through the Tabula declinationum; a large pen flourish at the head of the Tabula ascensionum rectarum. In the Apianus: ‘Octava sphaera’ written at the ring of the Schema praemissae divisionis, ‘Wittenberga’ underlined in the German place table; on fol. 53r ‘Elzingborgum 35 46. 57 0’ (a superscript c above the name) and ‘Lunda 36 30 57 23’, on fol. 53v ‘Vesbÿ Gotlandiæ 47 5. 59 50’ and the fourth place, its letters R-?-n-s-f-a-l-?-h-?, ‘46 35 60 15’, all four in one ink and ductus. The plant names stand at the head of the preface leaves (Pulmonaria, Ranunculus aquaticus, Hedera arborescens …) in a later hand, and the envelopes of plant remains lie at their openings; read letter by letter from the frames on 21 October 2026: the purchase note is ‘Eptꝰ thaliro & 4 Groſs.’ — emptus thalero et 4 grossis — the sign after ‘Ept’ being the -us abbreviation, not a g; the pastedown rule reads in full ‘Aſcens. decl {Merid. [Adde, blotted out by the writer] / Septen. Sub} ex Aſc. Recta / in deſcenſionibꝫ contrario modo’, the same rule as the verso's bracket memorandum, whose surviving case labels are ‘…rom:’ and ‘…nes’; above the rule a darker ‘Angl. 5.’, unexplained; the smudged word above ‘Sum Paüli’ reads ‘Brÿſſe’ or ‘Chrÿſſe’ and stands inside a wet-wiped erasure of an earlier inscription, the head-right word ‘to bra[h/n][e/o]’; the heavy black strokes through the recto name and through the verso's ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ are one ink and one campaign, a later owner's cancellation of both Brahe names, while the thin stroke through ‘tico brade ven:’ is earlier and different; the herbarium hand also wrote ‘Lamiꝫ’, ‘Liſimachia flore luteo’ and ‘Hÿacinthꝰ’; on fol. 53 ‘Lůnda lůndt’ and ‘Veſbÿ Gotlandiæ’ carry the u-mark and the diaeresis, and the fourth place is the museum's ‘Rumefalche’ (the tall letter is an f with a cross-bar), identified on 21 October 2026 as Schöner's — Luculentissima quaedam terrae totius descriptio (Nuremberg 1515), fo. 34r, ‘Gotlandiae insu. civita.: Bespue 47.5.59.50. Rumefalche 46.35.60.15.’ — a Clavus-derived pseudo-toponym of Gotland from the Ulm Ptolemy of 1486, so that both added lines on fol. 53v are copied, name and figures, from Schöner or from his source; a pencil ‘choo’ on the rear pastedown | binding period: Period 1 (student bindings, 1560–1567)
survivors.identified_by: Prandtl, Die Bibliothek des Tycho Brahe (Verzeichnis B); the museum's record and photographs (the binding stamps, the inscriptions leaf by leaf, the purchase note, the added positions on fol. 53 of the Apianus); examined and photographed at the museum on 20 October 2026 (the stamps TVCHO BRADE and ANNO 1561, the fly-title's inscriptions and purchase note on both sides of the leaf, the fol. 53 entries, the museum's accession note)
survivors.notes:
Prandtl’s Band II, the student binding of 1561: Regiomontanus’s Tabulae directionum (Tübingen, Ulrich Morhart, 1550) bound before Apianus’s Cosmographia in Gemma Frisius’s recension (Paris, Vivant Gaultherot, 1553; the colophon dated 1551). Prandtl recorded it in 1932 at Antiquariat Weiss & Co., Munich, and as sold to America; Gingerich (2002, p. 325) still placed it at an undisclosed location, calling it ‘the 1561 edition’ of the Apianus after the date on the binding. It had in fact returned to Denmark within a generation: the Handels- og Søfartsmuseet på Kronborg reported it among the acquisitions of 1956–57 as the gift of Lia Ekman and her late husband, the engineer Oscar Ekman, and Norlind placed it there in 1970 (pp. 338 and 361).

The museum’s record (Museernes Samlinger, inventory 1957:0030, priref 400004307, revised 16 June 2026) describes the volume leaf by leaf. The Regiomontanus: title, [43] pp. text, [268] pp. tables, a few notes in the head margin. The Apianus: title woodcut, fol. 1–74 with the volvelles, the cordiform world map inserted between fol. 34 and 35, the tables of positions from fol. 37; on fol. 53r–v Tycho has added four places with their figures, which the museum reads ‘Elzingborgum 35 46. 57 0 / Lunda Lundt 36 30 57 23 / Vesby Gotlandiæ 47 5. 59 50 / Rumefalche [?] 46 35 60 15’ — Helsingborg, Lund, Visby, and a fourth place the museum could not read. Quarto; stained, water-stained and wormed. Brown calf, blind-ruled mirror panels on both boards with originally gilt floral stamps, TVCHO BRADE stamped on the front board and ANNO 1561 on the rear, three raised bands, and on the spine the remnant of a label with the library shelfmark 204 — an owner between Tycho and the Munich trade whom no source names. The inscriptions: a note in ink on the front pastedown; on the fly-title, struck through, ‘tico brade ven:’, then ‘Tycho Brade’ and further ownership inscriptions, the leaf half torn and repaired; on its verso ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ [I am Tycho Brahe's], struck through, the purchase note ‘Eptg [emptus] thalero & 4 Groshj’ [bought for a thaler and 4 groschen], and beneath it an astronomical note, partly lost. Prandtl’s ‘Vorsatzblatt’ [endpaper] with the note and the name three times is thus placed: the purchase note is on the verso of the fly-title, not on the pastedown. Kept in a cloth-covered box; restored in 1957 by Birgitte Dall, Copenhagen. The record’s two photographs show the front board, and the volume open in its box at the Regiomontanus title with the fly-title raised, its verso with the purchase note and the astronomical note towards the camera. The record is filed in the museum’s case ‘Deponeringer div:’ (deposits), which agrees with the Royal Library deposit of 1986.

The Danish record of the volume, in order. Klem’s museum report for 1956–57 (Årbog 1957, p. 8) lists it among the year’s acquisitions as ‘en gave fra fru Lia Ekman og afdøde ægtefælle, civilingeniør Oscar Ekman’ [a gift from Mrs Lia Ekman and her late husband, the engineer Oscar Ekman], bought by Tycho ‘i 1561’ for ‘1 Thaler, 4 Groschen’. Erik Dal in Bogvennen (1966, p. 205), reviewing the Ekman sale (Bruun Rasmussen auction 186, 1–4 November 1965), names among the show-pieces withdrawn as bequests ‘en bog fra Tycho Brahes bibliotek (til Kronborg — Rundetaarn bød samtidig meget højt, men forgæves på en lignende hos Sotheby)’ [a book from Tycho Brahe's library (to Kronborg — Rundetaarn at the same time bid very high, but in vain, on a similar one at Sotheby's)]: the volume was still the museum’s in 1965. The Kronik of Magasin fra Det Kongelige Bibliotek (2:1, 1987, p. 31) records its deposit in the Royal Library’s Håndskriftafdeling, the contact arranged by museumsleder Claus Thykier of Ole Rømers Museum, the museum on Kronborg remaining the owner — an earlier witness to the deposit than Björklund 1992. The Kronik prints the front-board stamp as ‘Tycho Brahe’, a normalisation of the museum’s reading TVCHO BRADE; it reports ‘adskillige notater med flere hænder, deriblandt Tycho Brahes’ [several notes in more than one hand, among them Tycho Brahe's], and gives the herbarium use as a suggestion that had not been examined (‘foreslået … endnu ikke kunnet undersøges’ [suggested … not yet possible to examine], p. 33), which Björklund 1992 then states as fact. The Royal Library’s newsletter of November 2001 shows the volume still on deposit (Acc. 1986/116), lent to the Ole Rømer Museum’s exhibition of that autumn, and the Nationalmuseet catalogue of 2006 reproduced it from a Royal Library photograph. The deposit has ended: the museum’s curator, Thorbjørn Thaarup, confirmed in writing on 13 October 2026 that the volume is part of the museum’s collection and is kept at the museum (‘en del af vores samling og opbevares hos os’ [part of our collection and kept with us]); when it returned from the Royal Library is not stated.

The twentieth-century route, established on 20 October 2026: Prandtl’s ‘sold from Munich to America’ was wrong about the first step. Maggs Bros. of London offered the volume in Catalogue 582 (1933), item 155, at £125 — the entry collates both works, gives the stamps, transcribes ‘Sum Tychonis Brade / Epts thaliro & 4 Gross’ [I am Tycho Brahe's / bought for a thaler and 4 groschen], notes the half-torn fly-leaf and the Helsingborg note, and cites Prandtl for ‘our volume’ — again in Catalogue 600 (1934), item 260, and still in Catalogue 666 (1938), item 451, p. 166, always at £125, the figure pencilled on the front pastedown; the New York Times reviewed the 1933 catalogue on 28 May 1933. It reached New York only with Herbert Reichner’s first catalogue ([1939], item 72, probably $850) and is in none of his later ones. Between about 1940 and 1956 nothing is known.

Three published readings do not hold. The Kronik’s argument of 1987 that the price in thaler and groschen is Saxon coin and that the Leipzig matriculation register enters Tycho under 16 October 1561 fails on both points: the Copenhagen Ptolemy of 1560 is itself priced in Joachimsthaler, and 16 October is the winter-semester heading, the rector entering the term’s students at its end (Norlind 1970, p. 16); the binding’s ‘Anno 1561’ and every other witness put the purchase in Copenhagen. The Helsingborg and Lund figures on fol. 53r are the book’s own printed values from the Scania table on fol. 41v, transcribed beside the Zealand–Scania island entry; Visby and the fourth place stand beside the printed Gotland entry on fol. 53v. Christianson 1967 (Isis 58, p. 201), citing Prandtl, puts the ‘Anno 1561’ stamp on the spine — a slip; it is on the rear board. The provenance is set out in the deep-research dossier of 20 October 2026.

Claus Thykier’s report of 13 January 2003 (Ole Rømer Museet; absorbed 20 October 2026) is the examiner’s own account: he inspected the volume at the museum’s library in 1985, arranged its deposit at the Royal Library in 1986 (acc. 1986/116), and records the gift as January 1957 from civilingeniør Oskar Ekman with further provenance unknown. He reads the front of the fly-title (his ‘forperm’) as ‘Tyge Brahe’ struck through and ‘tico brahe ven’ struck through, and in another hand ‘Sum Paul…’, the rest lost on the torn-off part; the price, under a struck line where ‘Brade’ can be glimpsed, as ‘… 4 taliro & 4 Gross.’ in Saxon coin, which led him to leave open a journey abroad in 1561 or a book sent by courier (both answered by the semester convention: Norlind 1970, p. 16). He describes the herbarium: plant names at the head of 36 unpaginated pages in a hand not Tycho’s, remains in the gutter of 26 of them identified under the microscope by Jette Baagøe and re-housed in envelopes with the modern names, one name unattested before c. 1623 (Peter Wagner), so that the user ‘formentlig ikke har haft kontakt med Tycho’ [probably had no contact with Tycho]; and an astronomical note in Tycho’s hand in the margin of the preface’s tenth page. The book is to be kept horizontal in its capsule so that the plant remains do not fall out.

Examined and photographed at the museum on 20 October 2026, the volume, its box and the examiner’s report of 2003 brought from the store. What the leaves settle: the fly-title recto carries ‘tico brade ven:’ in a thin early hand, struck through once in the same ink; a name obliterated under heavy black strokes, which Thykier read as ‘Tyge Brahe’; and, in a firmer hand with a flourish, ‘Sum Pauli’ [I am Paul's] — complete to its final letter, so the owner’s first name is all the leaf ever carried of him, and what stood on the torn-away part was not the rest of it; two further short words, one smudged, one at the head right, stay unread. The verso’s struck line is the museum’s ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ — ‘Sum’ and ‘Brade’ are legible beside the bar — so the museum’s transcription and Thykier’s ‘a struck line where Brade can be glimpsed’ describe one line, and the recto’s ‘Sum Pauli’ is one of the museum’s ‘further ownership inscriptions’: the three witnesses agree once the two sides of the leaf are told apart. Beneath the purchase note the astronomical memorandum is intact — a two-branch rule in bracket form for passing from right to oblique ascension by the sign of the declination, ‘obliqua’ struck and ‘Recta’ written above it — and the ink note on the front pastedown is a companion rule in the same early hand. The front pastedown also carries a pencil collation in German, the trace of the Munich trade, and the Royal Library’s accession number in pencil, which stands again as ‘Acc. 1986/116’ at the head of the fly-title and on the slip kept in the box.

The spine label is a paper slip with the figures written in ink, ‘20’ and a damaged third figure consistent with 4; nothing else is lettered on the spine, and the larger label or patch that Prandtl’s plate of 1932 showed at the tail is gone. The rear flyleaf carries a faint ‘N 36’ at the head and a small blind-stamped cartouche near the gutter — a second earlier number and a dealer’s or restorer’s mark, both unread. The box is a brown cloth clamshell box with a gilt spine label lettered in English, ‘Tycho Brahe’s copy with autograph ownership notes, etc.’ — made in the English-speaking trade or for the American owner between 1933 and 1956, the one physical trace of that interval. The rear pastedown has the museum’s accession note in ballpoint, ‘Gave jan. 1957 fra civiling. Oskar Ekman’ [gift, January 1957, from the engineer Oskar Ekman], with the Kronborg stamp and ‘30:57’, the inventory number in its old form: the gift was entered in January 1957 under Oscar Ekman’s name, four months after his death on 16 September 1956 — which reconciles Klem’s ‘fru Lia Ekman og afdøde ægtefælle’ [Mrs Lia Ekman and her late husband], Thykier’s ‘January 1957 from civilingeniør Oskar Ekman’ and Dal’s ‘testamentarisk bortgivet’ [given away by bequest]: a gift in the dead man’s name, made by his widow.

The herbarium is confirmed: the plant names stand at the head of the preface leaves (Pulmonaria, Ranunculus aquaticus, Hedera arborescens …) in a later hand, and the envelopes of plant remains lie at their openings, so the box must stay flat. The four places on fol. 53r–v are in one ink and ductus, written in one campaign: ‘Elzingborgum’ with a superscript c, ‘Lunda’, ‘Vesbÿ Gotlandiæ’, and the fourth, whose letters read R-?-n-s-f-a-l-?-h-? and whose figures, set against the printed values, put it about half a degree west of Visby and a little north — the Swedish coast opposite Gotland, if the figures are to be trusted; the name, not the figures, must decide. The reader’s marks — tallies, a red stepped line through the declination table, a pen flourish, ‘Octava sphaera’, ‘Wittenberga’ underlined — are of several hands and dates, and none is attributed. Nothing here has been compared with a dated specimen of Tycho’s hand: ‘Tycho’s hand’ remains the attribution of Prandtl, the museum and Thykier. Read letter by letter from the frames on 21 October 2026. The purchase note is ‘emptus thalero et 4 grossis’ — the sign that the museum, Thykier and the examination of 20 October took for a g is the 9-shaped -us abbreviation. The ink rule on the front pastedown reads in full: oblique ascension, for a southern declination add, for a northern subtract, the ascensional difference from the right ascension; in descensions the contrary way — the writer blotted out his first ‘Adde’ and wrote the rule again on the fly-title verso as a bracket table, there striking ‘obliqua’ and writing ‘Recta’ above it. The smudged word above ‘Sum Pauli’ stands inside a wet-wiped erasure of an earlier inscription and reads ‘Brÿſſe’ or ‘Chrÿſſe’; the heavy black strokes through the recto name and through the verso's ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ are one ink and one campaign — a later owner cancelled both Brahe names, and the thin stroke through ‘tico brade ven:’ is an earlier, different cancellation. Three more plant names were read (Lamium, Lysimachia flore luteo, Hyacinthus), the Octavum problema column in full, and the fourth place on fol. 53v confirmed as the museum's ‘Rumefalche’ (the tall letter has a cross-bar: f, not a long ſ; a first reading of 21 October took it for ſ and is withdrawn). The same day the name was identified: ‘Bespue 47.5.59.50.’ and ‘Rumefalche 46.35.60.15.’ are the two ‘cities’ of Gotland on fo. 34r of Johannes Schöner's Luculentissima quaedam terrae totius descriptio (Nuremberg 1515), the text to his globe, and Schöner's northern towns come from the Ulm Ptolemy of 1486, whose Scandinavian names are Claudius Clavus's (Bjørnbo and Petersen 1904, pp. 115 and 118) — Rumefalche is one of Clavus's invented Gotland names, not a place, and its figures are a position on a map, not an observation. Helsingborg and Lund carry Schöner's figures too (Elebogum 35.46.57.0, Lunda 36.30.57.23), which Apian's printed Scania table repeats; so all four lines on fol. 53 are Schöner's values, copied by the student from Schöner, or from Apian and Schöner together. The Visby name form points to the exemplar: the 1515 printing reads ‘Bespue’ alone, the later Nuremberg reprint Bjørnbo used (undated, 1518) reads ‘Bespue uel wisbuy’, and the writer put the real name ‘Vesbÿ’ — so either the reprint or the Ulm Ptolemy itself stood on his desk at Leipzig; which, is open. The hands are labelled descriptively: A the thin early hand of ‘tico brade ven:’, B the grey-brown hand of ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ and the purchase note, C the firm dark hand of the pastedown rule, the verso memorandum and the fol. 53 places, D ‘Sum Pauli’, E the herbarium hand, F the German pencil collation. Hand C was compared feature by feature with the dated specimens of the Graphonomicon of Tycho Brahe — the horoscope prose of 1583, the observation narrative of 1597, the album leaf of 1599 — and with the unattributed index of 1563–65 in the Uppsala volume of 1563: ten concordances with the atlas (the looped uncial d, the u-mark, the diaeresis on y, the single-storey a, the long-ſ/round-s distribution, the ſc connection, the looped e, the capital A, a slant of 15–24 degrees inside the atlas band) and no discordance, but none of high distinctiveness, and the display forms that would decide do not occur in a working memorandum; against the Uppsala index the concordances are preponderant, but that hand is itself unattributed between Tycho at Leipzig and Vedel. The verdicts are inconclusive on both pairings. No hand is attributed: ‘Tycho's hand’ remains the attribution of Prandtl, the museum and Thykier, now recorded as contradicted by no feature and supported in kind by every one; a secure Vedel autograph of the 1560s–80s is what would decide it. Christianson (1967, p. 201) counts it with the pigskin volume of 1560 ([[vol:s-kl-47|18 J 318]]) as ‘two of his own “textbooks”’ still preserved; it is the earliest book to carry a purchase note beside an ownership entry in Tycho’s name — the hands of both unattributed, the comparison of 21 October 2026 inconclusive. The volume is not digitised; the museum’s record carries its two photographs (the front board; the volume open at the Regiomontanus title), and the examination of 20 October 2026 photographed the boards, the edges and the inscribed leaves. || 29 October 2026 — the six student volumes judged in the lecture session (the literature pack of this volume: 175 passages, 84 documents): this is the one surviving volume documented as Tycho’s before he left Denmark on 14 February 1562, by the boards alone. The place of purchase is an inference from the year, not a document; the groschen of the price are German money of account, unexplained for Copenhagen by any source, the house’s Joachimsthaler argument answering only the thaler; the tools of the binding have not been set against the Uppsala binding of 1563; ‘Sum Pauli’ is an owner no source dates. The volume’s return to Denmark — Oscar Ekman’s bequest, entered in January 1957 by his widow Lia in the dead man’s name — makes the one Copenhagen student volume a Danish holding, at Helsingør. || 29 October 2026 — the Ekman sale catalogue read in a copy in a private collection (Bruun Rasmussen 186, p. 111, lot 497): the volume is entered under ‘En Bog fra Tycho Brahe's Bibliotek’ for completeness only, not for sale, ‘given to the Handels- og Søfartsmuseet at Kronborg according to the last will of ingeniør Ekman’, and on view there in a showcase in 1965. The catalogue repeats the trade's description (‘en af de første, Tycho Brahe har ejet … han har skrevet sit navn deri samt et par notater og den pris’); what it adds is custodial — the bequest — not palaeographic. The catalogue will be shown at the talk of 19 November 2026.

holding_record.source: Slots- og Kulturstyrelsen, Museernes Samlinger — the object record of M/S Museet for Søfart
holding_record.basis: the record the store already links (priref 400004307): inventory 1957:0030, the museum's own description of the binding stamped TVCHO BRADE and ANNO 1561, the purchase note 'Eptg thalero & 4 Groshj' and Tycho's added positions on fol. 53 of the Apianus — Prandtl's Band II

custody.basis: The route out of Tycho's hands is undocumented. The fly-title (Thykier's ‘forperm’) carries two struck ownership lines — ‘tico brade ven:’ on the recto and ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ [I am Tycho Brahe's] on the verso, as the museum reads them (Thykier 2003 read the recto's as ‘Tyge Brahe’ and ‘tico brahe ven’) — which may mark a transfer in his lifetime or a later owner's cancellation. A third inscription in a firmer hand, ‘Sum Pauli’ [I am Paul's], is the only name of a later owner the volume yields: Thykier read it as ‘Sum Paul…’ with the rest lost on the torn-off part of the leaf, but the examination of 20 October 2026 shows it complete to its last letter, so the owner's first name is all the leaf ever carried of him. The book was used as a herbarium by a hand other than Tycho's, one of whose plant names is unattested before c. 1623 (Thykier 2003, after Wagner and Baagøe), so it was in a plant-collector's hands after Tycho's death. It stands in no Prague catalogue and its first title carries none of the Jesuit, Chomutov or Crusius marks of the Bohemian roads. The spine label, a paper slip with the figures ‘20[4]’ written in ink, records a library between Tycho and the Munich trade that no source names (Thykier: ‘formodentlig katalognummeret i Tychos eller et senere bibliotek’ [presumably the catalogue number in Tycho's or a later library]; the dossier of 20 October 2026); the rear flyleaf adds a faint ‘N 36’ at the head and a small blind-stamped cartouche near its gutter — a second earlier number and a dealer's or restorer's mark, both unread (examined 20 October 2026).

Prandtl 1932, the captions of his plates (pp. 2–3: ‘Seinerzeit im Besitze des Antiquariats Weiss & Co., München’ [at the time in the possession of the antiquarian firm Weiss & Co., Munich]) and p. 3 (‘kürzlich von München aus nach Amerika verkauft’ [recently sold from Munich to America] — wrong about the first step, see the next station); the Verzeichnis B entry for Band II names no location. The volume is in none of the firm's four digitised catalogues (1926–1930).

Catalogue 582 (1933), item 155, p. 92, £125, with every copy-specific identifier (the stamps, the half-torn fly-leaf, the purchase note, the Helsingborg note) and Prandtl cited for ‘our volume’; Catalogue 600 (1934), item 260, £125; Catalogue 666 (1938), item 451, p. 166, still £125, the entry reprinting Catalogue 600's text. The pencil ‘+125’ at the head of the front pastedown is this price. The firm's archive (British Library Add MS 89311) would name the seller.
Catalogue 1 ([1939]), item 72, probably $850 — Reichner was Prandtl's publisher in Vienna and emigrated to New York in 1938–39; the volume is in none of his Catalogues 2–9 (1940–48).

The buyer from Reichner is not recorded; no American auction appearance 1930–58 (American Book Prices Current); Rare Book Hub has no record. Mortensen (1955, p. 25) knew of no such volume in Denmark, which bounds nothing: the volume was then in private hands, and the Tycho literature took no notice of the museum's report of 1957 until Norlind 1970. The one physical trace of the interval is the volume's box: a brown cloth clamshell box with a gilt spine label lettered in English (‘Tycho Brahe's copy with autograph ownership notes, etc.’), made in the English-speaking trade or for the American owner (examined 20 October 2026).

custody.station: Oscar Ekman, engineer, and Lia Ekman, Copenhagen
custody.basis: The museum's report of its acquisitions of 1956–57 (Klem, Årbog 1957, p. 8; Thykier 2003 dates the gift to January 1957 and names Oskar Ekman alone): ‘en gave fra fru Lia Ekman og afdøde ægtefælle, civilingeniør Oscar Ekman’ [a gift from Mrs Lia Ekman and her late husband, the engineer Oscar Ekman]. Oscar Ekman (b. Copenhagen 13 October 1885, owner of Nordisk Elektricitets Selskab from 1913, d. 16 September 1956) had been a life member of the museum's friends' society since 1944–45; Lia Ekman (née Pouplier, b. Hamburg 1894, d. 1965) remained one to her death. Their source for the volume is not recorded; at the sale of their library (Bruun Rasmussen 186, November 1965) it was shown as a withdrawn show-piece, as Erik Dal reported in Bogvennen 1966. The museum's accession note on the rear pastedown, ‘Gave jan. 1957 fra civiling. Oskar Ekman’ [gift, January 1957, from the engineer Oskar Ekman] (read 20 October 2026), enters the gift in January 1957 under Oscar's name, four months after his death: a gift in the dead man's name, made by his widow — which is what Klem's wording, Thykier's and Dal's ‘testamentarisk bortgivet’ [given away by bequest] each describe. The sale catalogue itself (Bruun Rasmussen 186, p. 111, lot 497, read 29 October 2026) lists the volume under ‘En Bog fra Tycho Brahe's Bibliotek’ for completeness only — ‘This copy will not be sold as it was given to the “Handels- og Søfartsmuseet” at Kronborg according to the last will of ingeniør Ekman’; the Danish text ‘foræret … af ingeniør Ekman og kan beses der i en af udstillingsmontrerne’ — so the gift was a bequest under Oscar's will, executed by his widow in January 1957, and the volume stood in a showcase at Kronborg in November 1965.

custody.station: M/S Museet for Søfart (Handels- og Søfartsmuseet på Kronborg), Helsingør, inventory 1957:0030
custody.basis: The Ekmans' gift of 1956–57 (Årbog 1957; the museum's record); restored 1957 by Birgitte Dall. Deposited at the Royal Library's Håndskriftafdeling in 1986 as Acc. 1986/116 (the Kronik of 1987; the department's newsletter of November 2001), lent from there to the Ole Rømer Museum's exhibition ‘Tycho Brahes mange ansigter’ [Tycho Brahe's many faces], 25 October – 31 December 2001; in the museum's own keeping again, confirmed 13 October 2026, the date of return unrecorded. Examined and photographed at the museum on 20 October 2026: the Kronborg stamp and ‘30:57’ on the rear pastedown, ‘Acc. 1986/116’ in pencil on the fly-title and the pastedown and on the slip in the box, the plant envelopes in place, the box lettered in English.

open_questions: Who owned the volume between Tycho and the Munich trade: the spine label is a paper slip in the second compartment with ‘20[4]’ written in ink, and nothing else is now lettered on the spine — the larger label or patch at the tail in Prandtl's plate of 1932 is gone; the rear flyleaf adds a faint ‘N 36’ at the head and a small blind-stamped cartouche near the gutter, both unread (examined 20 October 2026). The two numbers and the stamp, read under raking light and set against the shelf-numbering of Danish and north-German libraries of the seventeenth to nineteenth centuries, would decide.

What ‘ven:’ abbreviates in ‘tico brade ven:’ — ven[didit] or vēnit (a sale), ven[dicat] (an ownership claim, as in Jacob Ulfeldt's ‘Vendicat sibi’ of the same decade), Ven[usinus] — and with it whether the book left Tycho in his lifetime. The photographs of 20 October 2026 settle the leaf itself: the line is struck through once, in the same ink as the writing, and a second name beside it is obliterated under later black strokes; two further short words on the recto, one smudged, one at the head right, are unread.

27 Oct 2026 [narrowed] - the leaf is settled by the photographs of 20 October 2026 (one thin stroke in the line's own ink; the second name obliterated under a later black campaign); the expansion itself is a reading question no examination can add to — it stays open as a question of Latin, with ven[dicat] the reading that makes the line an ownership claim in the idiom of the decade.

Who ‘Pauli’ was: the owner whose ‘Sum Pauli’ stands in a firm hand on the fly-title recto, complete to its last letter (examined 20 October 2026, confirming Thykier's ‘Sum Paul…’), what followed lost with the torn-away part of the leaf; whether his hand is that of the plant names (after c. 1623) — the photographs of both now allow the comparison, which has not been made. The smudged word above it reads ‘Brÿſſe’ or ‘Chrÿſſe’ and stands inside a wet-wiped erasure of an earlier inscription (21 October 2026) — a surname, or a trace of the erased owner.

27 Oct 2026 [narrowed] - a desk test is now possible and not yet made: the photographs of 'Sum Pauli' and of the plant names (both 20 October 2026) allow the comparison of the two hands; the identity itself needs a document.

Whether the purchase note, the two astronomical memoranda and the fol. 53 entries are in Tycho's hand of 1561–65: compared on 21 October 2026 with the dated specimens of the Graphonomicon (1583, 1597, 1599) and with the unattributed index of 1563–65 in the Uppsala volume — ten concordances, no discordance, none decisive; inconclusive on both pairings. A secure autograph of Anders Sørensen Vedel of the 1560s–80s, the other candidate owner of the Uppsala volume and Tycho's companion at Leipzig, would decide; so would a metered forensic comparison for the record once a comparator at pillar scale exists.

27 Oct 2026 [narrowed] - restated for chapter 3 (27 October 2026): Hand C stands as a candidate, consistent with the pillars and with the Uppsala index on every feature compared; the decisive control is a secure Vedel autograph of the 1560s–80s, and the next physical step is raking-light frames at the museum for the ascender/descender ratio.

Which exemplar supplied the Visby and Rumefalche lines on fol. 53v: the figures are Schöner's (Luculentissima quaedam terrae totius descriptio, Nuremberg 1515, fo. 34r) and the name Rumefalche is Claudius Clavus's pseudo-toponym from the Ulm Ptolemy of 1486 (Bjørnbo and Petersen 1904, pp. 115, 118), but the writer's ‘Vesbÿ’ for Schöner's ‘Bespue’ fits the later Schöner printing (‘Bespue uel wisbuy’, the undated Nuremberg reprint of 1518) or the Ulm Ptolemy's map better than the 1515 printing. Neither Schöner nor a Ptolemy Geographia is in Prandtl's list; a Schöner or an Ulm Ptolemy among the student's books would be a new entry.

Who bought the volume from Herbert Reichner about 1940, and from whom the Ekmans had it by 1956: the box, lettered in English, is the one physical trace of the interval; the Maggs archive (British Library Add MS 89311), Reichner's Catalogue 1 in paper, the Bruun Rasmussen catalogue of 1965 (no. 186) and Sahl's chapter on the Ekmans (Bogvennen 2011–12) are the witnesses to read.
When the volume returned from its deposit in the Royal Library's Håndskriftafdeling (Acc. 1986/116; still there in December 2001) to the museum; the deposit file of either institution would decide.

Whose tools the binder used: the upper board lettered TVCHO at the head and BRADE at the foot, the lower ANNO and 1561, a foliate centre-stamp on each board, fleur-de-lis corner stamps outside the double-ruled frame and small floral stamps flanking the lettering, no gilt surviving (photographed 20 October 2026); the comparison with the tools of the Uppsala binding of 1563 has not been made.

27 Oct 2026 [unchangeable] - both image sets exist in the house (the Helsingør frames of 20 October and the Uppsala Alvin TIFFs of 12 October 2026) and the comparison has not been made; a tool-by-tool comparison of the lettering punches and the centre/corner stamps, then EBDB, would decide — a desk task, not a visit.

The full reading of the German pencil collation on the front pastedown (the Munich trade's note): ‘£125’ at the head, ‘I: 158 unn. Bl. (das erste weiss) …’, ‘70 (von 1–74) wo in der Foliierung über…’, ‘II: 2 unn. Bl. (Bl. 31–34 …) + 1 doppel[bl.] …’ read on 21 October 2026; the rest needs the volume under raking light. The two astronomical memoranda are read in full (21 October 2026).

Who cancelled the Brahe names: the heavy black strokes through the recto name and through the verso's ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ are one ink and one campaign (21 October 2026), unlike every other ink on the leaf — a later owner who wished the Brahe ownership gone, Paulus or another; the thin stroke through ‘tico brade ven:’ is earlier and different. The darker ‘Angl. 5.’ above the pastedown rule and the pencil ‘choo’ on the rear pastedown are unexplained.

Open question of 27 October 2026 (the afterlife record): the two unrecorded intervals — from ‘Sum Pauli’ to the Munich trade before 1932, and from Reichner's New York catalogue of 1939 to the Ekmans before 1957; the Maggs archive (British Library Add MS 89311) would name the seller of 1933, and the Ekmans' papers or the museum's correspondence of 1956–57 the source of the gift.

29 Oct 2026 [narrowed] - the Bruun Rasmussen catalogue of 1965 is read (lot 497: a bequest under Oscar Ekman's will, not sold, on display at Kronborg); the source from which the Ekmans had the volume is still unnamed — the Maggs archive, Reichner's Catalogue 1 in paper and Sahl's chapter on the Ekmans remain the witnesses to read.

survivors.marks_securing_id: upper board blind-stamped at the head TY ✿ BRAD, a rosette between the words (the library's photographs, October 2026; the year 1563 that Prandtl, Norlind and Mortensen read with the name is not legible in them — in raking light, 13 October 2026, the band beneath the panel shows only the remains of stamped forms on an abraded surface, a looped figure at its right end that may be the 6 — but is plain to the eye with the book in hand: the library's Rare Books Librarian, asked, read 1563 on the band without doubt, 14 October 2026; the LIBRIS note gives ‘TY BRAD 1563’); light tanned leather over boards, blind-tooled with a portrait-medallion roll of the Reformers type (one medallion lettered IOANNES HVS), a foliate roll and rules, an Annunciation panel on the upper board (legend VIRGO · MARIA · DEI · MATER · SANCTISSIMA · SALVATORVM) and a Baptism-of-Christ panel on the lower (HIC EST FILIVS MEVS DILECTVS IN QVO MIHI COMPLACITVM EST); two brass clasps, the catches on the upper board, the straps lost; five raised bands; edges plain. The numerals ‘1.’, ‘2.’, ‘3.’ on the three titles are the later librarian's, matching the contents note on the front flyleaf | binding period: Period 1 (student years, to 1565): a Saxon binding of the Wittenberg–Leipzig type, consistent with a Leipzig binder in 1563
survivors.identified_by: Walde 1920 (Storhetstidens litterära krigsbyten II, p. 329, the first report, cited after Mortensen 1942, p. 25, and Mortensen 1955, p. 27); Prandtl 1932, Verzeichnis B, Band III; Norlind 1970, pp. 347, 356, 366; Mortensen 1955, p. 27; the library's catalogue (holdings revised 11 September 2026) and the EOD facsimile of October 2026; the library's Alvin record 805325 (former owners De la Gardie, Brahe, Vedel; photographs of binding, endleaves and edges, 12 October 2026)
survivors.notes:
Prandtl’s Band III, the Sammelband of 1563: Camerarius’s Hippocomicus with his Latin Xenophon (Leipzig 1556), Osius’s Historia excidii Hierosolymorum (Wittenberg 1558) and Garcaeus’s Tractatus de erigendis figuris coeli (Wittenberg 1556), in that order, the three titles numbered ‘1.’, ‘2.’, ‘3.’ in ink. Light tanned leather over boards with rich blind tooling and traces of clasps, the front board stamped TY BRAD and dated 1563; Vedel’s name ‘Andreas Seuerinus Velleius’ at the head of the first title; Magnus Gabriel De la Gardie’s red seal inside the front board; a handwritten index on the rear endleaf (the library’s catalogue; the LIBRIS note common to the three records: ‘På främre pärmen tryckt: "TY BRAD 1563"; på titelsidan handskrivet: "Andreas Seuerinus Welleius"; Magnus Gabiel De la Gardies röda sigill på främre pärmens insida’). Walde, who came upon the volume at Uppsala, took it for a book Tycho procured on the study journey of 1563 and soon gave or exchanged to Vedel, his companion on that journey — in an exchange Tycho may have received the Glareanus of 1536 that Vedel bought in August 1564, now at Prague (19 G 20); Mortensen followed him; Norlind read it the other way, as Vedel’s book given to Tycho, who had it bound with the two others.

The library’s facsimile of October 2026 (the text block only; binding, pastedowns and endleaves not photographed) shows the annotation leaf by leaf. The Camerarius carries a red-brown subject heading at the head of sig. A2 recto, red-brown underlining of the Greek style-terms in the preface (image 24) and of the opening of De nominibus equestribus (p. 97), and pen strokes against a passage on p. 141; the Osius nothing beyond its ‘2.’ and a small numeral ‘7’ at the foot of one page (image 58); the Garcaeus the ‘strödda marginalanteckningar’ of the catalogue — subject headings and section numbers in the calendar chapters (images 19–37 of the Garcaeus), the solar cycle for 1555 worked by long division (33), the dominical-letter table numbered by hand with the years 1488–1501 and a 1–7 counter (34), ‘obliquam’ correcting the misprint ‘aliquam’ (124), figures checking the Elector August’s nativity and part of fortune (129, 143, 155), the rule of the part of fortune written out (136), the revolution of 1556 recomputed from Reinhold’s tables (171: ‘Ego R[…] juxta Reinholdum ☉ in 16 37 ♌’), a note on the meridian of Reinhold’s equinox table (174: Königsberg at longitude 44¼ against 53½, ‘37 circiter min[uta]’), ‘Directionis finis’ with underlining at Propositio XXII (176) and a faint unread note (152). These are two registers of a sixteenth-century hand, in brown and black ink; whether they are Tycho’s student hand of 1563–65 or Vedel’s is not decided. Thoren (1990, p. 17) and Christianson (2020, p. 24) record that Tycho, during his Leipzig studies, bought ‘an astrological work by Johannes Garcaeus’ and began a notebook of horoscopes on its model; Thoren’s note points to this copy.

The library’s photographs (Alvin record 805325) show the rest: the upper board with TY ✿ BRAD at the head and the Annunciation panel, the lower board with the Baptism-of-Christ panel, the Reformers roll, the brass catches of the lost clasps, five raised bands, plain edges; on the front pastedown the library’s labels (‘Script. graeci (Xenophon)’, ‘Pp. IX. 2. 398’) and Magnus Gabriel De la Gardie’s red wax seal; on the front flyleaf verso the older shelfmarks ‘V. XI. 4.’ and ‘238’ and a contents note in an eighteenth- or nineteenth-century library hand (‘Accedunt: 2. Hieron. Osius … Witeb. 1558. 3. Joh. Garcaeus Jun. … Witeb. 1556’), whose numbering is the ‘1.’, ‘2.’, ‘3.’ written on the three titles; and on the rear endleaf, in a sixteenth-century cursive, an unfinished index of the Garcaeus — ‘Index monstrans quid quaelibet propositio in hoc libello contineat’, propositions I to V with their signatures (B, C, D …), a pen flourish beneath. The index is in the same hand, and belongs to the same work, as the marginal headings and section numbers of the Garcaeus, and it was written in the bound volume: whoever annotated the Garcaeus did so after the binding of 1563 — the owner of the bound book, Tycho in 1563–65 or Vedel afterwards; the index is the longest specimen of that hand.

The year 1563, read on the upper board by Prandtl, Norlind and Mortensen, is not legible in the photographs, nor in the three raking-light photographs the library supplied on 13 October 2026: the band beneath the panel, where a Saxon binder stamps the year under the owner’s name, carries the remains of stamped forms — a looped figure at its right end that may be the 6, the rest on an abraded surface — but no numeral can be read from them. With the book in hand the year is plain: Peter Sjökvist, the library’s Rare Books Librarian, confirmed in October 2026 that 1563 is seen quite clearly with the naked eye and that there is no doubt that is what stands on the binding. The year therefore stands on four readings of the book itself — Prandtl, Mortensen, Norlind and Sjökvist — and on the library’s catalogue note; the photographs fail to reproduce it, they do not contradict it. The Alvin record names De la Gardie, Tycho Brahe and Vedel as former owners. A Sammelband at KB, RAR:142 A, bound with Peucer 1553, is a different volume. The volume is kept in Specialsamlingar; the Osius also carries the older control number Pp:398 (2). Sjökvist (2024, p. 35) supplies the mechanism the chain lacked: in the Danish war of 1658–60 De la Gardie ‘acquired … big parts of the collections of Gunde Rosenkrantz (1604–1675), in which large portions of books previously owned by Holger Rosencrantz (1574–1642) and Anders Sörensen Vedel (1542–1616) could be found’ — Vedel's books as a body, not this volume, are named (added 27 October 2026).

custody.basis: His name ‘Andreas Seuerinus Velleius’ at the head of the first title. No owner is recorded between Vedel and De la Gardie. A mechanism for the gap: in the Danish war of 1658–60 Magnus Gabriel De la Gardie ‘acquired … big parts of the collections of Gunde Rosenkrantz (1604–1675), in which large portions of books previously owned by Holger Rosencrantz (1574–1642) and Anders Sörensen Vedel (1542–1616) could be found’ (Sjökvist 2024, p. 35) — Vedel's books as a body, not this volume, are named; a Rosenkrantz mark in the volume would raise it (C-04).

27 Oct 2026 [narrowed] - compared on 21 October 2026 with the Helsingør Hand C of 1561–65 (register a: concordant throughout, no discordance; register b: the digit 4 differs) — two unattributed hands of the same years now stand together; a secure Vedel autograph of the 1560s–80s is the one control that would decide both (Graphonomicon borderline.md).

Whether the volume was Tycho’s, given or exchanged to Vedel (Walde, Mortensen), or Vedel’s, given to Tycho and bound by him with the two other works (Norlind); the attribution of the annotating hand, which post-dates the binding of 1563, would bear on it.
What the faint note on image 152 of the Garcaeus reads; examination of the leaf itself would decide.
27 Oct 2026 [unchangeable] - the 2× render of the EOD image does not resolve it (checked for the chapter 3 sheet); only the leaf itself, in raking light, would.

Open question of 27 October 2026 (the afterlife record): whether the volume reached De la Gardie with Gunde Rosenkrantz's collection, which De la Gardie acquired in the Danish war of 1658–60 and in which ‘large portions of books previously owned by … Anders Sörensen Vedel’ stood (Sjökvist 2024, p. 35) — the one documented road from Vedel's library into De la Gardie's, at C for this copy; a Rosenkrantz mark in the volume, or the volume in the Rosenkrantz–De la Gardie lists, would decide.

survivors.marks_securing_id: plain binding; marginal notes by Tycho; on the Cardanus the censor’s note ‘Prohibiti in indice 2dae Classis, donec prodeat expurgatio’; no accession inscription on the leaves, the Chomutov college’s signature on the spine (Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 37, p. 93); ‘constat 5 lb 15 d.’ inside the upper board (Studnička 1901, Bericht, p. 20) | binding period: unmarked binding || Prague catalogue (National Library, Staré tisky), copy-level provenance note, verbatim: Podle Flory Kleinschnitzové mohl tisk patřit Tychonu Brahe, na základě rukopisné poznámky v závěru tisku se signaturou 19 G 20. | Podle Flory Kleinschnitzové mohl tisk patřit Tychonu Brahe, podle rukopisné poznámky v závěru tisku se signaturou 19 G 20. | Na přídeští modře rukou: T.B. 7 || Read on the Manuscriptorium facsimile, 27 October 2026: the leaves of 14 F 16 carry no Tycho mark and no 1642 Clementinum inscription (canvases 1, 155, 315); the Albubater title (canvas 155) carries the year ‘1671’ in ink at the upper left — probably the Chomutov catalogue year without its words; the Cardano title (canvas 315) carries ‘prohibiti in Indice / 2dæ Classis, donec / prodeat expurgatio’. The facsimile (536 canvases, NoC-NC) begins at the Gauricus title and ends on a blank leaf: neither the ‘constat 5 lb 15 d.’ inside the upper board nor the front pastedown's notes and ‘T.B. 7’ are in it.
survivors.identified_by: Studnička 1901 (Bericht), pp. 17–31; Prandtl, Die Bibliothek des Tycho Brahe (Verzeichnis B), and the National Library's former-owner index
survivors.notes: Bound volume IV, in Studnička’s reconstruction of its original make-up four constituents, nos. 41, 20, 1 and 11: the Sacrobosco manuscript, the Gauricus, the Albubater and the Cardanus. The manuscript was separated from Sign. 14 F 16 before 1901, at an earlier revision of the manuscripts (Prusík 1901, pp. 198–199; Studnička 1901, p. 21; Kukula 1906–07, p. 22). Studnička described the volume in 1901 as Tycho’s astrological study-book, brought to his notice by the custos Josef Truhlář: a manuscript compendium of Sacrobosco’s Sphaera first (now Sign. VII E 29), then the Gauricus, the Albubater and the Cardanus (Bericht, pp. 17–18, 30). He reports ‘constat 5 lb 15 d.’ on the inside of the front board — the sum of the cost note on the first leaf of the manuscript, which lists a Glareanus, the Gauricus with Montulmo, the Albubater, the Cardanus and the binder’s fee (pp. 20–21; the boards are not in the facsimile) — and reproduces as Tycho’s own work eight pages from the leaves bound at the end of the Albubater (pp. 22–29) and a horoscope from the Cardanus with a line of manuscript above it (p. 30). The first page he reproduces is the nativity of Andreas Schöner, cast for Nuremberg (‘Anno M.D.XXX die XXI Junij … natus Andreas Schönerus. Dies Martis’; 21 June 1530 fell on a Tuesday), and the cost note is headed with the same name. Which of the annotations in the volume are Tycho’s has not been established by a comparison of hands. Prusík 1901, group A, no. 3: Sign. 14 F 16, ‘ein Sammelband ohne besonderen Wert’, to which the Sacrobosco manuscript (now MS VII E XXIX) originally belonged; Kukula told in 1906–07 how the custos Truhlář, finding the price list on the manuscript’s flyleaf, recovered the Sammelband it had been taken from, its upper board marked ‘constat 5 15’, the sum of the list. The National Library’s digital facsimile of Sign. 14 F 16 shows the volume as it now stands: the three Petreius imprints — the Gauricus, the Albubater and the Cardanus — and nothing else; the Sacrobosco manuscript is at Sign. VII E 29. || Re-read of the June 2026 census positives, 27 October 2026 (ch. III), complete in two parts: 211 manuscript pages, 1 possible, 6 printed only of 218. The nativity on canvas 304 reads ‘Anno M·D·X·X·X·’ with a fourth X overwritten by a dark mark; ‘Dies martis’ fits 21 June 1530 (Tuesday, Julian), not 1540 (Monday). Besides the Schöner layer the re-read finds at least three later annotating layers — the bridge leaf (canvas 314, a rapid German cursive), a red ‘An: 1560:’ (canvas 246) and ‘Locus Stellae ex Copernici Doctrina’ (canvas 329) — none compared with any hand.

annotation_scan.state_note: Re-read 27 October 2026 (ch. III), complete (both parts): 211 manuscript, 1 possible, 6 printed only of the 218 June positives; the substantive layer is the pre-Tycho Schöner hand, never Tycho's.
