custody.basis: The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931).

No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 76) supposed that the college came by Tycho’s books in a way similar to the Clementinum’s gift; Císařová Smítková, Paličková and Vackářová (2021, p. 30) suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under Joannes Jüngling, who kept the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766; the college’s dated catalogue entries on Tycho’s volumes are of 1645 to 1675.

No accession inscription on the leaves; the college’s signature on the spine, which Kleinschnitzová read as the Chomutov provenance also written on the Glareanus 19 G 20, once part of the same Sammelband (1933, no. 37 and p. 93).

custody.station: The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague
custody.basis: Brought to the Clementinum with the library of the dissolved Chomutov college after 1773; Kleinschnitzová counted nineteen volumes of that provenance in 1933 (p. 81).

open_questions: Which of the annotations in the volume — the eight pages after the Albubater, the horoscope in the Cardanus, the cost note — are in Tycho’s hand, given that the first page Studnička reproduces is Andreas Schöner’s nativity and the cost note is headed with the same name; a comparison of hands against dated specimens would decide.

27 Oct 2026 — the eight pages after the Albubater (canvases 303–311: the 1535–45 diary, Andreas Schöner's nativity of 1530 and its tables) and the cost note belong to the pre-Tycho Schöner layer and are excluded for Tycho (Debunked Claims Register, 20 October 2026; dossier of 6 June 2026, scribe-compare run 3 consistent with Johann Schöner's autograph in ÖNB Cod. 10745). Still open: the Cardano horoscope Studnička reproduced (p. 30), not yet located on a canvas, and three later layers the census re-read of 27 October 2026 surfaces (canvases 246, 314, 329) — the only places a Tycho hand could be sought; a Graphonomicon comparison of those specimens against the 1561–65 working hands and the 1583/1599 pillars would decide.

Open question of 27 October 2026 (the afterlife record): by what road the volume reached the Chomutov college — the Clementinum's duplicates under Jüngling (Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021, p. 30), a second gift from the heirs (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 76), or the private hands that gave the college 5 G 92 and 5 J 103 in 1654. Two documented ties now frame the question without closing it: the heirs' claim was assigned in 1623 to the tax arrears of Chomutov and Kadaň among four royal towns — the instructions to the towns to pay from arrears are dated Chomutov 26 September 1623 and Kadaň 3 July 1626 (Volf 1932, part 2, p. 23), and the college itself had lost its library to the Saxon plunder of 1631, partly bought back in 1632, before the first dated Tycho accession of 1645 (Veselá 2025, pp. 27–29). The college's own catalogues of 1645–1675 and the Clementinum's duplicate lists of 1773–1782, if they survive in the Národní archiv or the National Library's archive, would decide.

What the ‘četné rkp. poznámky’ on the front pastedown are and whether the board's ‘constat 5 lb 15 d.’ is in the cost-note hand — neither is in the facsimile; NK ČR's photographs of the pastedown and the inner board (the reproduction desk, quote awaited since 27 October 2026) would decide.

Whether the bridge-leaf note (canvas 314), the red ‘An: 1560:’ (canvas 246) and the star note ‘Locus Stellae ex Copernici Doctrina’ (canvas 329) are one later owner's hand and whose — a Graphonomicon comparison against Tycho's 1561–65 hands (MFS Band II hand C) would test it.

Whether the June census reading ‘Anno 1572’ on canvas 409 or the re-read's ‘Anno 1524’ is right — a full-size reading of canvas 409 decides; a post-1547 year there would be the first dated post-Schöner annotation.

survivors.notes: Kukula first published the volume in 1906–07 (no. V of the seven found since 1902, Sign. XIV F 8): the Arithmetica communis with Peurbach’s and Gmunden’s algorithms (defective), Strabo’s Hortulus (Nuremberg 1512), the Liber diversarum rerum ascribed to Ptolemy (Venice 1509) and Faber’s Meteorologia Aristotelis (Nuremberg 1512), ‘T. B.’ on the first title; the binding without special character. The National Library’s owner index lists the volume under Sign. 14 F 8 with the Strabo, the Ptolemy and the Faber among its constituents. The National Library’s provenance survey of 2021 counts 215 volumes with Chomutov inscriptions and ‘at least four books from Tycho’s estate’ among them, all stamped ‘TBO 1576’; its authors suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under P. Jan Jüngling in the eighteenth century; the dated Chomutov notes of 1645 (44 F 38) and 1654 (Crusius’s gifts) are earlier. There is no digital facsimile of the volume; the library’s record offers five photographs (title page, front pastedown, boards, spine). || The library's convolute record (Manuscriptorium NKCR__-NKCR__14_F_000008_17OOHAF-cs, from Aleph docs 000155813, 000155815, 000155817, 000155823) lists four prints bound together today — the Arithmetica communis host ([Vienna: Singriener, 1515], 'neúplné'), Strabo's Hortulus as adl. 1 ('neúplné'), the ps.-Ptolemy Liber diversarum rerum as adl. 2 and the Meteorologia as adl. 3 — in the order a–d in which Kukula described them in 1906–07 (Prandtl's Band V: 21, 47, 32, 7); Kleinschnitzová's no. 36 omits the Strabo. The volume is intact as described since 1906; an earlier worklog note that it was disbound across several 1933 shelfmarks is contradicted by every source. The library records red manuscript marginal notes and red-highlighted capitals in the ps.-Ptolemy (adl. 2), attributed by no source.

survivors.marks_securing_id: Tycho's autograph entry on the blank leaf after the pasted-in leaf of Apianus's later arms: Psalm 19:1, a distich of his own ('Cui negat esse Deum, coelos et sidera spectet / Esse etenim monstrat stella vel una Deum') and the subscription 'Tycho Brahe scripsi Anno 1599 Junij die 14, quo Vitebergâ discessi Pragam a Caesare vocatus'. A dated motto of the album kind, not an ownership mark; no owner's name on the title, no annotation in the text | binding period: rebound in plain brown calf at Gotha in 1967, after the volume was taken apart for the Edition Leipzig facsimile; the original leather was plain, with traces of ties
survivors.identified_by: Rauch 1914, pp. 223–224 (the first publication of the entry); Prandtl 1932, Verzeichnis B, Band VI; the Forschungsbibliothek Gotha copy record (K10plus, revised 2024). Ownership doubted by Norlind 1970, pp. 337–338
survivors.notes: What the volume shows. The only trace of Tycho is one inscription, on the recto of the blank leaf that follows the pasted-in leaf of Apianus’s later arms (image 123 of the Jena facsimile): Psalm 19:1 (‘Coeli enarrant gloriam Dei et opera manuum eius annunciat firmamentum’), a distich whose hexameter Tycho had used in his Copenhagen oration of 1574 (‘Cui negat esse Deum, coelos et sidera spectet’, here with the pentameter ‘Esse etenim monstrat stella vel una Deum’), and the subscription ‘Tycho Brahe scripsi Anno 1599 Junij die 14, quo Vitebergâ discessi Pragam a Caesare vocatus’ — written on the day he left Wittenberg for Prague. The hand is that of his Wittenberg album entries of 1598–99, and a separate album leaf of the same day carries the same departure formula. The title page bears no owner’s name, the text no annotation, and the binding is a Gotha rebinding of 1967, made after the volume had been taken apart for the Edition Leipzig facsimile; the restoration report pasted inside the lower board records that the original leather was plain. The copy also carries, in a sixteenth-century hand close to the Apian family, captions on the old and the new arms and red crossings through the old shield on the title — the apparatus of a copy completed after Apianus’s ennoblement of 1541. What it proves, and what it does not. The inscription proves that Tycho held the book on 14 June 1599 and wrote in it. It is a dated motto entry of the album-amicorum kind (‘scripsi’, not ‘emi’ or ‘possidet’), not an ownership mark, and nothing else in the volume connects it to his library. Prandtl listed the volume among Tycho’s books on the strength of the entry alone. Norlind thought it more likely the book of someone else, perhaps of Duke Friedrich Wilhelm of Saxe-Weimar, Administrator of Electoral Saxony and Tycho’s patron at Dresden in November 1598, in whose book Tycho would have written as in an album. The Gotha library records the volume as Tycho’s gift to the duke and the duke as its recipient; the duke’s other Tychoniana — the Mechanica Memb. I 110 and the star catalogue Chart. A 984, both with dedications to him — are in the same library, and the library of his line at Altenburg came to Gotha in 1672. On either reading the volume is a book that passed through Tycho’s hands, not one shown to have stood on his shelves; hence grade B. Rauch, who first published the entry in 1914 on information from the Gotha librarian Rudolf Ehwald, wrote that the book had come to Gotha from Munich; nothing later explains the remark. Gingerich, who examined the copy for the facsimile, reports the entry as ‘written in what is now the Gotha copy’. Catalogued by the Forschungsbibliothek Gotha at Math gr2° 00038/02; the copy record transcribes the inscription and names the duke as recipient. Digitised by the Forschungsbibliothek Gotha; the page-by-page facsimile is served in the ThULB Jena viewer (URN urn:nbn:de:urmel-ufb-191132). || Chapter 3 state sheet, 27 October 2026: the ThULB facsimile has a IIIF Presentation manifest (dhb.thulb.uni-jena.de/api/iiif/presentation/v2/ufb_derivate_00019113/manifest) and a level-2 Image API; image 123 is 4955 × 7256 px native — the sharpest reproduction of any Tycho writing among the surviving volumes' facsimiles — and its text was read in full on the image: DAVID REX PSAL. XIX / Cœli enarrant Gloriam DEI / et opera manuûm eiûs / annûnciat Firmamentûm. / Qui negat esse DEVM cælos et sidera spectet / Esse etenim monstrat Stella vel una DEVM. / Tycho Brahe / scripsj / Anno 1599 / Jûnij die 14 / quo Vitebergâ / discessj / Pragam / a CÆSARE vocatûs. (with a pen flourish). The entry served the same day as the comparator for the 14 J 176 purchase note of June 1601.

survivors.notes: Kukula first published the volume in 1906–07 as no. VI of the seven Tychoniana found since 1902, under the shelfmark XIV A 63: Stoeffler’s Calendarium Romanum magnum (‘Tubingae 1518’ in Kukula; the book was printed at Oppenheim by Jacob Köbel in 1518, as Kleinschnitzová, no. 33, and the library’s record give it), Peurbach’s Tabulae eclipsium (Vienna 1514), Apianus’s Pronunciata (Nuremberg 1541) and an Introductorium astronomicum (Paris 1517), with ‘T. B.’ on the first title; the binding is without special character. The volume is Prandtl’s Band VII of 1932: the library’s owner index lists it under Sign. 14 A 63, Kleinschnitzová’s 1933 shelfmark for the Stoeffler and the Peurbach is 14 A 63, and the Stoeffler, the Peurbach and the Apianus are confirmed as its constituents. The volume is digitised in full view in the National Library’s programme with Google Books, the whole Sammelband under one digitisation id attached to the library’s record and to the four adligata records; the Manuscriptorium record is catalogue-only. The National Library’s provenance survey of 2021 counts 215 volumes with Chomutov inscriptions and ‘at least four books from Tycho’s estate’ among them, all stamped ‘TBO 1576’; its authors suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under P. Jan Jüngling in the eighteenth century; the dated Chomutov notes of 1645 (44 F 38) and 1654 (Crusius’s gifts) are earlier. || The library's record gives the title and flyleaf initials ‘T. B.’ as pencil (‘Na předsádce a na titulní straně tužkou iniciály: T. B. (Tycho Brahe)’), beside the pencil ‘T.B. 28.’ on the pastedown, while Kukula, Prandtl and Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 90: ‘eigenhändig von Brahe’) give the title initials as Tycho's own; which is right, or whether two sets exist, is not decidable from the records (27 October 2026). Kleinschnitzová's no. 33 lists four pieces and no Apianus; the library's record has the Apianus Instrumentum sinuum (1541) as adl. 2. The authority-field chronology ‘1576’ for Tycho on the record has no stated basis; Kukula and Prandtl call the binding plain.

Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 76) supposed that the college came by Tycho’s books in a way similar to the Clementinum’s gift; Císařová Smítková, Paličková and Vackářová (2021, p. 30) suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under Joannes Jüngling, who kept the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766; the college’s dated catalogue entries on Tycho’s volumes are of 1645 to 1675.

custody.basis: Brought to the Clementinum with the library of the dissolved Chomutov college after 1773; Kleinschnitzová counted nineteen volumes of that provenance in 1933 (p. 81).

open_questions: Open question of 27 October 2026 (the afterlife record): by what road the volume reached the Chomutov college — the Clementinum's duplicates under Jüngling (Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021, p. 30), a second gift from the heirs (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 76), or the private hands that gave the college 5 G 92 and 5 J 103 in 1654. Two documented ties now frame the question without closing it: the heirs' claim was assigned in 1623 to the tax arrears of Chomutov and Kadaň among four royal towns — the instructions to the towns to pay from arrears are dated Chomutov 26 September 1623 and Kadaň 3 July 1626 (Volf 1932, part 2, p. 23), and the college itself had lost its library to the Saxon plunder of 1631, partly bought back in 1632, before the first dated Tycho accession of 1645 (Veselá 2025, pp. 27–29). The college's own catalogues of 1645–1675 and the Clementinum's duplicate lists of 1773–1782, if they survive in the Národní archiv or the National Library's archive, would decide.

What the two entries struck out on the front free endleaf below the ‘T. B.’ read (canvas 1) — a UV or raking-light photograph from NK ČR could recover them; a pre-Tycho owner's name would change the volume's provenance.

Whose are the ink numerals 1–5 on the five adligate titles (canvases 131, 263, 387, 447, 471) — Tycho's binder's collation or the Chomutov cataloguer of 1671; a comparison with the Chomutov inscription on canvas 3 at full size would test the second.

The number 2781 that Studnička read on the spine in 1901 as Tycho's own shelf number in his hand is no longer visible, in direct or in raking light, and Prandtl's own photograph of the binding, the frontispiece of his catalogue of 1932, already shows the four panels of the spine without any number | binding period: Period 4 (gilt supralibros)
survivors.identified_by: Studnička 1901 (Bericht), p. 7 and note (the volume in Gustav Laube's possession at Prague, its binding with the portrait, arms and distichs, the number 2781 on the spine); Prandtl 1932, Verzeichnis B, Band XXI, and the frontispiece plate of both boards; Norlind 1970, pp. 335 and 348; Gingerich 2002, p. 325 (the Texas location); examined and photographed at the Harry Ransom Center by Benjamin Gross, Head of Fellowships and Scholarly Programs, 7 October 2026 (the binding as in Prandtl's plate, Laube's stamp on the title page)
survivors.notes: Gesner, De omni rerum fossilium genere (Zürich 1565, 8vo): the parchment Prachtband that Prandtl owned himself and reproduced, spread open with both boards, as the frontispiece of his catalogue of 1932; his Verzeichnis B lists it as Band XXI, ‘Prachtband, Pergament’, with the previous owner Prof. Dr. G. C. Laube of Prague, who had bought it from a Leipzig antiquarian bookseller. The volume was first noticed in 1901 by Studnička, who saw it in Gustav Laube's possession and read the number 2781 written on the spine as Tycho's own shelf number in his hand, remarking that the binding, unlike those of the Clementinum volumes relabelled in 1642, was intact — the single datum behind every estimate of several thousand volumes for the library (Norlind 1970, p. 335; Gingerich 2002, p. 323, ‘at best speculative’); the hand is Studnička's attribution. Gingerich (2002, p. 325) places the volume at the University of Texas at Austin (Harry Ransom Center), acquired with Prandtl's collection in the 1950s; his ‘private hands in Moravia’ is a conjecture, Prandtl's own account being the Leipzig trade. Catalogued by the University of Texas Libraries at QE 362 G391d 1565, Harry Ransom Center Book Collection, with the local note ‘Wilhelm Prandtl Collection’; the record names neither Tycho nor the binding, and the volume is not digitised. Examined and photographed at the Ransom Center on 7 October 2026 (twenty photographs: both boards with a ruler, the spine straight on and in raking light, the pastedowns and flyleaves, the title page, and the leaves that carry marks). The boards, about 17.5 × 11.5 cm, are as in Prandtl's plate: the portrait oval with the distich Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei / pulchrius enitet quae latet interior on the upper board, the arms with its distich on the lower, each within a lozenge of gilt foliate roll, with corner fleurons and a border roll; the portrait oval measures about 8 × 6 cm against the ruler, which is the larger of Mortensen's two dies (7.6 × 5.8 cm), not the smaller (5.9 × 4.3 cm in Mortensen’s measurement of 1931, 5.8 × 4.3 in that of 1955). The spine, in four panels between gilt-ruled bands with a gilt foliate tool in each, carries no lettering, label or number at all, in direct or in raking light: the 2781 that Studnička read in 1901 is no longer visible, and whether it was inked on the parchment and has faded, or stood on a label since lost, cannot be told from photographs. The title page bears Laube's blue stamp ‘Prof. Dr. G. C. Laube, Prag’ at the foot and no other inscription; the Jesuit inscription of 1642 is absent, as Studnička's remark on the intact spine implied. The front flyleaf carries a pencil note in a modern German hand, ‘Aus Tycho Brahes Bibliothek!’, the front pastedown a pencilled ‘760’ within an oval (a bookseller's or collector's number), the title verso a pencilled ‘HS-67’ and the gutter of leaf a2 the Texas call number in pencil; the rear pastedown has the printed bookplate ‘The University of Texas — The Wilhelm Prandtl Collection — The History of Science Collection’; the rear flyleaf is blank. A leaf-through of the whole volume found one marginal entry, on p. 103 of Gesner's De figuris lapidum: beside the woodcut of the goat-engraved gem that Francesco Calzolari of Verona had sent Gesner, a pen drawing of a goat copying it, and below the paragraph a single word in a German cursive hand, apparently ‘mein’, with a long flourish — a reader's doodle in a German hand, with nothing in it to suggest Tycho, whose marginalia are Latin in a humanist cursive; pp. 16–17 of Cordus's De halosantho show only hair-thin curving lines without ink, a dry pen rather than writing. Prandtl, who noted Tycho's hand systematically in other volumes, recorded none here, and the examination confirms it: the volume carries no annotation attributable to Tycho. Walde noted in 1938 that whether the number 2781 came from Tycho himself or from some cataloguing in his library was undecided, and that if it did the library must have run to several thousand works. Prandtl's photograph of 1932 — the book opened flat, lower board, spine and upper board — shows the spine without a number (the journal impression, Philobiblon 5, p. 299, and the offprint's frontispiece agree), and Prandtl, who cites the Bericht, says nothing of one: the number was gone before he bought the book, 'some years' before 1932, that is between Laube's death on 12 April 1923 and the sale of his books. Studnička's page is specific — the number stood on the spine, written, in Tycho's manner — so something was there in 1901; what it was, a dealer's or an owner's pencil number or label cleaned off in the trade, or Tycho's own, the photographs cannot say. The three edges of the text block have not been photographed. || Chapter 3 state sheet, 27 October 2026: the 'about 80 × 60 mm' of the Ransom Center photographs is a reading in the ruler's plane before parallax correction (Gross's own caveat), not a third die size — the oval is the large die (76 × 58 mm of the six concordant sources); the volume is intact as bound for Tycho (one imprint, seven parts); the edges remain unphotographed and the spine untested under ultraviolet.

survivors.notes: Kleinschnitzová no.1; Manuscript. A parchment manuscript in its original binding with the initials T. B. O. and the year 1582 (Norlind 1970, p. 340); Studnička counts it, in brown leather with the initials, to the second period of the bindings (Bericht, 1901, p. 7). He published the tables as Tycho's autograph and held them copied from Regiomontanus's sine tables of 1541 in the Archimedes volume, Sign. 5 C 31 (Bericht, p. 47); Norlind describes them as a copy and reworking of Copernicus's ‘Canon semissium subtensarum rectarum linearum in circulo’. Šíma and Valeška (2002) assign the tables to a professional writer; of the short inscriptions on the end leaves they conclude that they can neither prove them Tycho's nor exclude him. Prusík described the manuscript in 1901 as MS VI E IX: eighteen strong parchment leaves, the brown binding of the middle period full of ornament with ‘T. B. O.’ at the top of the upper board, the title ‘Tabulae sinuum 1582’, no distich on the title but at the lower right, added later in Tycho's hand, the words ‘οἰστέον καὶ ἐλπιστέον’; written for his own use and much worn; Kukula added Studnička's conjecture that the words were set down at the parting from the library on leaving Denmark. || The census re-read of 27 October 2026 counts 24 'manuscript' pages, but in this volume that includes the tables themselves; the added marks are the front-pastedown press-marks (canvas 2: 'Tres. M 1', the struck-through 'TB / [L]I cim. 52.', 'Cim D 82', the label 'E. VI. 9.'), the 1642 inscription and Greek line on f. 1r, 'Numerorum scientia' on f. Iv, the 'Tres. M 1' label on the back board and a short pen stroke above the table on canvas 29. The tables are seven-figure sines in 1' steps (sin 1° = 0174524 on canvas 5; sin 60° = 8660254 on canvas 29) with the differences written between the columns in the same hand.

Manuscript: six folio leaves, the third item of a volume of manuscripts which, according to Studnička, was made up when the Jesuit library was put in order in 1642, the lower and right margins folded in to fit the boards; headed in red ‘Cap. IIII. Quare his disciplinis prae ceteris prima et indubitata sit concludendi ratio’, with sections De puncto, De linea recta, De angulo and De figuris. Found by the custos Josef Truhlář and published by Studnička as Tycho’s autograph, the first page in facsimile in 1901 (Bericht, pp. 51–53) and the whole in 1903 as Brevissimum planimetriae compendium; Kleinschnitzová listed it as an autograph in 1933. Dreyer rejected the hand and the ownership alike — ‘manus non est Tychonis … neque ullum adest indicium, quod in hujus potestate libellum umquam fuisse ostendat’ — and reported from J. L. Heiberg that the text is taken from Proclus’s commentary on the first book of Euclid (Basel 1533) (Opera omnia I, p. 317). Šíma and Valeška (2002) assign the hand to a professional writer. Prusík listed the fragment in 1901 as the third manuscript, ‘eine mathematische Schrift ohne besonderen Titel’, beginning ‘Cap. IIII’, the binding without special character, under the shelfmark MS XII A XII (p. 198), the composite from which Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 83) reports it taken out and bound alone. The manuscript has not been digitised. || Truhlář's printed catalogue (retro-converted in Manuscriptorium, fetched 27 October 2026) places the six leaves at ff. 225–230 of the composite XII A 12 ('Fragmentum hoc manu scriptum nunc separatim asservatur sub sign. XVI/XVII, ff. 6, 30 × 21 cm; Prusík (1901) still found it in XII A 12, so the separation falls between 1901 and 1905–06. Brahe’ (typed) and ‘6’ (by hand), the number of Kleinschnitzová’s catalogue; adl. 1 is Maestlin’s Heidelberg disputation De astronomiae principalibus et primis fundamentis of 1582, and adl. 3 a Prague Jesuit thesis, Problema mathematicum de fontibus, defended by Ferdinand Ernst von Buckau under Theodor Moretus in August 1641 (Prague: typis academicis, 1641) — so the composite was bound no earlier than 1641. || The library's record reads the 1642 Clementinum inscription twice: on the Heron (adl. 2) with 'Ex Bibliotheca Tychonis', and on the Aristarchus host — a piece Kleinschnitzová marks 'Kein Tychonianum' — without any Ex Bibliotheca line but with 'Musei Mathem.'; the 1642 college formula alone therefore does not mark a Tycho book in this volume. open_questions: Whether the Werner's marginalia are Tycho's — first imaged (the annotated openings, especially De motu octavae sphaerae, the tract he sought the book for), then compared against the Graphonomicon's 1580s–1590s pillars; and whether this is the copy he received through Hagecius in 1589 (Kleinschnitzová's 'dürfte … identisch sein'), which a dated note or a Hagecius mark would decide.

survivors.identified_by: Hanslik 1851, pp. 612–613; Friis 1868–69, p. 266; Prusík 1901; Kleinschnitzová 1933, no. 12; Šolc 2002
survivors.notes: Friis described the volume in 1868, brought forward for him by the custos Dambeck: the Rheticus of 1551 with the Jesuit inscription, and ‘en Snees Blade’ (a score of leaves) of manuscript appended — the Praxis, dated at the Calends of January 1591 and ‘A. C. 1595, 13 Cal. Xbris’ — in a hand ‘som man hidtil, men vistnok med Urette, har anseet for den berømte Astronom’; a photograph of the volume had been sent to Copenhagen in 1862 by Dr Joseph Böhm (Berlingske Tidende, 9 March 1863), and Hanslik's history of the library (1851, p. 612) had noticed it (Friis 1868–69, p. 266). Šíma and Valeška (2002) established the hand as a professional copyist's. Prusík listed the Praxis first among the four manuscripts in 1901: a paper manuscript of twenty quarto leaves bound as the first appendix to the printed work at 14 C 20, the binding of the earliest period without special character, ‘Tycho Brahe Calend. Jannuar. 1591’ and the distich dated ‘A. C. 1595. 13 Cal. Xbris’ under the title; its authenticity, doubted by Dreyer, he held proved by Studnička. Hanslik's catalogue of 1851 (pp. 612–613) already printed the appended manuscript as Tycho's autograph, ‘Dogmata geometrica’, found by the custos Dambeck in the mathematical section of the library. || The Praxis (14 C 20/adl.1) is not in the Manuscriptorium facsimile: 26 canvases = the Rheticus's 12 leaves + 2 blanks (verified 27 October 2026); the only reproductions remain Studnička's facsimile of 1886 and Opera omnia I pp. 283–293. The column heads 'sin', 'cos', 'sec' (canvas 12) and 'tg', 'cosec', 'cotg' (canvas 13) pencilled above the Rheticus table are modern function names, a later reader's.

annotation_scan.state_note: Re-read 27 October 2026: no reader's annotation; the positives are the title inscriptions and later pencil function names (canvases 12–13). The census never covered the Praxis, which is not digitised.

survivors.notes: Kleinschnitzová no. 14, shelved as 14 H 188 in 1933; the library’s incunabula shelfmark is 40 F 39 (Boldan 2025, no. 33.b, the library’s own census of its Ratdolt astronomica). Boldan describes the volume as lacking its first gatherings a4 and a10 — the prefaces and Mariensüss’s exposition — which survive, with the same inscription of 1642, bound before the Augsburg 1492 Ephemerides at Strahov (DR VII 19): the two volumes are halves of one Tycho book, divided either in his time or in the Clementinum. || The library's own record of 40 F 39 (Manuscriptorium NKCR__-NKCR__40_F_000039_1OTU6W2-cs, Aleph stt20110039972, read 27 October 2026) states that the volume stood at 14 H 188 in the former Public and University Library and was re-shelved to the incunabula department after the mid-twentieth century — Kleinschnitzová's no. 14 is this volume. It lacks the opening gatherings a4 (Ratdolt's dedication, Regiomontanus's preface) and a10 (Mariensüss's introduction and dedication to Ladislav Černohorský of Boskovice); the title on the blank fol. [b1r] is in Tycho's hand per the record, with the damaged 1642 inscription below it. The marginalia — family entries, deaths of friends of the Leipzig–Dresden–Meissen circle, weather notes, many dated 1487–1506 — are the unknown first owner's. The 16th/17th-century rebinding (light leather over pasteboard, blind-tooled, German Scripture quotations, a foreign workshop, the boards mounted upside down) has a rear board of waste Danish manuscripts of the 16th century (Kleinschnitzová: 17th century); the spine carries the Clementinum's white-grey paint with the red title and shelfmark; ff. [b1–b3] are badly damaged by damp.

custody.basis: Brought to the Clementinum with the library of the dissolved Chomutov college after 1773; Kleinschnitzová counted nineteen volumes of that provenance in 1933 (p. 81).

open_questions: Open question of 27 October 2026 (the afterlife record): by what road the volume reached the Chomutov college — the Clementinum's duplicates under Jüngling (Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021, p. 30), a second gift from the heirs (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 76), or the private hands that gave the college 5 G 92 and 5 J 103 in 1654. Two documented ties now frame the question without closing it: the heirs' claim was assigned in 1623 to the tax arrears of Chomutov and Kadaň among four royal towns — the instructions to the towns to pay from arrears are dated Chomutov 26 September 1623 and Kadaň 3 July 1626 (Volf 1932, part 2, p. 23), and the college itself had lost its library to the Saxon plunder of 1631, partly bought back in 1632, before the first dated Tycho accession of 1645 (Veselá 2025, pp. 27–29). The college's own catalogues of 1645–1675 and the Clementinum's duplicate lists of 1773–1782, if they survive in the Národní archiv or the National Library's archive, would decide.

Whether the white-painted spine carries the Chomutov college’s ink title and class-mark, and whether the flyleaf and title initials T. B. stand as Kleinschnitzová and the library describe them — a reproduction of the spine, the flyleaf and the title from the National Library would close it.

Whether the limp green parchment binding with leather ties is of the sixteenth century (and so the binding the volume had in Tycho’s library) — photographs of the boards, or the library conservator’s dating, would close it.

survivors.notes: A cost note on the first leaf of the Sacrobosco manuscript Sign. VII E 29, which was once bound before the Gauricus of Sign. 14 F 16, is headed ‘Andreas Schöner’ and lists ‘Henricus Glareanus constat 21 ₰’, then the Gauricus and Montulmo, the Albubater, the Cardanus and the binder’s fee (reproduced by Studnička 1901, Bericht, p. 20); the binder's instruction on the last leaf of this volume names the Gauricus with Montulmo and the Albubater. Walde suggested in 1938 that the Glareanus, bought by Vedel in August 1564, may have come to Tycho in exchange for the Sammelband of 1563 now at Uppsala. The library’s records of the three adligata (docs 000082484–000082486, read 20 October 2026): Apianus, Cosmographia, ed. Gemma Frisius, Antwerp: Gregorius Bontius, 1545, inscribed on the title ‘Cubiculi Mathematici Pragae ad S. Clementem A[nn]o 1719’, with Joannes Walthrinus as an earlier owner; Theodosius, De sphaericis, ed. Vögelin, Vienna: Singriener, 1529, with the Charles College ex-libris ‘Col. Caroli IV Mathema. n° 30’; Stöffler, Cosmographicae aliquot descriptiones, ed. Dryander, Marburg: Cervicornus, 1537, inscribed ‘Dom[us] Professae Soc. Jesv ad S. Nicol. Pragae. Catalogo inscriptus 1733’. Each adligatum thus carries a later Prague provenance of its own, which indicates that the composite was assembled in the Clementinum after 1733 (an inference from the inscriptions; the records themselves say only that the three are bound with the Glareanus). No source held attributes these glosses.

survivors.notes:
The earliest dated binding attributed to Tycho anywhere — on the cipher T·B and the year alone, with no inscription, no annotation and no note of 1642, the one Tycho volume inscribed by the Jesuit professed house on the Malá Strana, so the ownership of its three works is graded C (29 October 2026; B on 28 October) — and, now that the Ptolemy 5 B 70 is carried as Pratensis’s, the earliest book attributed to him, if the cipher is his. Christianson (1967, pp. 200–201), reading the student volumes against the Copenhagen curriculum, counts it with the volume of 1561 as ‘two of his own “textbooks”’ still preserved, the Sacrobosco being the text Scavenius lectured on. Šolc’s photographs (2018, figs 1a–b) show on the front board the letters T and B, separated by small ornaments, above a panel stamp of a half-length figure, with the year 1560 below; on the rear board a second figured panel stamp and the paper label ‘Tres. M 47’. The library’s record reads the faint year on the board as 1560 and gives 1567 only in its former-owner field. The volume has no digital facsimile: the National Library’s catalogue record carries no link to a digitised copy, its Manuscriptorium record is a catalogue entry without images, and no copy at Google Books answers to the library’s digitisation identifier. Reproduced in colour by Šolc (2018, figs 1a–c, pp. 194–195 (the boards with ‘T.B. 1560’ and the label ‘Tres. M 47’, the Bayrus title)). Re-checked 25 October 2026: the Manuscriptorium image service answers ‘can’t get list of images’ for the record and the OAI repository does not hold it — there is no digital copy. || The binding's year 1560 rests on readings of the board (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 94; the library: ‘málo znatelný letopočet 1560’; Šolc's text), not on an image: Šolc's plate does not resolve it at its printed size. Google Books returned no record for NKP:1002596125 on 27 October 2026.

Material: blind-stamped pigskin (alum-tawed), the compiler's reading of Šolc's photograph on 28 October 2026; every printed description says ‘white leather’. Photographs of the boards, the three edges and the three title pages at 600 dpi were requested from the National Library on 28 October 2026 (the reproduction request of 23 October, item 6).

|| 29 October 2026 — the literature pack read whole (39 passages, 24 documents): every author after 1933 derives from Kleinschnitzová (Norlind 1970 p. 339, adding a letter O the board does not carry; Šolc 1999, 2006, 2018, with the Bayrus misdated 1559 in two of the three; Christianson 1967 pp. 200–201 and 2020; Thoren 1990; Pařez 2009), and none adds a mark, a hand, a note or an argument. Kleinschnitzová herself (pp. 76–78) counts the twenty-three Clementinum volumes with the note of 1642 and lets this one ‘verirrt sich’ — stray — into the professed house, which is the conclusion restated as a route. The library’s former-owner field gives Tycho and the professed house the year 1567, unexplained beside its own binding note ‘málo znatelný letopočet 1560’. No source asks whether another T. B. owned a Basel 1560 imprint bound in 1560. Ownership C until the boards, edges, title pages and pastedowns are read on the photographs requested on 28 October 2026.

Wholly in Tycho's hand: probable — Mortensen's verdict (‘egenhændige Tilskrift’), the signature built as the secure Wittenberg leaf of 8 May 1599 and the Duodo dedication of 1600, the address sharing the father's own prose idioms (the u-mark, the hooked descending J, the looped d), no calligrapher's marks, one ink and one planned block; the alternative of an address written at the same desk by a secretary over Tycho's signature is not excluded by the photographs — though Jessenius, the one documented secretary of such an address, is disfavoured on a word-for-word comparison with his album entry of 8 January 1599, and the father's own prose in the same album shares the address's 5-shaped round s and its L — and the son (who signed ‘T.F.’, ‘Filius’, ‘junior’ and never had a channel to a Lindenov) is excluded on context | binding period: Period 4 (gilt supralibros)
survivors.identified_by: Harald Mortensen 1955, pp. 25–27 (the volume acquired by the Royal Library from America through Hjalmar Bruhn: the small portrait-and-arms supralibros and Tycho's dedication to his cousin Hans Lindenov); Norlind 1970, p. 341, from Mortensen; examined and photographed in the Royal Library's reading room on 21 October 2026 — the library's copy eks. 2, 88, 201 01801, identified by the pencil catalogue signature 88,-201 on its front pastedown, the small dies on both boards, the dedication on the verso of the free endpaper and the Theocritus of 1596 bound second; the accession mark ‘1954 g. 230’ in pencil on the free endpaper
survivors.notes: A Tycho Sammelband, a Prachtband containing Calvin’s Epistolae et responsa (Hanau 1597) and the Theocritus of 1596, repatriated from the USA through the ship-broker (skibsmægler) Hjalmar Bruhn, the Royal Library’s benefactor (Mortensen 1955, p. 25: ‘Det kongelige Biblioteks altid redebonne Velgører Skibsmægler Hjalmar Bruhn’); the first book from Tycho’s own library to enter the Royal Library, which until then had owned none apart from the autograph observations (Mortensen 1955, p. 25: ‘har det hidtil ikke ejet en Bog fra hans egen Bogsamling (bortset fra de haandskrevne Observationer)’). Given by Tycho to his cousin Hans Lindenov after the Calvin edition of 1597 had appeared — probably before 1599, Mortensen supposes, unless the book was sent to Lindenov later (pp. 26–27). The dedication stands on the verso of the free endpaper facing the title; the supralibros is small. Mortensen describes the binding (1955, pp. 25–26): ‘et slidt Pergamentbind med Spor af grønne Bindebaand’, the portrait and arms plaques on the two boards, ‘derudenom en ret bred rektangulær Ramme trykt med Rullestempel, og inden i Rammens Hjørner Rosetter. Den udekorerede Ryg har haandskreven Titel fra senere Tid.’ His expansion of the dedication’s abbreviation is corrected by the corrigenda in Fund og Forskning X (1963), p. 155: ‘bør forkortelsen ddt opløses til dono dedit eller dedicavit’. The Royal Library’s catalogue lists two copies of the Hanau 1597 edition (VD16 C 304): 88, 201 01800, in the ordinary stacks, with the provenance of L. M. Schavenius, and 88, 201 01801, kept in the library’s store of rarities and lent only to the reading room, with no provenance or item note. The library’s copy of the Theocritus (Commelinus, 1596) at 168, 370 02401 is a separate copy; a constituent of the Sammelband would be shelved under the Calvin call number. The library has not confirmed that 88, 201 01801 is the volume acquired through Bruhn in 1954. Examined and photographed in the Forskningslæsesal on 21 October 2026: Photographed in the Forskningslæsesal on 21 October 2026, both Royal Library copies of the Hanau 1597 Calvin on the table: the Sammelband is eks. 2, 88, 201 01801 (barcode 201003563960), kept in the box store and, by the library's word, in Håndskriftsamlingens arkiv; eks. 1 is Scavenius's copy of 1665. Binding 175 × 120 × 75 mm, leaves 171 × 106 × 70 mm. What the volume carries beyond Tycho's marks, read on the object: the Royal Library's pencil catalogue signature ‘88,-201’ at the head of the front pastedown and again on the inner board edge (the Udenlandske Afdeling's Ældre Samling signature, two numbers with comma and dash); the accession mark ‘1954 g. 230’ in pencil along the fore-edge of the free endpaper — the accession year (or the financial year 1954/55) and a serial number, the letter unexplained, the only witness to the year of the purchase, which no printed source gives; ‘Boghist. Saml.’ (the Boghistorisk Studiesamling, the locked selection of the Ældre Samling started in the 1950s for books of provenance or annotation), ‘BOX’ (the climate-controlled box store funded in 1976 and filled in 1977–78), ‘S-1977’ (a marking of the security and revision campaign of 1977), and between them an earlier location of four pointed capitals beginning ‘D.A.’, struck through in the same pencil; ‘1597’ in pencil at the foot of the Calvin title; ‘dupl’ in pencil at the head of the Theocritus title — most simply the library's own duplicate check of 1954 against its separate Theocritus of 1596 (168, 370 02401), which is why the Sammelband is catalogued under the Calvin alone; the alternative, that the library had once owned and sold the volume as a duplicate and bought it back, is unsupported (duplicates were not signed before separation; Ilsøe records no Calvin of 1597 or Theocritus of 1596 in any duplicate sale; the catalogues of 1783 and 1786 are unread). Beneath the library's marks a continental layer of unknown origin: ‘fol. 9781’ at the foot of the rear pastedown, a graphite or ink number in a nineteenth- or early twentieth-century hand whose 7 is crossed (not the library's own pencil series of c. 1663, which runs only to c. 9200, has no prefix and covers Frederik III's stock), a pencil ‘36’ at its head, a two-letter pencil code ‘fij’ at the foot of the Theocritus title (a bookseller's cipher, or ‘ij’ for the second piece), an erased pencil note on the free endpaper, illegible even in the raw frames, three label-shaped areas at the head of each pastedown where paper has been removed (the library's pencils run over them, so they are earlier), and a scraped, thinned spot with brown specks immediately above the device on the Calvin title — the usual place for an owner's name, and not the library's practice, which stamped and did not erase; no library stamp is visible on either title. The spine carries an ink title in a round upright italic of the seventeenth century, ‘Johannis Caluini | Epistolae et Respons[a] | Theocriti | Idyllia et Epigra[m]ata’, not the dedication hand (Mortensen's ‘haandskreven Titel fra senere Tid’) and not the library's — a private owner of the Danish custody, to be set beside the Scavenius spine titles of eks. 1. No American mark is identifiable: the owner ‘fra Amerika’ either left none or removed it. The binding: gilt parchment over stiff pasteboard, three laced thongs, a flat untooled spine, two pairs of green silk ties (remnants in the slits at the fore-edge), all edges stained red and plain, plaited natural-thread endbands; on each board a gilt leaf roll with a twisted central line (band c. 7–8 mm, leaf pitch c. 5 mm, the corners overrun, not mitred) with four five-petalled heraldic double roses with hatched barbs, c. 11 mm, in the corners and the oval at centre, the gilt mostly worn. The dies place nothing (they were at Hven by 1588, in Prague after 1599 and in use after Tycho's death); the roll is a laurel garland of 6 mm pitch of the type Gigas saw on the Epistolae of 1596 and GKS 307, and the roll frame without a lozenge has its parallel in Gigas's plate of the Epistolae for Duke Johan Adolf; the rose punch is not that of GKS 307 (c. 18 mm) and probably not that of the Epistolae (c. 14 mm), nor the star-in-circle of Strahov Σ VI 3, the other small-die carrier; its nearest relative is the rose on the Magini De mundi of Hven, the same five-petalled barbed design a tenth smaller. The structure — stiff parchment, three laced thongs, flat spine, green ties, a rectangular frame with corner roses — is that of the Hven parchment family, not of the Prague leather bindings, so the evidence tilts to Tycho's own tool-kit used after Hven, at Wandsbek in 1597–98 or in Copenhagen in the spring of 1597, with Prague the less likely; the plain red edges have no parallel on any Hven binding the edition can see. The rose punch at 1:1 against the Magini rose and the rose on Astr. 1100 would decide. The dedication, read at native resolution and tested by refutation: one ink and one planned block (the ſ of the second line fitted into the space above the y of the third, the T's arch filling the indent of the second line); the signature constructed as the secure Wittenberg leaf of 8 May 1599 and the Duodo dedication of 1600; the address sharing the father's informal-prose idioms; no diaeresis on the y, as on two other secure specimens; the formula after the name, unparalleled among the store's dedications but explained by the sentence order; the doubled stroke over ‘ddt’ paralleled by the Duodo ‘DDt.’. The photographs cannot separate two writers sharing one inkwell at one desk, so an address written by a secretary over Tycho's own ‘Tycho Brahe ddt’ (the practice of the Mosbach Mechanica, where the signature came first and Jessenius added the address later at Wittenberg) remains the one live alternative, decided only by the order of the strokes where the second line crosses the third — and that alternative is now disfavoured for Jessenius himself: his own entry in the album of Tycho's son (Národní muzeum VI F 44, fol. 24r, Wittenberg, 8 January 1599), set word for word against the address, has an I in ‘Iohan:’ that is a straight oblique stroke without descender or foot where the address's J descends and hooks, an h whose right limb descends where the address's sits on the baseline, a sigma-form round s, a small hooked u-mark and a joined cursive ductus, while the father's own prose on the first leaf of the same album shares with the address the 5-shaped round s (‘suo’ beside ‘Sortis’), the construction of the capital L (‘Lindenouio’ beside ‘Laborem’), the arc u-mark, the baseline h and the lifted, letter-by-letter ductus, with no disagreement of construction found; the untested hands are Longomontanus and Tengnagel; the son, who in 1598 gave a cousin a Mechanica under a bare ‘Tycho Brahe’, is excluded on context — in Italy in 1601, Prague in 1602 and northern Bohemia from 1603, the only Copenhagen entry in his album dated 28 October 1599, no channel to any Lindenov, and every specimen of his own hand marked ‘T.F.’, ‘Filius’ or ‘junior’. Where and when the gift was made: Kancelliets Brevbøger reach Hans Lindenov on Bornholm throughout 1597–1602 — a new lensbrev from 1 May 1597, the Swedish-muster alert of 20 June 1597, the Bilde complaint of 26 July 1597, the new lensbrev from 1 May 1599, and in November 1600 his castle clerk, not he, ‘nu var her med Hans Lindenovs Regnskab’; no herredag met in 1597, no letter summons him to Copenhagen, and he had needed royal leave to go home in February 1596 — so a meeting in Copenhagen in the spring of 1597, when Tycho lodged there, is possible but undocumented, and a sending to Bornholm or Ørslev from Wandsbek, Wittenberg or Prague, through the Lindenov–Bille kin who were in letter contact with Tycho in 1598–1600, is the more economical reading. The Royal Library's own record of the acquisition (the file behind accession 1954 no. 230, which should name the seller) has not been asked for. The rose punch, tested the same evening against every Tycho binding imaged at a known scale: the rose of the Hven presentation bindings is a punch of about 14.5 mm with line-hatched outer petals and a seeded centre — on the Stockholm De mundi of 1588 (Dudith's copy, RAR 106 A, 14.1–14.9 mm against the ruler in the Swedish digitisation), on the Dibner Epistolae of 1596 (14.4–15.2 mm against the Kodak scale in the Smithsonian's photograph), on the Epistolae presented to Duke Johan Adolf (the Royal Library's LN 430 4°, eks. 1, the copy Gigas knew as Astr. 1100; 13.8–14.6 mm on the cover image in Early European Books, scaled on the large oval and checked on the roll's 6.4 mm pitch) and, by size, on the Mechanica presented to Jan Zbyněk z Hazmburka (Strahov AG XI 56, 14.2–15.0 mm); the rose on the Magini De mundi is a second punch of 9.5–10 mm; the rose on this volume, 11 mm with smooth petals and a bossed centre, is a third. The binding was therefore not made with Tycho's presentation tools: a binder working in the same idiom, with his own rose and a laurel roll of the same type and nearly the same pitch (6.0 against 6.2–6.6 mm), bound the two books. Where is still open — Copenhagen in 1597, Rostock, Wandsbek or Hamburg in 1597–98, Wittenberg in 1598–99 — with Prague low, since the other small-die carrier at Strahov has a star and raised bands; a dated Wandsbek binding imaged at high resolution (the Mechanica presentation copies, the Royal Library's LN 432) is now the comparator to seek.

custody.basis: Tycho’s dedication ‘Johanni Lindenouio consobrino suo Tycho Brahe ddt’ on the verso of the free endpaper facing the title. The recipient is Hans Christoffersen Lindenov til Ørslevkloster (d. by 7 April 1610): lensmand at Bergenhus 1578–86, where the four royal letters on Tycho's Nordfjord fief were addressed to him (29 May 1579, 10 August 1580, 8 January 1581, 16 March 1586; TBOO XIV, pp. 9, 14, 19; Friis 1871, p. 161), landsdommer in Nørrejylland from 1587, holder of Ørslev Kloster by exchange with the crown from 1584, lensmand at Hammershus 1594–1610, the fief withdrawn on 3 January 1610 for infirmity (DAA 1902, pp. 286–287; Bricka X, pp. 316–318). He crossed to Hven with Tycho in the night of 3–4 July 1594 and left on the 5th — ‘rediit D. T. cum Hans Lindenov et D. G.’, ‘Abiit Johannes Lindenow’ — his one visit in the diary (Friis ed. 1876, pp. 218–219). Tycho's consobrinus: Mortensen read the word strictly, Hans a son of Christoffer Lindenov's first marriage with Margrethe Clausdatter Bille (b. 1525), sister of Tycho's mother Beate, against DAA 1902, which lists him under the second wife Ide Rantzau; DAA dates neither marriage and no later Rettelser took the point up, so Mortensen's reading stands unrefuted (Mortensen 1955, p. 27; DAA 1890, p. 87). The Calvin edition was on sale at the Frankfurt Lent fair of 1597 (Lutz, A2v, under ‘Libri Calvinianorum’) and cannot have been among the books registered at Uraniborg on 21 March 1597 (the diary, p. 263; Mortensen prints 10 March); Mortensen puts the gift probably before 1599, unless the book was sent to Lindenov later (pp. 26–27: ‘sandsynligvis har han faaet Bogen i Tiden før 1599, hvis den da ikke paa et senere Tidspunkt er blevet sendt til ham’). Lindenov sat on Bornholm from 1594, so the book was handed over elsewhere or sent; the strict window is 1597 to October 1601. Examined 21 October 2026: the dedication read on the leaf (see the marks). Kancelliets Brevbøger place Lindenov on Bornholm throughout 1597–1602 — the lensbrev from 1 May 1597 (pp. 126–127), the missives of 20 June and 26 July 1597 (pp. 171, 187), the new lensbrev from 1 May 1599 (p. 419), the Gæsteri letters of November 1600 in which his castle clerk brought the account to Copenhagen (pp. 561, 563–564), the stranded munitions of 12 November 1601 (p. 684) — and record no summons to Copenhagen; no herredag met in 1597, and he had needed royal leave to go home in February 1596 (the 1593–96 volume, p. 585). A hand-over in Copenhagen in April–May 1597 is therefore possible but undocumented, and a sending to Bornholm or Ørslev from Wandsbek, Wittenberg or Prague the more economical reading; the chancery, Tycho's own papers (the index of the Opera omnia has no Hans Lindenov after 1586) and the son's album give no trace of him in Germany or Bohemia. The enfeoffment with Hammershus dates from 20 June 1594, two weeks before he crossed to Hven with Tycho; the landsdommer's office in Jutland was no longer his in 1597–1601, when the chancery addresses the landsdommere Mogens and Iver Juel separately.

No owner is recorded between Lindenov and the volume’s appearance in America. Lindenov's widow Elsebe Jensdatter Juel held Ørslev to her death in 1626/27 and the estate stayed with his son and grandson to 1642 (DAA 1902); no sale of his books is recorded, no second volume with his name is known, and the auction databases hold no Tycho-marked Calvin or Theocritus at any date (Rare Book Hub transaction history, searched 21 October 2026). Mortensen's ‘fra Amerika’ names a place, not a dealer, an auction, a private owner or an institution. The object adds the first physical trace of the road: on the rear pastedown ‘fol. 9781’ in a continental hand of the nineteenth or early twentieth century (the 7 crossed) and a pencil ‘36’; at the foot of the Theocritus title the pencil code ‘fij’; an erased pencil note on the free endpaper; three label-shaped areas at the head of each pastedown where paper has been removed, earlier than the library's pencils of 1954–77; and a scraped inscription above the device on the Calvin title — one or more European trade or institutional passages before America, none named. The spine title in a seventeenth-century Danish hand stands between Lindenov and that road (examined 21 October 2026).

Acquired from America with the support of the ship-broker Hjalmar Bruhn (Mortensen 1955, p. 25: ‘Ved virksom Støtte af Det kongelige Biblioteks altid redebonne Velgører Skibsmægler Hjalmar Bruhn er det lykkedes fra Amerika at hjemføre en Bog, der har tilhørt Tycho Brahe’); ‘for få år siden’ in 1959 (Paulli & Dal 1959, p. 15). The year is not stated anywhere: Bruhn (1881–1959) is already the library's benefactor in January 1952 (Paulli 1954, p. 7) and the volume is ‘det nu erhvervede’ in the article of 1955, so the purchase falls between 1952 and 1955 (Paulli & Dal 1958–59, p. 15: ‘for få år siden lykkedes Det kongelige Biblioteks at erhverve et tychonisk samlebind fra USA’). The accession mark in pencil on the free endpaper, ‘1954 g. 230’ (read 21 October 2026), gives the year — 1954, or the financial year 1954/55 — and the serial; the volume went into the Boghistorisk Studiesamling (‘Boghist. Saml.’), was moved to the box store (‘BOX’) in the security campaign of 1977 (‘S-1977’), an earlier location beginning ‘D.A.’ cancelled, and is catalogued as eks. 2 of the Hanau Calvin, 88, 201 01801, its Theocritus marked ‘dupl’ against the library's separate copy. Bruhn died on 21 December 1959 (‘Bruhn, Hj., Skibsmgl.’, Dødsfald i Danmark 1959); he had funded the library's purchases at the Maar auction of 1952 and given it a Steno quarto, a Pontoppidan psalm-book in a silver-filigree binding (1954) and two Andersen dedication copies (1955) — Danish-department benefactions, the Tycho volume the only Tychonian among them.

open_questions: Whether all four lines of the dedication are one hand or an address written by a secretary at Tycho's desk over his own ‘Tycho Brahe ddt’: the photographs of 21 October 2026 show one ink, one nib and one planned block, which excludes a composite made at a distance but not one made in one sitting; the order of the strokes where the second line meets the third (the ſ-tail against the T and y; the h of ‘Tycho’ against ‘Consobrino’) and at the bars over ‘ddt’, read under magnification, decides it, with ultraviolet or infrared reflectance of the two halves if the library's conservators will run it. Jessenius, the one documented secretary of such an address, is disfavoured on a word-for-word comparison with his entry in the album of Tycho's son (VI F 44, fol. 24r, 8 January 1599), and the father's own prose in the same album shares the address's 5-shaped round s and its L; Longomontanus (ÖNB Cod. 10703, f. 236v, reading room only) and Tengnagel (no image) are untested, and those two letters are the features to test them on. A side-by-side with the Otte Steensen Brahe Mechanica (Hielmst. 148 2° eks. 4) and the dated copy LN 432 copy 3 in the same reading room would test the hand against the one disputed and one secure comparator the library holds.

Where the volume was bound (Copenhagen 1597, Rostock or Wandsbek 1597–98, Wittenberg 1598–99, Prague 1599–1601): the corner rose is not Tycho's presentation rose (c. 14.5 mm on the Stockholm De mundi, the Dibner and Johan Adolf Epistolae and the Hazmburk Mechanica) nor the Magini rose (9.5–10 mm) but a third punch of 11 mm, so the binder worked with his own tools in the Hven idiom; the laurel roll (6.0 mm pitch) is of the type on the Epistolae and GKS 307 and cannot be told from it at the resolutions reached. A dated Wandsbek or Wittenberg binding imaged at high resolution — the Mechanica presentation copies, LN 432 — and, on the object, the sewing and any binder's waste against the library's own Tycho bindings on one table would decide; the dies travelled and outlived Tycho.

Where and when the book changed hands: Lindenov is on Bornholm in every chancery letter of 1597–1602, Tycho in Copenhagen only in April–May 1597; the Hammershus accounts and the Rentemester accounts at Rigsarkivet (travel, absences, the clerk's journeys) and Hübertz's Bornholm documents of 1597–1601 would show whether he left the island that spring.

The road from Lindenov's heirs to America: who wrote ‘fol. 9781’, ‘36’ and ‘fij’, what the erased endpaper note said, whose labels were removed from the pastedowns, whose name was scraped from the Calvin title, and who owned the book ‘i Amerika’ — the library's own file behind accession 1954 no. 230 should name the seller and the price — not asked for, by the editor's decision — and the annotated duplicate catalogues of 1742, 1783, 1786 and 1836 (archive E 23 and E 62; Ilsøe 1998) would retire for good the reading of ‘dupl’ as an earlier Royal Library passage.

The meaning of ‘g.’ in the accession mark, of ‘S-1977’, and of the cancelled location ‘D.A.?.?’; whether ‘fol. 9781’ is ink or graphite; whether a library stamp exists anywhere in the volume; the conjugacy of the dedication leaf with the pastedown and whether the red edge-stain runs onto it.

27 Oct 2026 [unchangeable] - the frames of 21 October 2026 show the marks but cannot answer what the library's own pencils mean (a second reading-room session with the library's duplicate catalogues and a stamp search; the conjugacy and the edge-stain by eye).
Whether the spine title's hand is Peder Scavenius's (the Scavenius books of eks. 1 are known by his spine titles) or another seventeenth-century Danish owner's.

Whether Scaliger's Emendationes (30 pp.) and Casaubon's Theocriticarum lectionum libellus (150 pp.), the second and third parts of VD16 ZV 14910, are bound in; the collation of both constituents was not made.

27 Oct 2026 [unchangeable] - the collation was not made on 21 October 2026 and no facsimile exists; a reading-room collation of the Theocritus (VD16 ZV 14910 parts 2–3) is the test, orderable while the volume is on loan to the reading room (to 13 November 2026).

Open question of 27 October 2026 (the afterlife record): the road from Lindenov's heirs at Ørslev to the American owner of the twentieth century; published sources only — the Lindenov estate's dispersal after 1642 (DAA 1902), the Danish and German sale catalogues that would carry ‘fol. 9781’, and the Royal Library's published accession report of 1954.

survivors.notes: Agrippa, Opera, tomus I (Lyon, c. 1550, 8vo): the parchment Prachtband with the gilt portrait-and-arms plaques that Prandtl listed in 1932 as Band XX in Harald Mortensen’s collection at Copenhagen. Bought in Germany by professor Sigurd Wandel, then Mortensen’s. Paulli and Dal (1959, pp. 15–16) print the letter to the museum’s director Otto Andrup of 30 December 1949 by which the testamentary promise became a gift in the donor’s lifetime: ‘selv om jeg hænger ved disse Ting, kan jeg jo have ligesaa megen Glæde af at se dem velforvaret udstillet paa Frederiksborg’. The gift was made in 1950, and the volume was shown in the museum’s Tycho Brahe case when Mortensen wrote in 1955. The museum confirmed in a communication of 28 September 2026 that it holds the volume in its library as inventory B3950a-b, not on display, and on 12 October 2026 that the suffix names two inventoried parts: the volume (a) and the slipcase it is kept in (b).

custody.basis: The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931).
Mortensen 1955, p. 30, from Dr Teichl’s report of 1943: ‘Bogen … har tidligere tilhørt Jesuiterkollegiet i Prag’. The library’s own record names no former owner.
How the volume reached Vienna is not documented.

survivors.institution_raw: Röhsska Museum, Göteborg
survivors.later_owners: Ludwig Rosenthal, antiquarian bookseller, Munich — who in 1906 sent the volume to the Zeitschrift für Bücherfreunde, where its two plaques were reproduced → Baron Per Hierta (1864–1924), Främmestad, Västergötland → Röhsska Konstslöjdmuseet, Göteborg, by 1955
survivors.marks_securing_id: Tycho's gilt portrait+arms superexlibris — the finely struck, well-preserved exemplar figured in the Zeitschrift für Bücherfreunde X (1906/07). On a Renaissance binding: the 1906 notice took it for Basel work made for Tycho, Bargum for Danish work made under his direction, Mortensen (1955, p. 28) for a binding Tycho acquired bound and then stamped. The 1906 description: brown leather over wooden boards, two chased brass clasps, seven raised bands, three blind-tooled frames (the inner one with fourteen scholar-portrait medallions), four gilt rosettes, the two gilt medallions with the distichs. | binding period: Period 4 (gilt supralibros)
survivors.identified_by: Prandtl 1932 (no.57 / Einzelband XXV); Mortensen 1955 (pp. 28–30)
survivors.notes: Theatri humanae vitae vol. XVIII (Basel 1587). Mortensen 1955 (pp. 28–30) identifies the volume Prandtl catalogued as no. 57, ex Per Hierta, with the one now at the Röhsska museum, Göteborg. The modern inventory number and the museum’s accession are not recorded. The volume was first published in 1906, when Ludwig Rosenthal of Munich sent it to the Zeitschrift für Bücherfreunde: wooden boards covered in brown leather, two chased brass clasps, seven raised bands, three blind-tooled frames, the innermost with fourteen portrait medallions of scholars, four gilt rosettes, and the gilt portrait and arms medallions with their distichs; a manuscript note inside the board called it a ‘Schweizer Ledereinband mit Blinddruck und Goldmedaillons’, and the writer supposed the binding made at Basel for Tycho. Bargum answered from Copenhagen in the same volume that the binding was Danish work made under Tycho’s direction — though he could not match the fourteen medallions on any other Tycho binding — that Tycho was not at Basel in 1587, that Gellius Sascerides may have procured the book at Basel or at the Frankfurt fair after the summer of 1588, and that Tycho may have taken from Zwinger’s title the name of his projected Theatrum astronomicum. Mortensen in 1955 took the volume for a Renaissance binding that Tycho acquired bound and then stamped, the reading followed here. Neither notice names the volume’s owner between Rosenthal and Hierta. || Chapter 3 state sheet, 27 October 2026: the object has never been seen by the house and no image exists beyond the two plaques of 1906; the museum's inventory number is unknown and its online catalogue unreachable; the enquiry to the museum (one letter: the accession record for chapter II, photographs of boards with a rule, spine, edges, pastedowns and title for chapter III) is drafted in the talk folder, unsent.

custody.basis: The route out of the library and to Sweden is undocumented (possibly the Swedish sack of Prague in 1648, but no evidence places the volume on that road).

Hierta's collection of bookbindings was bought by Hjalmar Wijk and given to the Röhsska in 1915 (SBL 19, p. 32; Nordisk familjebok, 4th ed., p. 528); Hierta died in 1924, so Prandtl's placing of the volume at Främmestad in 1932 was already stale (W9, 27 October 2026).

There by 1955 (Mortensen 1955, p. 30: ‘findes nu i Röhsska Konstslöjdmuseet, Göteborg’; p. 28: one of the Nordic volumes ‘har skiftet Ejer siden Prandtls Liste udkom’); the museum’s accession is not documented. Most probably with Wijk's gift of Hierta's bindings in 1915 (C: neither source names the Zwinger).

Open question of 27 October 2026 (the afterlife record): the road from the heirs to Rosenthal's stock of 1906 and from Hierta's Främmestad to the museum; the museum's accession ledger (asked for in the draft enquiry of 27 October 2026, unsent) would close the last step, and any owner's mark before 1906 the first.

Narrowed 27 October 2026 (the research round): Hierta's bindings reached the museum by Wijk's gift of 1915, so the accession to ask for is that gift's list; the step Rosenthal 1906 → Hierta is still undocumented — Prandtl cites ‘ZfB 1914, 224’, unread in the house (W9).

What the binding is in the museum's own description — materials, the die size (large or small plaques), the edges, any inscription or label of the owner before Rosenthal 1906 — and under what terms its photographs may be shown; the museum's answer to the drafted enquiry would decide.

survivors.institution_raw: Austrian National Library, Vienna
survivors.marks_securing_id: No Tycho mark. The ÖNB description records no former owner (only a 19th-c. half-parchment rebinding). The identification rests on Norlind's attribution and on the volume's Uraniborg-circle content — Longomontanus's 'Responsio ad Capnurianam apologiam' is bound in the same 16th-c. Sammelhandschrift — which is circumstantial, not a mark.
survivors.identified_by: Norlind 1970, p. 343 (a work-level attribution: Tycho's copy of the Commentariolus; the National Library's record of Cod. 10530 names no former owner, and the volume carries no Tycho mark)
survivors.notes: Walde showed in 1938 that the manuscript belonged to Johannes Eriksen of Hamburg, tutor to Tycho’s sons at Wittenberg in February 1598 and Tycho’s amanuensis at Prague in 1601: it carries the inscription, as Curtze transcribed it, ‘Dominus M. Christiernus Severinus Longomontanus reliquit amico suo Iohanni Ericksen [a Greek word] Benachia Bohemorum 18. Julii discedens A° 1600’ — Longomontanus’s parting gift at Benátky. Walde left open the assumption that it then passed to Tycho and with his papers to Vienna, observing that Eriksen’s other books and manuscripts went into Queen Christina’s library with the Prague booty (a Pitiscus of 1600 bought at Prague on 14 August 1601, now at Hanover; two chemical manuscripts at Leiden from Vossius’s share; a Lull of 1593 at Västerås with the Christina shelfmark), and supposed that his literary property came into Rudolf II’s hands. The manuscript is a sixteenth-century Latin Sammelhandschrift of 45 leaves containing the Commentariolus of Copernicus and the Responsio ad Capnurianam apologiam of Longomontanus, Tycho’s chief assistant. The Austrian National Library’s description records a nineteenth-century half-parchment rebinding and no former owner, and does not mention Brahe; Norlind’s attribution of the manuscript to Tycho’s library is not corroborated by the catalogue, and the link to Tycho rests on the Longomontanus text and the circle of Uraniborg. The library has published a full digitisation of the manuscript. || Chapter 3 state sheet, 27 October 2026: the National Library's facsimile has a IIIF v3 manifest (api.onb.ac.at/iiif/presentation/v3/manifest/DTL_2808861) of 100 canvases at 2257 × 2881 px, covers included; the cover-to-cover reading for a mark of ownership is the one test that can be made from home and is in progress.

survivors.institution_raw: Private American collector (acquired from Martayan Lan, New York, Catalogue 28, 2001, item 55; formerly Felix Mainx, Prague, acquired 1938, then ‘a private European collector’)
survivors.later_owners: Felix Mainx, Prague (acquired 1938; he told Harald Mortensen of it, and Mortensen printed the fact in Fund og Forskning 2, 1955, p. 30) → ‘a private European collector’ (Martayan Lan's provenance line, 2001) → Martayan Lan, New York, Catalogue 28 (2001), item 55, offered at US$ 300,000 → a private American collector (Gingerich 2002, p. 326 n. 16)
survivors.marks_securing_id: Tycho's autograph annotations throughout, from a word or two to a note filling the margin, incl. the long note written upside down in the lower margin of Book II, pp. 124–125 (the hand confirmed by Owen Gingerich, per litteras 25 May 2001, and studied by Anthony Grafton); Tycho's gilt portrait supralibros with the motto ‘Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei / pulchrius eniteat, quae latet interior’ on the front cover and the Brahe arms with ‘Arma genus fundi pereunt durabile virtus / et doctrina decus nobilitatis habent’ on the back | binding period: Period 4 (gilt supralibros): contemporary flexible vellum with yapp edges, the portrait-and-arms supralibros (Martayan Lan 2001)
survivors.identified_by: Harald Mortensen 1955, p. 30 (from Felix Mainx's report of 1938); Norlind 1970, p. 347; the annotations recognised as Tycho's by Owen Gingerich (per litteras, 25 May 2001) and Anthony Grafton (report for Martayan Lan, 2001); Gingerich 2002, p. 326
survivors.notes: Martayan Lan’s description (Catalogue 28, item 55, pp. 66–67, headed ‘Tycho Brahe reads & annotates the new star of 1572: unpublished notes on “the greatest cosmological crisis in Western history” – Grafton’): 4to; 229, (1) pp., (5) ff., 284 pp., 18 ff.; three woodcut star charts and several depictions of constellations and related astronomical phenomena in the text. Binding: contemporary flexible vellum with yapp edges, a gilt medallion portrait of Tycho in the centre of the front cover, worn, with ‘Hic patet exterior Tychonis forma Brahei / pulchrius eniteat, quae latet interior’ in the surround; the back cover with the Brahe family arms and ‘Arma genus fundi pereunt durabile virtus / et doctrina decus nobilitatis habent’; covers soiled, remnants of ties; an old shelfmark stencilled on the spine. Condition: front endleaf soiled, with unidentified later annotations; waterstain and soiling in the upper right corner of the title and on scattered leaves; a scored former ownership inscription and a later inscription dated 1647; even toning, occasional light browning; ‘for a working copy, very good’. The price asked was US$ 300,000. The annotations in Tycho’s hand range from a word or two to notes virtually filling the margin; on pp. 124–125 of Book II the lower-margin note was entered with the copy held upside down (the colour plate at the front of the catalogue, captioned ‘Tycho Brahe’s Annotated Copy No. 55’; Gingerich 2002, fig. 1). The dealer supplied a list of the annotated locations with a partial transcription, and Anthony Grafton’s detailed but preliminary report, available on request, which found a genetic relation to the Progymnasmata (Prague 1602); Owen Gingerich confirmed the hand (per litteras, 25 May 2001) and wrote that the book ‘contains source material used directly by Tycho in composing his Progymnasmata … this is a working text that is feeding directly into his published work, and we have nothing else like this’. The dealer called it ‘one of only two known copies of any book owned by the astronomer in private hands’. Provenance as given: ‘a private European collector. In 1955, the Danish librarian H. Mortensen described the present copy as being in the private collection of a professor in Prague’ – that professor is Felix Mainx, who told Mortensen in 1938 that he had acquired Tycho’s copy (Mortensen 1955, p. 30); Gingerich 2002, p. 326, which places the book in Mortensen’s own collection about 1955, misreads Mortensen’s paper. Gingerich 2002, p. 327: Tycho annotated heavily the section on Muñoz’s observations of the new star of 1572 and quoted the passage in the Progymnasmata; n. 16: now in the hands of a private American collector. References cited by the dealer: Norlind 1970, p. 347; Adams G-373; Durling 2042; Warner, The Sky Explored, p. 92; Daston & Park, Wonders and the Order of Nature, p. 175; Christianson 2000, p. 139; Prandtl 1932 (cited by the offprint pagination, pp. 1–16).

custody.basis: The route out of the library is undocumented: the library remained with Tycho’s heirs in 1601 (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76, 78), but nothing places this volume with them, and the first dated witness on the copy is the inscription of 1647.

open_questions: Open question of 27 October 2026 (the afterlife record): the two intervals — from the library to the inscription of 1647, and from 1647 to 1938; the inscriber of 1647 identified would place the volume on the private road (II) or in a Jesuit house, and the dealer of 1938 named would open the modern chain.

Which of the two oval dies the vellum carries (large 76 × 58 or small 58 × 43 mm): not stated by the dealer and not measurable from the catalogue plate; a photograph of the front cover with the quarto page as scale would decide.

survivors.institution_raw: An American collector, anonymous (bought about 2001–2002 from the Belgian owner who wrote to Gingerich about 2000; formerly a monastery library in the Low Countries, until about 1960)
survivors.later_owners: a monastery library in the Low Countries, until about 1960 (the star names written in French on the planisphere and a note partly in Dutch, partly in Flemish on the facing page place the volume around Antwerp or Brussels for a very long time) → a private owner in Belgium, who wrote to Gingerich about 2000 → an anonymous American collector, ‘who must have paid close to a million dollars for it’ (Gingerich 2002, p. 328)
survivors.marks_securing_id: Binding stamped ‘T.B.O.’ above the date ‘1583’; Tycho's annotations in the comet section near the end of the Astronomicum Caesareum (Gingerich 2002, fig. 2: f. O1 verso, a marginal heading reading, in the reproduction, ‘Motus diurnus Cometae in suo circulo’ beside Apianus's table of the comet's daily motion) | binding period: Period 3 (T.B.O. 1583; the binding is not otherwise described)
survivors.identified_by: Owen Gingerich, about 2000, from the Belgian owner's e-mail enquiry about the binding stamp (Gingerich 2002, pp. 327–328)
survivors.notes: Gingerich 2002, pp. 327–328: about two years before he wrote (so about 2000) an e-mail enquiry came from Belgium about a copy of Apianus's Astronomicum Caesareum bound with an even rarer equatorium, an earlier one by Johann Schöner: why, the owner asked, would books printed in 1521 and 1540 be in a binding stamped 1583, with the initials TBO above the date? Gingerich recognised Tycho's mark at once. Further enquiries showed several annotations by Tycho, all in the comet section near the end; fig. 2 (‘courtesy of another private collector’) is a detail of f. O1 verso with Tycho's marginalia beside the table of the comet's daily motion. Additional early annotations in other hands – the star names on the planisphere in French, a note on the facing page partly Dutch and partly Flemish – place the book around Antwerp or Brussels for a very long time; until about 1960 it was in a monastery library. Gingerich imagines it migrated to the Low Countries by the same Jesuit hands that brought the Wittich Copernicus to Liège. ‘This extraordinary volume has changed hands again, to an anonymous American collector who must have paid close to a million dollars for it.’ Gingerich, who had examined over a hundred copies of the Astronomicum Caesareum without finding one associated with Tycho, took this to be the copy Tycho retained when he gave Wittich his (the Chicago copy, with Tycho's presentation inscription; Tycho later complained it had cost him 20 florins). It is distinct from both the Chicago copy and the copy Tycho inscribed at Wittenberg on 14 June 1599, now at Gotha (Prandtl Band VI). Neither the monastery, the Belgian owner nor the American buyer is named.

custody.basis: The route out of the library is undocumented. The star names written in French on the planisphere and a note partly in Dutch, partly in Flemish place the volume around Antwerp or Brussels for a very long time; Gingerich supposed Jesuit hands, a conjecture (Gingerich 2002, pp. 327–328).
