survivors.institution_raw: University of Chicago Library
survivors.later_owners: Paul Wittich (Tycho's gift, inscribed 29 October 1580 on his departure from Hven) → his sister at Wrocław, from 1586; Tycho pursued the library from 1589 but did not reclaim the Apianus, and only the Copernicus copies reached him in 1600 → unknown owners; rebound in German half calf dated 1686 → Louis H. Silver, Chicago → the Newberry Library, which bought Silver's library in 1964 but never accessioned this volume → sold by the Newberry, Sotheby's, London, 8–9 November 1965, lot 4 → Joseph Halle Schaffner (1897–1972), buying through Warren Howell → his bequest to the University of Chicago Library, 1972
survivors.marks_securing_id: Tycho's presentation inscription, transcribed in the library's catalogue record: 'D[omi]no Paulo Witichio Wratislauiensj ob amicitam & comune[m] mathemati[cum] amorem d[ono] d[edit] Tÿcho Brahe Huanae anno 1580 29 Octobris.' — to Paul Wittich of Wrocław, for friendship and a shared love of mathematics, given at Hven on 29 October 1580 (on the title page according to Gingerich and Westman 1988, p. 17); Tycho's own account of the purchase for 20 florins and of the gift, in his letter to Hagecius of 1 November 1589 | binding period: half leather and marbled paper over boards, an armorial device pasted to the front cover, the date 1686 tooled on it (the catalogue record; 'German half calf; dated 1686' in the catalogue of 1977)
survivors.identified_by: The University of Chicago Library's catalogue record (bib 146807), which names Tycho as inscriber and Wittich, Silver and Schaffner as former owners and transcribes the inscription; its exhibition catalogue of 1977, entry 15 ('Silver 4. Presented by Tycho Brahe … to his pupil Paul Wittich, October 29, 1580'); Gingerich 2002, p. 327
survivors.notes: The volume carries Tycho’s presentation inscription, which the library’s catalogue record transcribes: ‘D[omi]no Paulo Witichio Wratislauiensj ob amicitam & comune[m] mathemati[cum] amorem d[ono] d[edit] Tÿcho Brahe Huanae anno 1580 29 Octobris.’ — to Master Paul Wittich of Wrocław, for friendship and a shared love of mathematics, Tycho Brahe gave this, at Hven, on 29 October 1580 (a Saturday). The record’s ‘amicitam’ and ‘Huanae’ are its own readings. Gingerich and Westman, who examined the book, place the inscription on the title page. The record further notes former owners’ manuscript annotations in two hands with underscoring, a manuscript pagination 1–46 beginning on page [2], the original silk threads to the volvelles ending in small pearls or coloured glass beads, the volvelle on page [17] lacking its moving parts, a cancel slip over two lines of page [75], some initials hand-coloured by a former owner, a paper tab at the first page of the Meteoroscopion, Louis H. Silver’s book label and Joseph Halle Schaffner’s bookplate. The binding is half leather and marbled paper over boards, with an armorial device pasted to the front cover and the date 1686 tooled on it, and fabric ties, one missing. Tycho’s own words settle the ownership: writing to Hagecius on 1 November 1589 about Wittich’s library, he says that among the books will be found ‘that Astronomicum of Apianus, which I bought for 20 florins and gave to him when he was here; I do not reclaim it after his death unless it can be bought at a fair price’, and that he has another copy to hand. The book was therefore Tycho’s, left his library by his gift on 29 October 1580 — two days after his return from Helsingborg, in the weeks of the comet he and Wittich had observed — and did not come back: what Monaw brought from Wrocław in October 1600 were the annotated copies of Copernicus. It is a documented gift in Tycho’s lifetime, with his autograph, not a survivor of the posthumous dispersal. Whether one of the two annotating hands is Wittich’s, or Tycho’s, is not stated. The record names the owners the inscription does not: Louis H. Silver of Chicago, whose library the Newberry Library bought in 1964 and from which this volume, never accessioned, was sold at Sotheby’s in London on 8–9 November 1965 as lot 4 (‘Silver 4’ in the catalogue of 1977); Joseph Halle Schaffner, who bought at that sale through Warren Howell and whose science library came to the University of Chicago by bequest after his death in August 1972 (exhibited 1977, entry 15). The owners between Wittich’s sister at Wrocław and Silver are not recorded; the binding of 1686 is the one fixed point. Catalogued by the University of Chicago Library at alc ff QB41.A639 1540 (the exhibit label gives alc ff QB41.A63). The volume has not been digitised. Dal's note on the Ekman sale (Bogvennen 1966, p. 205) records that Rundetaarn ‘bød samtidig meget højt, men forgæves på en lignende hos Sotheby’ — a Tycho-library book at Sotheby's in November 1965; the one Sotheby sale of that month the note names is the Silver/Newberry duplicates sale, whose lot 4 is this volume, so this lot is the candidate for the underbid (C; no bidding record seen; added 27 October 2026). Dal's note goes on in its next sentences to name the sale — November 1965, Louis H. Silver, the Newberry Library — and the Newberry's own account (Karr Schmidt 2023) says the copy was never accessioned and was sold to help defray the costs of the Silver purchase; Bruun Rasmussen 186 ran 1–4 November and the Silver sale 8–9 November 1965 (W10, 27 October 2026). || Chapter 3 state sheet, 27 October 2026: the volume is a single work in a later binding (the 1686 owner's), so it stands 'rebound' in the constituents register; no image of any leaf, board, spine or edge is held, and the two annotating hands and the underscoring the record reports remain uncompared until the Special Collections Research Center's images are ordered (ten colour TIFFs per volume at USD 10 each, on Christian's list). The Danish side of the 1965 sale: Dal's note on the Ekman auction (Bogvennen 1966, p. 205) says Rundetaarn ‘bød samtidig meget højt, men forgæves på en lignende hos Sotheby’; the one Sotheby's sale of November 1965 the note names is the Newberry Library's Silver-duplicates sale (8–9 November 1965, 369 lots, £288,998), whose lot 4 is this volume, bought by Warren Howell for Joseph Halle Schaffner (Schaffner catalogue 1977, entry 15) — so Rundetaarn's underbid most probably fell on this volume (C; no bidding record seen-02).

custody.basis: The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931).

No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 76) supposed that the college came by Tycho’s books in a way similar to the Clementinum’s gift; Císařová Smítková, Paličková and Vackářová (2021, p. 30) suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under Joannes Jüngling, who kept the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766; the college’s dated catalogue entries on Tycho’s volumes are of 1645 to 1675.

Open question of 27 October 2026 (the afterlife record): by what road the volume reached the Chomutov college — the Clementinum's duplicates under Jüngling (Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021, p. 30), a second gift from the heirs (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 76), or the private hands that gave the college 5 G 92 and 5 J 103 in 1654. Two documented ties now frame the question without closing it: the heirs' claim was assigned in 1623 to the tax arrears of Chomutov and Kadaň among four royal towns — the instructions to the towns to pay from arrears are dated Chomutov 26 September 1623 and Kadaň 3 July 1626 (Volf 1932, part 2, p. 23), and the college itself had lost its library to the Saxon plunder of 1631, partly bought back in 1632, before the first dated Tycho accession of 1645 (Veselá 2025, pp. 27–29). The college's own catalogues of 1645–1675 and the Clementinum's duplicate lists of 1773–1782, if they survive in the Národní archiv or the National Library's archive, would decide.

survivors.notes: The De revolutionibus mis-attribution copy; entered via the Wittich-library purchase. Friis had already denied the marginalia to Tycho in 1868: the notes ‘næsten paa hver Side’ cannot be attributed to him ‘som man hidtil har antaget’, though the book ‘kan hidrøre fra hans Samling’ (Friis 1868–69, pp. 266–267, citing Hanslik 1851, p. 274, and Hanuš, Zusätze, Prague 1863, p. 9); the hand was identified as Paul Wittich's by Gingerich and Westman in 1988. The library's own catalogue of 1851 (Hanslik, pp. 274–275) had given the glosses to Tycho; Prusík 1901 (group A, no. 6) and Kukula 1906–07 repeated the attribution, Kukula calling for a specialist's study of the glossed Copernicus; Prusík noted the quantity of blank paper bound in with the book. Binding, as the National Library describes and photographs it in 2026: pale leather over boards, blind-tooled with ornament rolls and a pictorial centre panel on each board — Christ on the cross under an arch, figures at the foot and a lettered plaque below, on the front board; the risen Christ with banner and soldiers beneath on the back — a binding that in its execution stands apart from the rest of Tycho's volumes (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 9 (scan 9), Obr. 5–6; the front board, a graphite frottage of the whole board made to bring out the blind stamp, and the two centre panels are reproduced). The description supports what the provenance already implies: the volume was bound before it reached Tycho, for Wittich or an earlier owner, and carries none of Tycho's marks. Exhibited: in the Copernicus year 1973 the volume was the principal exhibit of the Prague quincentenary exhibition, shown as Tycho's annotated copy and prized as from his estate — the showing that the reattribution of 1981–88 overtook (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 8 (scan 8); she names neither venue nor organiser). Facsimile: Horský's edition (Nicolai Copernici De revolutionibus … cum commentariis manu scriptis Tychonis Brahe, Cimelia Bohemica 16, Pragae 1971), printed for the Copernicus year 1973, is held by the National Library as BMMS Facs F 158: smooth leather boards with the gilt initials NC and TB in a line device, the spine lettered COPERNICUS · BRAHE · DE REVOLUTIONIBUS (Vackářová 2026, printed pp. 9–10 (scans 9–10), Obr. 7); its title perpetuates the attribution to Tycho that the Debunked Claims Register records as overturned. The first-person note on fol. 82 in which the annotator writes of a discovery he himself made — the note John Craig copied into the Edinburgh copy as made by ‘M. Witt’, the clue of 1977/78 — does not stand in this copy: the National Library's curator states expressly that the Clementinum volume lacks it (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 32 (scan 32)), consistent with Gingerich's placing of that note, on the mean motion of precession, in the Liège copy at ff. 81–83v. || The volume carries no mark of Tycho's own: the one trace leading to him is the college's 1642 line ‘Ex Bibliotheca et Recognitione Tichoniana’ (Vackářová 2026, p. 25). The tail label ‘B. 15.’ is one number off the shelfmark 14 B 16, in the form of the old shelfmark labels (‘I. 2.’ on 5 J 2, ‘F. 8.’ on 14 F 8); no source explains it. The ‘Musei Mathematici’ line the library records on the title is not identifiable in the Obr. 30 reproduction.

survivors.marks_securing_id: sewn among Tycho's own observation books, in the codex of his observations of 1600–1601; Tycho's autograph marginal notes on the leaf
survivors.identified_by: Dreyer, Opera omnia VIII (1925), p. 438, note to p. 295; Norlind 1970, p. 351. The two give different folios (157 and 159); neither has been checked on the codex
survivors.notes: One manuscript leaf, not a book. Its heading reads ‘Observationes aliquot Eclipsium Solis et Lunae per Joh. Krabbe, mathematicum ducis H. Julii factae’; it records seven lunar and six solar eclipses of 1581–1600 observed at Helmstedt, Berlin, Braunschweig, Wolfenbüttel and Gröningen, the times as a rule from star altitudes, and it carries in Tycho’s hand the mean times for Krabbe’s observations and for his own. Tycho had asked Georg Rollenhagen in Magdeburg in April 1600 to procure these observations and their method, in order to fix the meridian difference between Krabbe’s observing places and his own (Opera omnia VIII, 295); the last entry on the leaf is 30 June 1600. The leaf is sewn into the codex of Tycho’s observations of 1600–1601 and passed with the observation books from his heirs to Kepler, to Ludwig Kepler, and by sale to Frederik III in 1655 (Mortensen 1955, p. 31). The library’s record is that of the codex: it names Tycho’s Benátky and Prague observations and the observations Kepler sent from Styria, not the Krabbe leaf. The leaf is not printed in the Opera omnia; Dreyer’s commentary places it at fol. 157, Norlind at fol. 159. No digital facsimile of the codex exists: the library’s record for GKS 311–318 is a physical-only record, and of the observation codices only GKS 316 is digitised; the library’s microfilm is Ms. micro 555.

survivors.notes: Prandtl’s Band XXIX, Einzelband 40: Reinhold’s Prutenicae tabulae of 1551, the presentation copy to the Counts of Mansfeld, which Prandtl locates in the Prague University Library. Studnička described the volume in 1901 (Bericht, pp. 41–45) and reproduced Reinhold’s dedication and the two manuscript pieces on the flyleaf: a passage headed ‘Plato’ (‘Unum est naturae vinculum, doctrina numerorum, figurarum et motuum coelestium …’), and the draft of the epigram ‘Quamvis mortalis vescor mortalibus auris’, a first version corrected and struck through and a second written under ‘Aliter’. Dreyer and Ræder printed the epigram from this leaf (Opera omnia IX, p. 215; the cancelled version p. 316). Studnička supposed that Tycho had kept both pieces from an earlier time and inserted them here, and took the binding as proof that the stamps were Tycho’s own and had come with him to Prague (pp. 41, 45). Prusík 1901, group C (Prachtbände), white leather, no. 1, lists Sign. 14 J 176 as the Prutenicae with Reinhold’s dedication to the Counts of Mansfeld, Tycho’s note ‘Est manus Reinholdi. Emi Pragae anno 1601 mense Junio’, and a leaf of verses in his hand at the front; Kukula in 1906–07 described the two drafts of the distich with their deletions. Reproduced: the front board with the gilt portrait medallion — a faded red inscription above it — and the arms stamp of the back board, photographed by Zdeněk Rerych for the National Library's volume of 2026, which presents the binding as the ‘second variant’ of Tycho's bindings beside the ‘typical’ T·B·O leather of 14 J 190 (Vackářová 2026, printed p. 8 (scan 8), Obr. 4; she does not say there were only two). The photograph places the portrait die on the front board and the arms die on the back, as the Iconographia's supralibros records assume. Reproduced in colour by Šolc (2018, figs 3a–c, p. 197 (the portrait binding, Reinhold's dedication with Tycho's note, the title)). || The front pastedown (canvas 2) carries the library's marks in sequence: the printed label 'Veřejná a universitní knihovna v Praze' pasted over the German label of the k. k. Öffentliche und Universitäts-Bibliothek, 'T. B. 18.' in ink, the violet 'Tres.' with 'M 18' and a blue-crayon '10.', a struck-through '[?] D 83', the red-and-black 'XIV / J 176' and the modern NK barcode label 1002391364; a blue round stamp 'UNIVERS. PRAG. BIBL. C. R. PUBL.' stands on the dedication leaf and the Plato leaf. The re-read of 27 October 2026 finds 29 manuscript pages, beyond the preliminaries mostly red-ink corrections of the printed tables (hand unidentified) and pencil figures.

survivors.notes: This Sacrobosco-commentary manuscript was separated from Sign. 14 F 16 before 1901, at an earlier revision of the manuscripts (Prusík 1901, pp. 198–199; Studnička 1901, p. 21; Kukula 1906–07, p. 22), and shelved as VII E 29, while the three printed constituents (Gauricus A 20, Albubater A 1, Cardano A 11) remain in 14 F 16; Prandtl’s four-part Band IV is Studnička’s reconstruction of the volume’s original make-up. The first leaf (f. 1r) carries a cost note headed ‘Andreas Schöner’: ‘Henricus Glareanus constat 21 d. / L. Gauricus & Jo: De monte ulmo constat 24 d. / Albubater 42 d. / Cardanus 42 d. / 36 d. Ligatori’, summed to 165 pfennigs, that is 5 lb 15 d. at thirty pfennigs to the pound; beside it a large monogram in ink, read as T B, with an astronomical diagram and pen trials of the planetary signs below; at the foot, in a later library hand, ‘Antea praeligatum Tractatui Lucae Gaurici Norimbergae a. 1540 edito, sign. 14. F. 16.’ On the verso: ‘Nota. Tribus rebus res comprobantur. I Ratione. II Autoritate. III Experientia’, and under it, in a larger hand, the conclusion drawn for astrology (‘Ergo etiam astrologia vera erit …’). Studnička reproduced the cost note and the upper note of the verso in 1901 as Tycho’s (Bericht, p. 20): the custos Josef Truhlář had concluded from the cost note that the works it lists must be in the library and found them in the Sammelband Sign. 14 F 16, where the removal of the manuscript had left a gap (p. 21). The hands have not been compared with Tycho’s or with Schöner’s. Prusík listed the manuscript in 1901 as the fourth, ‘Sphaera Johannis de Sacrobusto in compendium digesta, Anno salutis nostrae MDXXXIX’, formerly bound in the printed volume 14 F 16 and newly bound as MS VII E XXIX. || The front pastedown (canvas 2) carries 'Tres. M. 24.', the accession note 'A. B. 5/1900', 'T B. 24.' in blue crayon over an erased 6, and 'ms. VII. E. 29.' — the new binding entered in 1900 (inference from the accession note), consistent with the separation from 14 F 16 before 1901. The facsimile (73 canvases, CC BY-NC-SA) is complete, covers and spine included; its leaf labels (modern endleaf = 'Ir', old flyleaf = 'IIr') differ from the record's foliation (old flyleaf = f. Ir).

open_questions: Whether the cost note and the notes on the verso are in Tycho’s hand or in Andreas Schöner’s; the hands have not been compared with Tycho’s or with Schöner’s.

27 Oct 2026 — read on canvases 6–7: 'Andreas Schöner' and the cost list stand in one small hand (the re-read concurs); the verso's two notes are in two different ductus; the T B monogram is in a bolder black pen; no comparison has been made. A comparison of the cost-list hand with the Schöner layer identified in 14 F 16 (dossier of 6 June 2026) and with a securely attributed Andreas Schöner autograph, and of the monogram and the verso's lower block with Tycho's 1560s pillars, would decide it.

Open question of 27 October 2026 (the afterlife record): by what road the volume reached the Chomutov college — the Clementinum's duplicates under Jüngling (Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021, p. 30), a second gift from the heirs (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 76), or the private hands that gave the college 5 G 92 and 5 J 103 in 1654. Two documented ties now frame the question without closing it: the heirs' claim was assigned in 1623 to the tax arrears of Chomutov and Kadaň among four royal towns — the instructions to the towns to pay from arrears are dated Chomutov 26 September 1623 and Kadaň 3 July 1626 (Volf 1932, part 2, p. 23), and the college itself had lost its library to the Saxon plunder of 1631, partly bought back in 1632, before the first dated Tycho accession of 1645 (Veselá 2025, pp. 27–29). The college's own catalogues of 1645–1675 and the Clementinum's duplicate lists of 1773–1782, if they survive in the Národní archiv or the National Library's archive, would decide.
What the round impression with a wreath border at the foot of the old flyleaf (canvas 6) is — a library stamp or an earlier owner's mark — a raking-light image of the leaf closes it.
Whether the binding of c. 1900 (half leather, marbled sides; accession 'A. B. 5/1900') was made at the separation from 14 F 16 — the library's accession register for 1900 closes it.

survivors.marks_securing_id: No Tycho autograph mark. The dense annotations are Paul Wittich's, not Tycho's -- Gingerich (Census, pp. 105-108) retracts the earlier Tycho-annotation belief, noting the flyleaf longitude list cites Vratislavia (Wittich's Wrocław) but neither Hven nor Copenhagen. Tycho ownership rests on Gingerich's documented acquisition history (one of the copies Monau brought to Prague for Tycho in Oct 1600 -- Gingerich, Census, pp. 105-108; Mosley p. 179 puts the number despatched at three), not on a Tycho mark.
survivors.identified_by: Gingerich, An Annotated Census of Copernicus' De revolutionibus (2002), 'Vatican 1' / Ottoboniana 1902, pp. 105-108
survivors.notes: The 1543 Nuremberg first edition, distinct from the Clementinum Wittich copy (Sign. 14 B 16, the 1566 Basel edition). Gingerich traces its passage (Census, pp. 105–108): from Wittich to his sister, and to Tycho, who ‘presumably he got it in October 1600 through the help of Jacob Monaw’; thence, by conjecture, to Rudolf II; taken in the Swedish plunder of the west bank of Prague under Königsmarck in July 1648; to Queen Christina, and with her to Rome in 1655; to Pope Alexander VIII (Pietro Ottoboni) in 1690; and so to the Vatican Library, the spine bearing the papal arms of Pius IX. Richly annotated by Wittich on four preliminary pages and on thirty pages after f. 196; the observation notes include a conjunction of Venus and Regulus on 16 September 1574 and of Jupiter and Fomalhaut on 8 November 1572, and ff. 197v–211v carry the proto-Tychonic geo-heliocentric diagrams dated 27 January to 17 February 1578 (Gingerich, ‘Vatican 1’). Digitised in full on the Vatican Library’s digital site as Ott. lat. 1902, with Wittich’s manuscript notes bound in at the end. || Chapter 3 state sheet, 27 October 2026: the DigiVatLib manifest (digi.vatlib.it/iiif/MSS_Ott.lat.1902/manifest.json) has 450 canvases at 1744–1962 × 2614–2618 px including the covers — canvas 1 is the front board of Pius IX's red-brown morocco with a gilt chain roll, canvas 3 a blank flyleaf; every image carries the library's 'ALL RIGHTS RESERVED' watermark.

survivors.notes: Euclid, Elementa, in the Zamberti–Campanus edition, Basel: Herwagen and Brand 1558, folio. The volume carries no Jesuit inscription; it belongs to the Clauser stratum, bought in 1775. The front board, of blind-tooled pigskin over wooden boards, bears the two-line TYCHO / BRAHE above and 1567 below a central panel showing a crowned shield with a radiant sun and the legend SOL·VIDET·OIA (a Sol-videt-omnia panel stamp); the Katalog Tritius describes it as ‘Supralibros Tychona Brahe z roku 1567’, and Pařez (2009) published a photograph. The title leaf carries the ink ‘Bibliotheca Strahoviensis’, two round purple BIBLIOTHECA STRAHOVIENSIS stamps, and at lower left the large graphite ‘G. Crusio ‹K›’ of Gabriel Crusius, mid-seventeenth century. Examination of the volume found one annotated opening: Book I, prop. 4 (Theon’s exposition, ‘Si duo triangula …’), with marginal and head-of-page notes and a lettered triangle, together with a short jotting in the Campanus section — the ‘few notes’ of Pařez, who attributes them to Tycho’s hand. The hand has not been established as Tycho’s. The volume was found by Hedvika Kuchařová and published by Pařez (2009); the Katalog Tritius provenance note reads ‘Brahe, Tycho; Clauser, Jan Josef’ (record 993601).

survivors.notes: Regiomontanus, Ephemerides 1492–1506 (Augsburg: Ratdolt 1492), with the prefatory gatherings a4 a10 of the Venice 1481 Ephemerides bound before it — the gatherings missing from the National Library’s copy (Kleinschnitzová 14). The identification as Tycho’s rests on the inscription at fol. a2r, ‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis Jesu Pragae Anno 1642. Ex Bibliotheca Tichoniana’ (Straka 1913; Boldan 2025, 33.c and 36.a; Tritius), the same basis as the Clementinum volumes; the authorship of the 34-line weather note at fol. e4v, which Straka (1913) attributed to Tycho’s hand, is the open question, and the note has not been subjected to a comparison of hands. Munzar and Pařez (2002, fig. 5) reproduce the weather note. The binding is a contemporary one, not from Tycho’s bindery: bare wooden boards with a strip of leather over the spine nailed to the boards with brass nails, the shelf label DR VII 19 at the foot; a marginal ink ‘156/2/1’ stands beside the Tabula regionum, above which is the reference-meridian note ‘Nota hec Ephemerides sunt supputate ad longitudinem …’. The Katalog Tritius (record 1064031) describes a late-gothic binding on wooden boards, 230 × 150 mm, leather over a third of the boards only, nailed, the blind-tooled frame worn away, ‘ALMANACH’ faintly on the front board, the clasp removed, yellow edges; the 1481 part reduced to gathering 1a4 and fol. a5–6 of 2a; three front flyleaves of mathematical calculations signed ‘Josephus Worel’ above a drawn basket, c. 1766, the same hand foliating the volume; a late-sixteenth-century ‘Ex libris Johanni Nachlovskij’ at fol. 1a1b, the 1642 formula at 1a2a, and Tycho’s ownership attested by an autograph note of meteorological character at fol. e14b (75v). The record states that the volume ‘then became part of the so-called Mathematical Museum in the Clementinum, from which it passed to Strahov’; the Strnad step of Straka (1913) is doubted because neither Seydl nor Kouklová lists it. The old shelfmark was AG VII 84.

custody.basis: The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931).

No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 76) supposed that the college came by Tycho’s books in a way similar to the Clementinum’s gift; Císařová Smítková, Paličková and Vackářová (2021, p. 30) suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under Joannes Jüngling, who kept the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766; the college’s dated catalogue entries on Tycho’s volumes are of 1645 to 1675.
‘Collegii Societatis Jesu Commotovien. catalogo inscriptus 1645’ on fol. <2>2r (Boldan & Kazanskii 2023, p. 28 and fig. 5).

custody.station: The Clementinum library after the suppression of the Society: the public University Library, since 1990 the National Library of the Czech Republic, Prague
custody.basis: Brought to the Clementinum with the library of the dissolved Chomutov college after 1773; Kleinschnitzová counted nineteen volumes of that provenance in 1933 (p. 81).

open_questions: Open question of 27 October 2026 (the afterlife record): by what road the volume reached the Chomutov college — the Clementinum's duplicates under Jüngling (Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021, p. 30), a second gift from the heirs (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 76), or the private hands that gave the college 5 G 92 and 5 J 103 in 1654. Two documented ties now frame the question without closing it: the heirs' claim was assigned in 1623 to the tax arrears of Chomutov and Kadaň among four royal towns — the instructions to the towns to pay from arrears are dated Chomutov 26 September 1623 and Kadaň 3 July 1626 (Volf 1932, part 2, p. 23), and the college itself had lost its library to the Saxon plunder of 1631, partly bought back in 1632, before the first dated Tycho accession of 1645 (Veselá 2025, pp. 27–29). The college's own catalogues of 1645–1675 and the Clementinum's duplicate lists of 1773–1782, if they survive in the Národní archiv or the National Library's archive, would decide.

When the National Library applied the labels ‘T. Brahe 49.’ (front board) and ‘Tres. M 49’ (rear board) — after the 2023 identification, or earlier, which would mean the library knew the volume as a Tychonianum before Boldan & Kazanskii; the incunable curator could say.

custody.basis: The library remained with the heirs when the instruments and the observation books were ceded to Rudolf II and taken to Vienna in 1604; during the long proceedings over the unpaid purchase price they were forced to part with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library passed into other hands: one part as a gift to the Jesuit college in the Clementinum, whose volumes carry the accession note of 1642, the Chomutov college’s Tychoniana apparently in the same way, and single works into private ownership (Kleinschnitzová 1933, pp. 75–76 and 78, after Volf 1931).

No owner is recorded between the heirs and the Chomutov college’s catalogue entry. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 76) supposed that the college came by Tycho’s books in a way similar to the Clementinum’s gift; Císařová Smítková, Paličková and Vackářová (2021, p. 30) suppose Clementinum duplicates passed on under Joannes Jüngling, who kept the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766; the college’s dated catalogue entries on Tycho’s volumes are of 1645 to 1675.
The inscription ‘Collegij Societatis IESV Commotouij Catalogo inscriptus A° 1671’ on the title (the scan), the formula of the Chomutov college found on 14 A 63, 14 H 225 and XV K 22.

The volume did not come to the Clementinum with the Chomutov library after 1773. The red stamp ‘Z Hankowych’ on the title is read by the Kórnik cataloguer as Václav Hanka's (1791–1861) (Muszyński 1977, no. 583 and index p. 253), and the entry's mark ‘[A. T. Działyński-kat. Kiel.]’ places the volume in Kielisiński's card catalogue of 1840–c. 1847: it passed from Chomutov to Hanka in Prague and from him, in his lifetime, to Tytus Działyński's Kórnik. When and how it left Chomutov, how Hanka came by it, and what the older shelfmarks ‘H. VI. 365.’ and ‘C: 157.’ denote (Muszyński omits the concordance) remain undocumented.

custody.station: Václav Hanka (1791–1861), Prague — his stamp ‘Z Hankowych’
custody.basis: The red stamp ‘Z Hankowych’ on the title, read as Hanka's by Muszyński 1977 (no. 583; index p. 253, after Encyklopedia Gutenberga 6, p. 86), who lists it on two further Kórnik volumes bound alike (Cim.Qu.2813–2814); the genitive plural (‘of the Hankas’) leaves a family stock possible (W4, 27 October 2026).
The library’s record and digitisation (Wielkopolska Biblioteka Cyfrowa, publication 518174). In Kielisiński's catalogue of 1840–c. 1847 (Muszyński 1977, no. 583, ‘kat. Kiel.’; Bolewska).

open_questions: Open question of 27 October 2026 (the afterlife record): by what road the volume reached the Chomutov college — the Clementinum's duplicates under Jüngling (Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021, p. 30), a second gift from the heirs (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 76), or the private hands that gave the college 5 G 92 and 5 J 103 in 1654. Two documented ties now frame the question without closing it: the heirs' claim was assigned in 1623 to the tax arrears of Chomutov and Kadaň among four royal towns — the instructions to the towns to pay from arrears are dated Chomutov 26 September 1623 and Kadaň 3 July 1626 (Volf 1932, part 2, p. 23), and the college itself had lost its library to the Saxon plunder of 1631, partly bought back in 1632, before the first dated Tycho accession of 1645 (Veselá 2025, pp. 27–29). The college's own catalogues of 1645–1675 and the Clementinum's duplicate lists of 1773–1782, if they survive in the Národní archiv or the National Library's archive, would decide.

Narrowed 27 October 2026 (the research round): the stamp is Hanka's and the volume was at Kórnik by c. 1847 (Muszyński 1977; Bolewska); what remains is the road Chomutov → Hanka (before or after 1773) and the Kórnik accession entry or Kielisiński card — the draft enquiry of 27 October 2026 to the Biblioteka Kórnicka asks exactly that (unsent).

channels.name: Left the library in Tycho’s lifetime: gifts and exchanges
channels.mechanism: Books that left the library in Tycho’s lifetime: the Apianus he gave Paul Wittich at Hven on 29 October 1580, the Apianus at Gotha in which he wrote a dated motto for Duke Friedrich Wilhelm of Saxe-Weimar on leaving Wittenberg on 14 June 1599 — his own book given at parting, as the Gotha library reads the entry, or the duke’s book in which he wrote, as Norlind thought more likely —, the Calvin–Theocritus Sammelband dedicated to his cousin Hans Lindenov in exile, and — if Walde and Mortensen are right against Norlind — the Sammelband of 1563 that carries Vedel’s name. These volumes left the library before it was dispersed and reached their holders by roads of their own.
channels.diagnostic_markers: Tycho’s presentation inscription or dated motto on the copy; a recipient’s name of his lifetime

channels.name: The Jesuit road: the Clementinum (1642), the colleges at Chomutov and Krumlov and the professed house, reunited in the Clementinum after 1773
channels.mechanism: Tycho's son-in-law Frans Gansneb Tengnagel — a Catholic convert who ran the posthumous editions — had intended to continue Tycho’s work and died in 1622 (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 76); the heirs, pressed by the lawsuit over the unpaid purchase price, parted with their possessions piecemeal, the earliest dated step out of the library being of 1623 (p. 76); a part of the library came as a gift to the Jesuit Collegium Caesareum at the Clementinum in Prague (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 76, after Volf). The volumes so given — twenty-three survive — carry on the title ‘Collegij Caesarei Societatis Jesu Pragae A° 1642’, in most cases with ‘Ex Bibliotheca Tijchoniana’ and ‘Musaei Mathematici’, and were shelved as the separately kept Musaeum Mathematicum, whose books are known by the red-brown double lines on their white spines (p. 78). A larger group came to the Jesuit college at Chomutov (Komotau), apparently in the same way (p. 76); a single volume each reached the college at Krumlov — by exchange in 1654 from Andreas Scherhackl of Budějovice, who had owned it since 1623 — and the professed house on Prague’s Malá Strana (pp. 76 and 78); the suppression of the Society in 1773 and the secularisation of the monasteries brought these fragments together again in the Clementinum (p. 78) — nineteen volumes of Chomutov provenance by 1933 (p. 81). Šolc's accounts of 1999 (§ 2.533, printed p. 150) and 2006 (printed p. 192 (scan 6)) give the nineteen the Chomutov inscription ‘Collegij Societis JESU Commotouij Catalogo inscriptus A.’ with a year between 1671 and 1675 — the 1645 entry of 44 F 38 and Crusius's gifts of 1654 lie outside that range — and add that four further Tychonic volumes reached the Clementinum itself as gifts (‘Stiftungen’) of private persons whose names stand on their title pages; he names neither the donors nor the volumes. The store's Crusius volumes (5 G 92, 5 J 103) were gifts to the Chomutov college, not to the Clementinum, so they are not Šolc's four; which four he means is open (see lead-crusius-layer). The National Library’s provenance survey of its Jesuit stocks (Císařová Smítková, Paličková & Vackářová 2021, p. 30) registers 215 volumes with Chomutov inscriptions, seven of them given to the college before 1600, and among them ‘minimálně čtyři knihy z pozůstalosti Tychona Brahe’, all with the supralibros ‘TBO 1576’ on the front board and the Chomutov inscription on the title; its authors connect the college’s unusual holding of mathematics and astronomy with P. Jan Jüngling (1705–1775), keeper of the Clementinum’s mathematical library in 1749 and prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–1766, and suppose these books to have been duplicates of the Clementinum college’s library. The Museum itself was removed after 1773 to the lodging of its last keeper, Joseph Stepling, and returned only after his death in 1778, a custody in which losses occurred, at Karel Rafael Ungar's cataloguing of the 1780s the Tycho volumes were then distributed among the University Library's subject departments, predominantly department 14 (Šolc 2006, printed p. 192 (scan 6)) — he does not say what the first element of a present shelfmark denotes —, and the librarians of the Clementinum later broke up some of Tycho's Sammelbände and bound his books with others' (p. 80), which is why some of his volumes now hold works that were never his. In the chains of custody the Mathematical Museum is named as a station only where the volume itself carries the words (‘Musaei Mathematici’, ‘Bibliothecae Mathematicae’ or the Museum's spine marking); the college alone is named otherwise. Gingerich's 2002 survey of the Clementinum volumes counts the marks as follows: sixteen carry the initials 'T.B.O.' tooled on the binding, six the gilt supralibros portrait, twelve the initials written in by hand, and two are author presentations (Bruno and Scaliger). Clear marginalia in Tycho's hand appear in only a few — among them the Ziegler In C. Plinii of 1531, in its Martianus Capella section, and Bartholomaeus Scultetus's Cometae of 1577. Šolc's own later wording (2006, p. 192) is ‘věnováno’ — donated — for the harder-to-sell, mostly astronomical remainder, with the Vitellio–Dürer volume reaching the Jesuits ‘probably by sale’ in 1636; the Handbuch's ‘gekauft’ (Faltysová 1999, § 1.13, after Tobolka) is the other reading, and neither cites a document. Two documents frame the Chomutov road without explaining it: in 1623 the heirs' claim on the Chamber was assigned to the tax arrears of four royal towns, Chomutov and Kadaň among them — the instructions to the towns dated Chomutov 26 September 1623 and Kadaň 3 July 1626 (Volf 1932, part 2, p. 23), and the college that received Tycho's volumes had lost its library to the Saxon plunder of 1631, partly bought back the next year (Veselá 2025, pp. 27–29), so that the first dated accession of 1645 entered a library being rebuilt. Whether either tie carried books is undocumented. The duplicates road under Jüngling cannot account for the dated Chomutov entries: he was prefect of the Chomutov library in 1765–66, a century after the inscriptions of 1645–1675, so for the inscribed volumes the choice is between the heirs, the college's own purchases and local private donors such as Crusius (the research round of 27 October 2026).
channels.diagnostic_markers: 'Collegii Caesarei Soc. Jesu Pragae 1642' / 'Ex bibliotheca Tychoniana' inscription; the initials 'T.B.O.'/'T.B.O. 1576/1583' tooled on the binding; gilt supralibros portrait
channels.current_locations: National Library of the Czech Republic (Clementinum), Prague — the largest surviving fragment, enumerated volume by volume. Kleinschnitzová (1933) catalogued 97 works in 47 volumes; Šolc (2002) extends this to about 110 titles in some 50 volumes. Two strays carry the same provenance outside the National Library: the Bianchini at Teplá, inscribed in 1642, and the Alphonsine Tables at TU Wien, formerly in the Prague Jesuit college. Šolc's own counts: more than 110 prints and 5 manuscripts in 52 volumes (1999, § 2.527); at the new cataloguing of the university library's fund in 1898 its then director Richard Kukula noted, in Šolc's words, 4 manuscripts and 50 prints of Tycho provenance (Šolc 2006, printed p. 192 (scan 6), citing no publication) — Prusík 1901 listed what that recataloguing had found as four manuscripts and sixteen printed works, and Kukula's own article of 1906–07 counts five manuscripts and fifty printed works in twenty-eight volumes, seven of them found since 1902 (Kukula 1906–07, pp. 17–25), so Šolc's figures pair Prusík's manuscripts with Kukula's prints and are not reconciled here; Kleinschnitzová 47 volumes with 97 prints, and ‘at least five further volumes’ have been added since (2006, p. 192).

channels.name: The heirs’ dispersal into private hands (after 1601)
channels.mechanism: During the lawsuit over the purchase price the heirs parted with their possessions piecemeal, and parts of the library with them: ‘so manches Werk wanderte auch in Privatbesitz’ (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 76). The volumes placed here are those whose first recorded owner after Tycho is a private collector of the seventeenth century; what else left by this road is untraced. Since 20 October 2026 the road also carries the Strahov Euclid of 1558 (AV II 2), formerly on a road of its own (VII): it passed from the heirs to Gabriel Crusius — his graphite ‘G. Crusio ‹K›’ on the title, the formula his gift volumes at Chomutov carry in ink — and from him by private hands to Jan Josef Klauser (1705–1771), whose library Strahov bought in 1775; it carries no Jesuit inscription. The Ramus AG XIV 7 began the same way, Crusius giving it to the Chomutov college on 5 August 1654. Kleinschnitzová's 2 A 8 (e-kl-43), inscribed by Andreas Scherhackl of Budějovice in 1623 and given by him to the Krumlov Jesuits by exchange in 1654, belongs here too, not on the Jesuit road: its first owner after the heirs is a private man.
channels.diagnostic_markers: later-owner inscriptions (e.g. Gabriel Crusius 1654/1673); Crusius's ‘G. Crusio inservio’ without a 1642 inscription; Klauser's library (bought by Strahov 1775)
channels.current_locations: Strahov Library, Prague (the Euclid AV II 2 and the Ramus AG XIV 7); the National Library of the Czech Republic (2 A 8, by way of Krumlov); private hands in the United States

channels.name: The Swedish booty of 1648 (Königsmarck’s capture of the west bank of Prague)
channels.mechanism: The 1648 Swedish capture of Prague carried off Rudolfine/Bohemian holdings, including Tycho material, to Sweden. The first Tycho items documented on this road are not books of the library: two manuscripts — a parchment copy of the star catalogue and a Solis et Lunae motus diarii of 1598–99 — and a printed book in a presentation binding, from Rudolf II’s collection at the Castle, shipped with the Castle’s books in 1648–49 and entered in the Stockholm royal library’s catalogue of 1650–51 under Frans Tengnagel’s name, all three untraced (Veselá 2025, p. 142). The Castle was the one Prague collection the Swedes confiscated systematically; the Old Town Jesuit college and the university libraries were untouched, which is why the core of 1642 was never at risk (p. 256). The recataloguing at Stockholm in 1650–51 stripped the booty’s spine marks, and Vossius removed the royal library’s signatures from the books he took in 1654: a volume without a Swedish mark is not thereby excluded from this road (pp. 208–214, 228). The database of the Swedish book plunder (Knihovna AV ČR, searched in full on 19 October 2026: 4,367 records) holds no Tycho imprint from its Prague-Castle group of 79 records (47 under Rudolf II, 20 under Ferdinand III) and no book of Tycho's own; its three Tycho imprints came by other roads — Dudith's De mundi with the Dietrichstein library of Mikulov (Stockholm KB), Hermann Bulder's De mundi and Tycho's dedication copy of the Mechanica to Petr Vok with the Rožmberk library (Stockholm University Library; Copenhagen). Tengnagel's name returns nothing.
channels.current_locations: The Vatican Library: the Wittich–Tycho De revolutionibus of 1543, by way of Queen Christina’s library and the Ottoboni collection. No located volume of the library is in Sweden by this road. The two manuscripts are registered among the observation codices as lost volumes.

channels.name: Rudolfine-imperial absorption
channels.mechanism: Rudolf II had the instruments and the manuscript observations ceded to him by contract (Kleinschnitzová 1933, p. 75), and books may have passed into the court’s orbit with them; none is documented. No located volume is placed on this road: the one candidate, the Vienna manuscript of the Commentariolus, enters the record by an undocumented step and stands on the road of unknown route. Veselá reads the three Stockholm items — two manuscripts and a print — as Tycho’s personal gift to Rudolf II on his arrival in Prague, an inference she marks as such (2025, p. 142). The one catalogue of the Castle library, of 1636 (Riegger 1795, pp. 214–230), is Ferdinand III’s library and not Rudolf’s, whose books had largely gone to Vienna after 1612, and a Habsburg supralibros is not proof of Rudolf’s ownership: any claim that a book of Tycho’s passed through Rudolf’s hands has to pass that test (pp. 140, 150).
channels.diagnostic_markers: imperial provenance — no located volume carries it

channels.name: Attrition / loss
channels.mechanism: War, fire and untraced dispersal account for the gap between the library as it stood at his death and the remnant located today — no single catastrophe, but a long attrition that left no mark to search by. No located volume belongs here by definition, and the titles without a located copy are not its measure: a title is unlocated because no copy has been identified, not because one is known to be lost; the size of the loss is bounded only by the size of the library, which is itself disputed.

channels.name: Out of the Jesuit stock after 1773 without staying in the Clementinum: Strahov (Strnad), Teplá, Kórnik
channels.mechanism: Two volumes carrying the 1642 inscription are now at Strahov, not in the Clementinum: Rheticus–Otho's Opus palatinum (Σ V 5/a) and the Regiomontanus Ephemerides (DR VII 19). The documented route out of the Clementinum is the one Boldan & Vackářová describe for the Mathematical Museum's library: after the suppression of 1773 Karel Rafael Ungar screened the incoming Jesuit and monastic books for duplicates, the observatory director Antonín Strnad bought part of the surplus astronomical volumes for himself, and from his estate they passed to Strahov, which bought the substantial part of his library after his death in 1799 (Munzar 2001). Straka gave exactly this chain for the Regiomontanus in 1913 — Clementinum → Strnad → Strahov — though Strahov's present cataloguer notes that the volume appears in neither published catalogue of Strnad's library (Seydl 1939; Kouklová 1989). The spine is the test: the Mathematical Museum's books carry no ex-libris, only red lines and an abbreviated title on the spine, and Strnad's books his handwritten name or name-stamp. Seydl identified the Strahov volumes from Strnad's library by matching his own book-list, in two hands, against the Strahov volume catalogue (Hyklová 2017, p. 49) — the method behind the cataloguer's finding that the Regiomontanus is in neither list. The library's own record of DR VII 19 nevertheless places the volume in the Clementinum's Mathematical Museum before it came to Strahov, and Munzar and Pařez (2002, p. 369) supposed the Strahov purchases from the Clementinum stock were made ‘probably not before’ 1773. Two volumes show the same leakage from other Jesuit stocks. The Bianchini of Teplá, inscribed at the Clementinum in 1642, is now in the Premonstratensians' library there by an undocumented step. Heidenstein's De bello Moscovitico (Basel 1588), in Tycho's portrait-and-arms binding and catalogued at Chomutov in 1671, never reached the Clementinum at all: it is at the Biblioteka Kórnicka (Cim.Qu.2812), its route there — the volume carries older shelfmarks and stamps not yet identified — still to be established. Kleinschnitzová (1933, p. 81) supposed that the Chomutov stock reached the Clementinum only in part; the Kórnik volume is the first located proof of it. The Bianchini's Teplá station closed in 2006–07, when the National Library bought the Teplá monastery's manuscripts, incunabula and paleotypes and the volume returned to the Clementinum (NK ČR STT 000005829, accession 07/ORST 394); the road keeps Teplá's name as the house it passed through.
channels.diagnostic_markers: the 1642 inscription on a book now outside the National Library; a Mathematical-Museum spine (red lines, abbreviated author/title); Antonín Strnad's name or stamp; a Clementinum or Chomutov inscription on a book now outside the National Library
channels.current_locations: Strahov Library, Prague — Σ V 5/a and DR VII 19 itemised here; the Strnad stratum at Strahov has never been sifted for further Tychoniana; Teplá (the Bianchini); Kórnik (the Heidenstein) Mainx's notice of 1940 (printed p. 43 (scan 4)) gives Strahov's original editions of Copernicus, Tycho Brahe and Kepler as ‘from the possession of the Prague astronomer A. Strnad’ — a statement one year after Seydl's catalogue of Strnad's library (not held) that the stratum holds astronomical first editions; Tycho's own works lie outside the Bibliotheca, but the sentence names the shelf to sift.

channels.name: With the observation books: Kepler, Ludwig Kepler, Frederik III (after 1604)
channels.mechanism: The manuscript observations went a road of their own: Kepler received them under a contract with Tengnagel of 1604 and never returned them; after his death in 1630 his son Ludwig held them as a pledge against the court’s bond of 1633 and sold them to Frederik III of Denmark — in 1655 on Mortensen’s account (1955, pp. 31–32), ‘at the latest in the beginning of 1662’ on Dreyer’s (1890, Appendix, pp. 370, 373). A leaf of another man’s observations sewn into Tycho’s own codex travelled with them.
channels.diagnostic_markers: bound or sewn into the observation codices of the Royal Library, Copenhagen

channels.name: Route out of the library unknown
channels.mechanism: Volumes identified as Tycho’s by their marks that surfaced in the trade or in a later collection with no documented step between his library and their first recorded later owner. The chain of custody records the gap as a gap; the later stations are given with their sources.
channels.current_locations: Helsingør; Hillerød; Göteborg; Austin; Prague (Strahov); private hands in the United States

sources.label: Prandtl 1932
sources.full: Wilhelm Prandtl, ‘Die Bibliothek des Tycho Brahe’, *Philobiblon: eine Zeitschrift für Bücherfreunde* 5 (Vienna, 1932), Heft 8, pp. 291–299, and Heft 9, pp. 321–329; issued separately, Vienna 1933. Verzeichnis A lists the surviving works by author; Verzeichnis B the bound volumes (Bände I–XXIX), ordered by acquisition period, with their locations in 1932. Cited here by the pagination of the Sonderdruck (the periodisation pp. 9–11, Verzeichnis A pp. 11–13, Verzeichnis B pp. 13–14, the literature p. 16); the *Philobiblon* pages are approximate (Rosen 1981 anchors *Philobiblon* p. 327 to Sonderdruck p. 16).

sources.label: Martayan Lan Cat. 28 (2001)

The description records the binding, the condition, the later inscriptions, the range of the annotations, Owen Gingerich's confirmation of the hand (per litteras 25 May 2001), Anthony Grafton's report, and the provenance line.

An introduction on the library’s growth, housing and fate (pp. 333–336) and an alphabetical catalogue of 211 entries (pp. 336–366) argued to have been in Tycho’s library, from the surviving volumes and from the books named in his writings and letters, with Prandtl, Kleinschnitzová and Zinner numbers.

sources.role: The inventory of the library on Hven in March 1597 and the departure into exile.

sources.label: Mosley 2007
sources.full: Adam Mosley, *Bearing the Heavens: Tycho Brahe and the Astronomical Community of the Late Sixteenth Century* (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2007), chapter 3, ‘Books and the heavens’, §II (ii), ‘The astronomical library’, pp. 166–182; the notes give the volume, page and lines of Tycho's letters in Dreyer's *Opera omnia* (TBOO).
sources.role: The acquisition of books through the Frankfurt fairs, correspondent-agents and the pursuit of dead scholars’ libraries (Ambrose, Brechtal, Dudith, Wittich), from the correspondence.

sources.label: Gingerich, Census 2002
sources.full: Owen Gingerich, *An Annotated Census of Copernicus’ De revolutionibus (Nuremberg, 1543 and Basel, 1566)* (Studia Copernicana, Brill’s Series 2; Leiden: Brill, 2002), esp. pp. 105–108 on the Vatican copy (Ott. lat. 1902).
sources.role: The copy-by-copy provenance of the *De revolutionibus* exemplars that passed through Tycho’s hands, and the identification of the ‘Tychonic’ marginalia as Wittich’s.

sources.label: Tycho’s correspondence (DSL)
sources.full: Tycho Brahe, *Epistolae*: the letters of J. L. E. Dreyer’s *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia*, vols VI–VIII (Copenhagen, 1919–1925), served as a digital edition by Det Danske Sprog- og Litteraturselskab, ed. Peter Zeeberg (tekstnet.dk): 509 letters as published, 350 by the edition’s own overview.
sources.role: The acquisition record by proxy: books requested, sent, given, lent or discussed in the letters. Each letter-attested entry links to the letter.

sources.label: NKP, Staré tisky (Aleph)
sources.full: Národní knihovna České republiky, Prague, catalogue of early printed books (base STT, Aleph), former-owner index ‘Brahe, Tycho, 1546–1601’ (CERL Thesaurus cnp01316674): 102 records, each with shelfmark, provenance note (field 561) and, where digitised, the Manuscriptorium record.
sources.role: The record-level catalogue links and the verbatim copy-level provenance notes quoted under the Prague volumes.

sources.label: Manuscriptorium
sources.full: Manuscriptorium (manuscriptorium.com), the digital library run by the National Library of the Czech Republic: the library's TEI P5 catalogue records of the Clementinum volumes (identification, contents, physical description, binding, provenance, former owners, the literature that cites the copy), the retro-converted entries of its printed manuscript catalogues, and the page-by-page facsimiles of the digitised volumes. Records CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Records consulted 9 September 2026.
sources.role: The catalogue-record fields, binding descriptions, former-owner entries, provenance notes and facsimiles quoted under the Prague volumes.

sources.label: Schrimpf & Verbunt 2021
sources.full: Andreas Schrimpf and Frank Verbunt, ‘The star catalogue of Wilhelm IV, Landgraf von Hessen-Kassel’, in G. Wolfschmidt (ed.), *Applied and computational historical astronomy* (Nuncius Hamburgensis 55, 2021); arXiv:2103.10801.
sources.role: Context for the Kassel observation material in the letters.

sources.label: Pařez 2009
sources.full: Jan Pařez, ‘Supralibros dánského astronoma Tycha Brahe ve Strahovské knihovně’, *Sborník pro exlibris a drobnou grafiku* 2009 (Spolek sběratelů a přátel exlibris, Praha), pp. 24–26, with photographs of the Euclid’s 1567 name-stamp and of the portrait and arms supralibros on Σ V 5 and Σ VI 3. The only description of the four Strahov volumes from Tycho’s library together; credits the discovery of the Euclid to Hedvika Kuchařová.
sources.role: The Strahov supralibros; the basis of the four Strahov entries.
sources.url_label: Spolek sběratelů a přátel exlibris — the whole Sborník as a PDF

sources.label: Straka 1913
sources.full: Cyrill Straka, ‘Zápis Tychona Brahe v knihovně Strahovské’, *Časopis Musea království Českého* 87 (1913), pp. 382–384. The discovery note on the Strahov Regiomontanus: the two Ratdolt incunables, the 1642 inscription, the 34-line weather note (Latin text in part, Czech paraphrase), the later owners Nachlovský and Worell, and the chain Clementinum → Strnad → Strahov.
sources.role: First publication of the Strahov Regiomontanus and of the attribution of its note to Tycho.

sources.label: Boldan 2025
sources.full: Kamil Boldan, ‘Ratdoltova astronomika v českých a moravských knihovnách’, *Knihy a dějiny* 32 (2025), no. 1–2, pp. 9–41 (DOI 10.23852/KAD.2025.32.01). A census of 104 Ratdolt astronomica in Czech libraries; entries 33.b, 33.c and 36.a describe the National Library’s Venice 1481 *Ephemerides* (40 F 39, Tycho’s, lacking its first gatherings) and the Strahov volume DR VII 19 (the Augsburg 1492 *Ephemerides* with the 1481 prefatory gatherings bound before it, the weather note at fol. e4v).
sources.role: The modern description of DR VII 19; establishes that the two 1481 gatherings bound before the Strahov *Ephemerides* of 1492 are those missing from the National Library's *Ephemerides* 40 F 39.
sources.url_label: Knihy a dějiny — the DOI opens the PDF

sources.label: Kroupa 2001
sources.full: Jiří K. Kroupa, ‘První vydání díla Tychona Brahe Astronomiae instauratae mechanica v českých knihovnách’, *Bulletin plus* (Národní knihovna ČR) 4/2001. The three Bohemian copies of the 1598 *Mechanica* compared (Strahov AG XI 56, Křivoklát III-a-18, NK ČR 14 A 291) with the three Paris copies; the Strahov copy’s green silk binding, dedication text and bound-in watercolour.
sources.role: The Strahov *Mechanica*’s binding and watercolour; the Křivoklát copy’s route through the Clementinum.
sources.url_label: Wayback Machine — the Bulletin plus page as it stood in 2012

sources.label: Strahov Katalog Tritius
sources.full: Knihovna Královské kanonie premonstrátů na Strahově, Katalog Tritius (strahovskyklaster.tritius.cz): the provenance field for ‘Brahe’ returns twelve records (read 8 September 2026); the records cited are 993601 (Euclid AV II 2: ‘Brahe, Tycho ; Clauser, Jan Josef’ / ‘Supralibros Tychona Brahe z roku 1567’), 1046995 (*Opus palatinum* Σ V 5/a), 1045270 (Ramus AG XIV 7: ‘vazba se zlacenou podobou Tychona de Brahe’) and 1064031 (Regiomontanus DR VII 19).
sources.role: The holding library’s own provenance record for each copy.

sources.label: NUSK — Slepí svědkové doby
sources.full: Univerzita Pardubice, NUSK database of blind-tooled bindings (nusk.upce.cz): workshop 33, ‘Knihvazač rudolfínského okruhu II’ (Schunke’s Dürerbuch-Meister; active 1587–1626), whose tools stamped the Strahov *Opus palatinum* Σ V 5 and the Lobkowicz Guntherus at Nelahozeves (II Gf 14), both 1599–1601.
sources.role: The binder attribution of the *Opus palatinum*.

sources.label: Voit 2020
sources.full: Petr Voit, *Vzácné knižní vazby Strahovské knihovny v Praze: od gotiky na práh baroka* (Praha: Královská kanonie premonstrátů na Strahově, 2020; *Bibliotheca Strahoviensis*, Series monographica IX), pp. 250–252 — the *Opus palatinum* binding and the group of presentation bindings made for Tycho.
sources.role: The published description of the *Opus palatinum* binding; not read at first hand — Novotný's review (2021) confirms that the monograph treats the group of presentation bindings made for Tycho.

sources.label: Munzar & Pařez 2002
sources.full: Jan Munzar & Jan Pařez, ‘Tycho Brahe as a Meteorologist’, in J. R. Christianson, A. Hadravová, P. Hadrava and M. Šolc (eds), *Tycho Brahe and Prague: Crossroads of European Science* (Acta Historica Astronomiae 16; Frankfurt am Main: Harri Deutsch, 2002), pp. 360–375 — the transcription, translation and dating of the winter-1495/96 note in the Strahov Regiomontanus (pp. 369–374), with a letter-by-letter comparison of its hand against the DG IV 25 motto and the AG XI 56 dedication. Figs. 4 and 5 (pp. 370–371) reproduce the 1642 leaf and the note itself; p. 369 counts ‘five books from Tycho's library in the Strahov book collection’ and supposes the Strahov purchases ‘probably not before the abolition of the Jesuit Order in 1773’.
sources.role: The argument that the note is Tycho’s: the hand ‘with a high probability’ his, and at the least a person of his immediate circle; the winter 1495/96 rather than 1595/96, from independent climate records, a reconstruction of the planetary positions at the 1495 solstice and the chronology of the venereal epidemic; the note read as a retrospective astrometeorological reconstruction, not a Bohemian weather record.

sources.label: Neškudla 2021
sources.full: Bořek Neškudla, ‘Přehled dosavadního bádání o knihovnách premonstrátských klášterů’, *Bibliotheca Strahoviensis* 14 (2021), pp. 227–244, at p. 229: Strahov bought the library of the Prague printer and gubernial archivist Jan Josef Klauser in 1775, Heidel’s in 1780, Riegger’s in 1794, and absorbed the Norbertinum’s in 1787.
sources.role: The date the Clauser books reached Strahov.

sources.label: Munzar 2001
sources.full: Jan Munzar, ‘200. výročí úmrtí astronoma Antonína Strnada (1746–1799)’, *Bibliotheca Strahoviensis* 4–5 (2001), pp. 269–271: Strahov bought the substantial part of Strnad’s library after his death; the three studies of it are Seydl 1939, Kouklová 1985/86 and Kouklová 1989.
sources.role: The route by which Strnad’s books reached Strahov.

sources.label: Studnička 1901
sources.full: František Josef Studnička, *Prager Tychoniana* (Prague, 1901). The Tycho relics in Prague as seen in 1901, among them the Ptolemy of 1551 (the purchase note read as Tycho’s hand, Pratensis taken for the seller, p. 39) and the annotated *De revolutionibus* of 1566.
sources.role: The Prague holdings before Prandtl and Kleinschnitzová; the first reading of the Ptolemy’s title page.

sources.label: Studnička 1901 (Bericht)
sources.full: František Josef Studnička, *Bericht über die astrologischen Studien des Reformators der beobachtenden Astronomie Tycho Brahe: Weitere Beiträge zur bevorstehenden Saecularfeier der Erinnerung an sein vor 300 Jahren erfolgtes Ableben* (Prague: Königlich Böhmische Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften, 1901), 54 pp. The Tychoniana found in the Prague University Library after his *Prager Tychoniana*, brought to his notice by the custos Josef Truhlář: the astrological Sammelband with facsimiles of its manuscript leaves (pp. 17–31), further astrological books by title (pp. 33–35), the Reinhold of 1551 with its dedication and flyleaf drafts (pp. 41–45), the Archimedes volume (pp. 46–50), a geometrical manuscript (pp. 51–53) and six more volumes by title (p. 54); p. 7 and note infer the size of the library from the number 2781 on the spine of the Gesner of 1565, then in Gustav Laube's possession, and distinguish three periods of binding. The digitised copy lacks p. 19.
sources.role: The first notice of the Prague volumes found after the *Prager Tychoniana* and of the Gesner volume; the facsimiles of the cost note and the flyleaf drafts; the sole source of the spine number 2781 behind every estimate of several thousand volumes for the library.

sources.label: Boldan & Vackářová 2024
sources.full: Kamil Boldan & Jana Vackářová, *Bibliotheca astronomica. Astronomické tisky 15.–17. století ze sbírek Národní knihovny ČR* (Prague: Národní knihovna ČR, 2024), pp. 88–103 (Tycho’s library and its marks) and 142–145 (the later fortunes of the books: Ungar’s duplicate screening after 1773, Strnad’s purchases, and the Ptolemy 5 B 70 read with Johannes Pratensis as first owner).
sources.role: The National Library’s own reading of its Tycho volumes and of the eighteenth-century routes out of the Clementinum.
sources.url_label: Národní knihovna ČR — the catalogue as a PDF, at p. 88

sources.label: Handels- og Søfartsmuseet, Årbog 1957
sources.full: Knud Klem, ‘Museets komité og beretning om regnskabsåret 1956–57’, *Handels- og Søfartsmuseet på Kronborg: Årbog 1957* (Helsingør: Selskabet Handels- og Søfartsmuseets Venner, 1957), pp. 5–21 (the report itself pp. 7–21; the volume at p. 8). The museum’s report for the year records, among the acquisitions of 1956–57, Regiomontanus’s *Tabulae directionum* (1550) bound with Apianus’s *Cosmographia* (1553) in a contemporary binding, ‘which belonged to Tycho Brahe’, as the gift of Lia Ekman and her late husband, the engineer Oscar Ekman, with Tycho’s own note that he bought it in 1561 for one thaler and four groschen.
sources.role: The acquisition record of Prandtl’s Band II, the student binding of 1561.

pages.via: tidsskrift.dk; the viewer opens on the page (scan page 6) with the paragraph on the Ekmans' gift.

sources.label: Museernes Samlinger (M/S Museet for Søfart)
sources.full: Slots- og Kulturstyrelsen, Museernes Samlinger (the SARA database of the Danish state-recognised museums): the object record of M/S Museet for Søfart, Helsingør, inventory number 1957:0030, priref 400004307, ‘Astronomi (bog fra Tycho Brahes bibliotek), indeholdende:’ (revised 16 June 2026). The museum's description, in Danish, gives the two works with their title transcriptions and collations (Regiomontanus, Tübingen 1550: title, [43] pp. text, [268] pp. tables, a few notes in the head margin; Apianus, Paris 1553, the colophon dated 1551, fol. 1–74, the cordiform world map inserted between fol. 34 and 35); Tycho's added positions for Helsingborg, Lund, Visby and a fourth place on fol. 53r–v of the Apianus, transcribed with their figures; the binding (brown calf, blind-ruled mirror panels, originally gilt floral stamps, TVCHO BRADE on the front board, ANNO 1561 on the rear, three raised bands, the remnant of a label with the library shelfmark 204); the inscriptions leaf by leaf (a note in ink on the front pastedown; on the fly-title ‘tico brade ven:’ struck through, ‘Tycho Brade’ and further ownership inscriptions, the leaf half torn and repaired; on its verso ‘Sum Thÿchonis Brade’ struck through, ‘Eptg [emptus] thalero & 4 Groshj’ and beneath it an astronomical note, partly lost); the condition, the cloth-covered box, the restoration by Birgitte Dall in 1957, and the museum's summary of Prandtl (cited as *Philobiblon* 1933). Two photographs: the front board, and the volume open in its box at the Regiomontanus title with the fly-title raised so that its verso, the purchase note and the astronomical note, faces the camera. Consulted 11 October 2026 and reproduced under the volume in the section on the surviving volumes.
sources.role: The holding museum’s own record and photographs of Band II.

pages.via: Museernes Samlinger (Slots- og Kulturstyrelsen): the museum's own record with its two photographs.

sources.label: Björklund 1992
sources.full: Per-Åke Björklund, *Tycho Brahe og Kamarillaen* (Copenhagen: Rhodos, 1992), p. 26: the Regiomontanus of 1561, lately come to light at the Handels- og Søfartsmuseet på Kronborg, ‘now deposited at the Royal Library’s manuscript department’; Latin plant names written at the head of the pages in another hand, and plant fragments still between the leaves — the volume had served as a herbarium.
sources.role: The deposit of Band II at the Royal Library, and its use as a herbarium.

sources.label: Grinder-Hansen 2006
sources.full: Poul Grinder-Hansen (ed.), *Tycho Brahes Verden: Danmark i Europa 1550–1600* (Copenhagen: Nationalmuseet, 2006), p. 42, fig. 5: the volume of 1561 reproduced — ‘Bogen tilhører Handels- og Søfartsmuseet. Det Kongelige Bibliotek foto.’
sources.role: The 2006 reproduction of Band II, photographed at the Royal Library.

sources.label: Friis (ed.) 1876
sources.full: *Tyge Brahes meteorologiske Dagbog, holdt paa Uraniborg for Aarene 1582–1597*, ed. F. R. Friis, with a summary by Poul la Cour and a register of the historical notices by H. F. Rørdam (Appendix til *Collectanea Meteorologica*, issued by Det Kgl. Danske Videnskabernes Selskab through its Meteorological Committee; Copenhagen: H. H. Thiele, 1876), the preface pp. I–IV, the diary text pp. 1–263; the entry of 21 March 1597, ‘Registeret vi alle junkers bøger’, on p. 263.
sources.role: The one record of the library as a whole: the registration of the books on 21 March 1597, and the household's move into the Copenhagen ‘Museum’ on 11 April.
sources.url_label: Royal Danish Academy — the Academy's own scan of the 1876 edition (PDF, 101 MB)

links.label: Internet Archive scan (University of Toronto copy)

sources.label: TBOO
sources.full: *Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera omnia*, ed. J. L. E. Dreyer, 15 vols (Copenhagen: Libraria Gyldendaliana, 1913–29): vols VI–VIII, the correspondence (1919–25), cited by volume, page and line; vol. IX (1927), the meteorological diary, pp. 1–146 (the day-by-day entries from p. 5), and the Carmina, among them (p. 175) the inscriptions around Tycho's portrait and arms. The letters are served with a facsimile of the edition by tekstnet.dk.
sources.role: The printed edition every letter reference in the history resolves to.

sources.label: Friis 1868–69
sources.full: F. R. Friis, ‘Tyge Brahes Haandskrifter i Wien og Prag’, *Danske Samlinger for Historie, Topographi, Personal- og Literaturhistorie* 4 (1868–69), pp. 250–268. The survey of Tycho's manuscripts in the Vienna Hofbibliothek (the nineteen quarto volumes of observation copies in Tycho's bindings; the list of his books in Cod. 10,688) and of the remains in Prague (14 C 20, 14 B 16), with the report of Tycho books in the Nostitz library.
sources.role: The first survey of the Prague and Vienna Tychoniana; the Nostitz report; the acquisition of the Vienna manuscripts about 1657. His ‘nye Nummer’ for the Vienna manuscripts were provisional, a recataloguing being under way; the ‘Cod. philos. Nr.’ he gives in parentheses is the stable cross-key of 1868.

sources.label: Nielsen 1921
sources.full: Lauritz Nielsen, ‘Tycho Brahes Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen’, *Nordisk tidskrift för bok- och biblioteksväsen* 8 (1921), pp. 175–214; p. 177 on the bindery and the paper mill, and the letter to Vedel of 16 February 1584 announcing the press.
sources.role: The press, the bindery and the paper mill as one establishment.

sources.label: Vellev 2002
sources.full: Jens Vellev, ‘Tycho Brahe's Paper Mill on Hven and N. A. Møller Nicolaisen's Excavations, 1933–1934’, in J. R. Christianson, A. Hadravová, P. Hadrava and M. Šolc (eds), *Tycho Brahe and Prague: Crossroads of European Science* (Acta Historica Astronomiae 16; Frankfurt am Main: Harri Deutsch, 2002), pp. 333–355; the dates of the mill from the inscribed stone (begun 1590, completed 1592; demolished 1602), pp. 334–335.
sources.role: The dates of the paper mill.

sources.label: Šafařík 1881
sources.full: ‘Bericht über die Versammlung der Astronomischen Gesellschaft zu Strassburg 1881’, first sitting, 22 September 1881, item 7, in *Vierteljahrsschrift der Astronomischen Gesellschaft* 16 (1881), p. 273: the secretary’s minute that Vojtěch Šafařík distributed to those present photolithographs of the only original portrait of Tycho extant in Prague, a watercolour in folio on parchment bound before a copy of the *Progymnasmata* with an autograph dedication to Johann Zajíc von Hasenburk, ‘gegenwärtig im Kloster Strahow zu Prag’.
sources.role: The only description of the Strahov *Progymnasmata* and its watercolour.

sources.label: Gingerich & Westman 1988
sources.full: Owen Gingerich and Robert S. Westman, *The Wittich Connection: Conflict and Priority in Late Sixteenth-Century Cosmology* (Transactions of the American Philosophical Society 78, part 7; Philadelphia, 1988). The identification of Paul Wittich's hand in the annotated copies of *De revolutionibus*, among them the Prague copy 14 B 16 and the Vatican copy Ottob. lat. 1902, and the history of Tycho's pursuit of Wittich's books (pp. 17–22).
sources.role: The Wittich hand; the gift of the Astronomicum Caesareum in 1580 and Tycho's second copy of 1589; the pursuit of the library 1589–1600 and its endgame; the three other Wittich survivals and the Breslau sale of 1606; Gingerich's 1978 count of the Clementinum Tychoniana; the Triangulorum praxis and Tycho as a stinting annotator.

sources.label: Šíma & Valeška 2002
sources.full: Zdislav Šíma and Jiří Valeška, ‘Analysis of Tycho's Handwritings’, in J. R. Christianson, A. Hadravová, P. Hadrava and M. Šolc (eds), *Tycho Brahe and Prague: Crossroads of European Science* (Acta Historica Astronomiae 16; Frankfurt am Main: Harri Deutsch, 2002), pp. 150–167: the three Prague manuscripts published by Studnička as autograph are the work of professional copyists; the dedication in the Strahov *Mechanica* is a calligrapher's text with Tycho's signature.
sources.role: The scribal hand of the Prague manuscripts.

sources.label: Paulli & Dal 1959
sources.full: R. Paulli and Erik Dal, ‘Harald Mortensen og hans bogsamling’, *Fund og Forskning i Det kongelige Biblioteks Samlinger* 5–6 (1958–59), pp. 7 ff.; p. 15 on the objects Mortensen gave Det Nationalhistoriske Museum på Frederiksborg in 1950 (the museum's report for 1949–50): Tycho's *De mundi* (Uraniborg 1588 with the Frankfurt 1610 title) and *Progymnasmata* (Uraniborg 1592 with the Prague 1602 title), an album leaf in Tycho's hand, a woodcut portrait Mortensen knew in two other impressions, both in Germany, and Agrippa's *Opera I* ‘i pergamentbind med Tychos portræt og våben i guld’, bought in Germany by Sigurd Wandel.
sources.role: The record of the 1950 gift and of the Agrippa's Danish owners before the museum.

sources.label: Danmarks Adels Aarbog 1902
sources.full: *Danmarks Adels Aarbog* XIX (1902), the Lindenov stamtavle, pp. 277–290, with the Henvisninger pp. 493–495.
sources.role: The recipient's own line: Christoffer Johansen Lindenov's three marriages (Margrethe Clausdatter Bille, Ide Rantzau, Anne Bjørn) with Hans listed under the second; Hans's offices (Bergenhus 1578–86, landsdommer 1587, Hammershus 1594–1610), the fief withdrawn 3 January 1610, dead by 7 April 1610; his wife Elsebe Jensdatter Juel, buried in Ørslev church; his sons.

sources.label: Danmarks Adels Aarbog 1890
sources.full: *Danmarks Adels Aarbog* VII (1890), the Bille stamtavle, pp. 86–87.
sources.role: Claus Bille's children: Margrethe, born 28 February 1525 at Lyngsgård, married Christoffer Johansen Lindenov til Drenderup; Beate, born 29 April 1526, married Otte Brahe — the two sisters through whom Hans Lindenov is Tycho's first cousin.

sources.label: Bricka, DBL X (1896)
sources.full: C. F. Bricka (ed.), *Dansk biografisk Lexikon*, 1st ed., X (Copenhagen 1896), pp. 316–318 (A. Thiset: Christoffer Johansen Lindenov; Hans Lindenov til Gavnø; Hans Lindenov til Ørslevkloster, the privateer).
sources.role: Christoffer Lindenov's seats, death at Drenderup 11 April 1585 and three marriages in order, Margrethe Bille first; the son's article naming the father Hans Christoffersen Lindenov til Ørslevkloster, lensmand on Bornholm, and the mother Elsebe Juel.

sources.label: Lutz, Lent-fair catalogue 1597
sources.full: Tobias Lutz, *Catalogus novus nundinarum vernalium Francofurti ad Moenum anno M.D.XCVII celebratarum* (Frankfurt: Johann Saur, 1597), leaf A2v. Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Rar. 1639 Beibd. 14.
sources.role: The Calvin edition on sale at the Frankfurt Lent fair of 1597, listed under the heading ‘Libri Calvinianorum’: ‘Ioan. Caluini fideliss. Doctoris Epistolæ & responsa, cum eiusdem vita à Theod. Beza descripta. Hanouiæ. 8.’ — the terminus for the volume's availability, after Tycho had left Hven.

sources.label: Paulli 1954
sources.full: Richard Paulli, ‘Fra Bartholin til Struensee’, *Fund og Forskning i Det kongelige Biblioteks Samlinger* 1 (1954), pp. 1 ff.
sources.role: Hjalmar Bruhn as the library's benefactor before the Tycho purchase: ‘en af bibliotekets trofasteste venner og velgørere’, who pledged the costs of the Vilhelm Maar auction of January 1952 and filled gaps in Steno's spiritual works (p. 7).

sources.label: DBL, ‘Dan Folke’
sources.full: *Dansk Biografisk Leksikon*, 3rd ed., ‘Dan Folke’ (lex.dk).
sources.role: The benefactor's dates: ‘skibsmægler Hjalmar B. (1881-1959)’, father-in-law of the composer Dan Folke.

sources.label: Frederiksborg 2026
sources.full: Det Nationalhistoriske Museum på Frederiksborg, the collections department: written answers of 28 September and 12 October 2026 to an enquiry of 9 September 2026 about the objects Harald Mortensen gave the museum in 1950, listing each with its inventory number and present keeping — Agrippa, *Opera I* (B3950a-b, the museum library), *De mundi* (B3948, the museum library), *Progymnasmata* (B3947, the museum library), the album leaf in Tycho's hand (B3949, in store), the woodcut portrait (P-10178, the print collection), the oak column capital from Uraniborg (B3954, in store) and Gassendi's life of Tycho, The Hague 1655 (B3951, the museum library). The second answer, of 12 October 2026, to three questions of 28 September: the suffix of B3950a-b denotes the volume (a) and the slipcase it is kept in (b); the museum's register transcribes the album leaf B3949 as ‘Themistocles / perieram ni sic periissem / Tycho Brahe scripsi Witebergis Ao 1599 febr. die 16.’; the woodcut P-10178 is dated 1586 in the register and its sheet measures 22.5 × 14 cm. Unpublished; copies are kept with the edition's working papers.
sources.role: The holding museum's own confirmation of the Agrippa's custody and inventory number.

sources.label: Ransom Center 2026
sources.full: Harry Ransom Center, The University of Texas at Austin: examination and photographs of QE 362 G391d 1565 by Benjamin Gross, Head of Fellowships and Scholarly Programs, 7 October 2026, with his report of 8 October 2026 — twenty photographs (both boards with a ruler in the frame, the spine straight on and in raking light, the pastedowns and flyleaves, the title page recto and verso, leaf a2, the opening pp. 102–103 of *De figuris lapidum* with its marginal drawing, and pp. 16–17 of Cordus's *De halosantho*), and the report that no trace of the spine number could be found and that a leaf-through of the whole volume turned up one marginal drawing. Unpublished; copies are kept with the edition's working papers.
sources.role: The holding library's own examination of the volume: the binding and its die measured, the spine without its number, Laube's stamp and the later notes, and the one marginal entry.

sources.label: NK ČR, catalogue photographs
sources.full: Národní knihovna České republiky, Prague: the photographs attached to the library's own catalogue records of early printed books (base STT, Aleph, 'Obrazová příloha') — for the Tycho volumes, Sign. 5 H 65 (record 000057198: spine, and one edge of the text block), 5 J 2 (000058701: spine), 14 F 8 (000155813: spine, spine with the front board) and 14 B 16 (000059267: spine). Read 22 October 2026.
sources.role: The only photographs of the spines of these volumes, and the one photograph of a lettered edge: the Chomutov college's painted spines and shelfmarks, the library's labels, and the titles stamped on the edge of 5 H 65.
sources.url_label: NK ČR Aleph — the record of 5 H 65 with its photographs

sources.label: Philobiblon 1932, Weimar copy
sources.full: Philobiblon: eine Zeitschrift für Bücherfreunde 5 (1932), the copy of the Herzogin Anna Amalia Bibliothek, Weimar, digitised page by page (record 1467327069_1932000500): Heft 8, pp. 291–300, and Heft 9, pp. 321–330, Prandtl's article in its journal printing, with the plates — p. 292 the binding of Band II (the Weiss & Co. photograph), p. 293 its flyleaf and title, p. 298 the Palingenius leaf, p. 299 the Gesner, Einzelband XXI, opened flat with both boards and the spine. Read 22 October 2026.
sources.role: The journal impression of Prandtl's plates, sharper in its greys than the offprint; the only image of the Gesner's spine before 2026.

sources.label: Uppsala UB, Alvin (Vedel, Obr. 46:500)
sources.full: Uppsala University Library, Alvin records 183783, 183841 and 183784: the front board, the spine and the inside of the front cover of Obr. 46:500, Baccanelli's De consensu medicorum (Lyon 1558) in a blind-tooled binding dated 1564 with the initials of Anders Sørensen Vedel, later Magnus Gabriel De la Gardie's (his seal inside the cover). Alvin also lists Obr. 49:169, a composite volume of prints of 1572–78 from Vedel's library. Photographs read 23 October 2026.
sources.role: The holding library's photographs of a Vedel binding, the comparandum for the dated bindings of 1576–82.
